patient_voice.pain: Vaginal itching, dryness, dyspareunia

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with vaginal itching.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.

100.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with vaginal itching, dryness, burning, dyspareunia, and increased urinary frequency. Postmenopausal. Exam reveals pale, thin vaginal mucosa with loss of rugae. Atrophic vaginitis results from estrogen deficiency → thinning of vaginal epithelium → decreased glycogen → loss of lactobacilli → increased vaginal pH → susceptibility to infection and irritation. Diagnosis is clinical. Wet mount may show increased WBCs and parabasal cells. Rule out other causes: candidiasis, bacterial vaginosis, trichomoniasis, STIs. Treatment: vaginal estrogen therapy (cream, ring, or tablet — first-line, minimal systemic absorption). Non-hormonal moisturizers and lubricants. If systemic vasomotor symptoms also present → consider systemic HRT.
100.clinical_tip: Atrophic Vaginitis (Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause) — follow CCS review orders.
100.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Atrophic Vaginitis (Genitourinary Syndrome of Menopause).

patient_voice.chief_complaint: High fever, sore throat, drooling, stridor, tripod position
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset high fever, severe sore throat, drooling, muffled 'hot potato' voice, stridor, and tripod positioning (leaning forward, chin thrust out). Epiglottitis is a …
patient_voice.pain: High fever, sore throat, drooling, stridor, tripod position

exam: Ill-appearing with frequent cough; speaks in short phrases between paroxysms.
RR 22; SpO₂ 94%; productive cough with scattered rhonchi; increased work of breathing.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Warm skin with fever; no purpura on initial survey.
101.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset high fever, severe sore throat, drooling, muffled 'hot potato' voice, stridor, and tripod positioning (leaning forward, chin thrust out). Epiglottitis is a life-threatening airway emergency. Historically caused by H. influenzae type B (now rare due to Hib vaccine) — now more commonly Group A Strep, S. pneumoniae, Staph. Do NOT examine the throat or agitate the child — can trigger complete airway obstruction! Let the child remain in position of comfort. Immediate management: keep child calm, avoid invasive exam, arrange for controlled airway management in OR by anesthesia/ENT (awake fiberoptic intubation). Croup (laryngotracheitis) is viral, slower onset, barky cough — epiglottitis is rapid, toxic-appearing, no cough. Lateral neck X-ray shows 'thumbprint sign' (swollen epiglottis) but do NOT send child to radiology unattended. Treatment: IV antibiotics (ceftriaxone + vancomycin), steroids (dexamethasone).
101.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Epiglottitis.

interventions.why: Awake fiberoptic intubation. Keep child calm.

interventions.label: Ceftriaxone + Vancomycin
interventions.why: IV antibiotics.

interventions.label: Dexamethasone
interventions.why: Reduce airway edema.

102.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 9:00 Temperature: 37.0 C (98.6 degrees F) Pulse: 110 beat/min, Regular rhythm; bounding Respiratory rate: 18 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 122 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 74 mm Hg Height: 175.3 cm (69.0 in) Weight: 65.8 kg (145 lb) Body Mass Index: 21.4 kg/m2
exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with generalized weakness.
Altered mental status with attention and command-following documented.
No rash; hydration and perfusion assessed
102.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with episodes of confusion, diaphoresis, tremors, palpitations, and generalized weakness — relieved by eating (Whipple's triad: hypoglycemic symptoms + low glucose <50 mg/dL + relief with glucose administration). Insulinoma is a neuroendocrine tumor of pancreatic beta cells causing inappropriate insulin secretion → fasting hypoglycemia. Diagnosis: supervised 72-hour fast — will develop hypoglycemia with inappropriately elevated insulin + C-peptide levels (endogenous insulin). Insulin:glucose ratio elevated. Sulfonylurea screen negative (rules out factitious hypoglycemia). Localization: CT/MRI abdomen, endoscopic ultrasound, or selective arterial calcium stimulation. Treatment: surgical resection (enucleation). If unresectable or metastatic: diazoxide (suppresses insulin secretion), octreotide, everolimus. Frequent small meals, avoid prolonged fasting.
102.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Insulinoma.

104.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with localized lower back pain, fever, chills, malaise, and point tenderness over the affected vertebrae. Vertebral osteomyelitis is a bacterial infection of the vertebral body — most commonly S. aureus. Risk factors: IV drug use, recent bacteremia, indwelling catheters, DM, immunocompromised. Diagnosis: MRI spine with contrast (gold standard — high sensitivity). Plain X-ray may be normal early (need 30-50% bone loss to see). Blood cultures x2 (positive in 50%). If blood cultures negative → CT-guided or open biopsy for culture. ESR and CRP elevated. Treatment: IV antibiotics (empiric: vancomycin + ceftriaxone or cefepime — cover MRSA and gram-negatives) x 6 weeks minimum, tailored to culture results. Surgical debridement if abscess, neurologic deficit, spinal instability, or failure of medical therapy.

105.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset severe unilateral pelvic/abdominal pain following activity (intercourse, exercise). May have vaginal bleeding. Exam reveals peritoneal signs, adnexal tenderness, possible palpable mass. Ruptured ovarian cyst → bleeding into peritoneal cavity → hemoperitoneum → hypovolemia and acute abdomen. Most common: ruptured corpus luteum cyst. Differential: ectopic pregnancy (MUST rule out — HCG), PID, appendicitis, ovarian torsion. Diagnosis: HCG negative (rules out ectopic). Transvaginal ultrasound shows free fluid in pelvis/abdomen, ruptured cyst, possible adnexal mass. CBC for anemia from blood loss. Type and screen. Management: stable → observation, analgesia, serial hematocrit. Unstable/hypotensive → IV fluids, blood transfusion if needed, surgical consult (laparoscopy vs laparotomy for hemostasis). If on anticoagulation → reverse.

patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with fever (single temp >38.3°C or sustained >38.0°C for 1h) and absolute neutrophil count <500 cells/µL. This is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY — mortality high without immediate anti…
patient_voice.pain: Fever with known neutropenia

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with fatigue.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
106.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with fever (single temp >38.3°C or sustained >38.0°C for 1h) and absolute neutrophil count <500 cells/µL. This is a MEDICAL EMERGENCY — mortality high without immediate antibiotics. Most commonly seen post-chemotherapy. Often no localizing signs of infection because there are no neutrophils to create pus/inflammation. Blood cultures x2, UA + culture, CXR. Calculate MASCC score for risk stratification (low-risk may be outpatient). Treatment: empiric IV antibiotics within 1 HOUR — monotherapy with anti-pseudomonal beta-lactam (cefepime, meropenem, pip-tazo). Add vancomycin if: hemodynamic instability, suspected catheter infection, skin/soft tissue infection, known MRSA colonization, severe mucositis. If persists >4-7 days → add antifungal coverage. G-CSF may be considered. Admit. Reverse isolation (neutropenic precautions).

107.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with paranoia, auditory hallucinations (hearing voices), disorganized speech/behavior, negative symptoms (flat affect, social withdrawal, avolition), and functional decline >6 months. Schizophrenia is a chronic psychiatric disorder — symptoms for ≥6 months with ≥1 month of active symptoms. Must rule out substance-induced psychosis, medical causes (CNS tumor, infection, autoimmune encephalitis, thyroid), and other psychiatric disorders (bipolar with psychosis, schizoaffective). Diagnosis is clinical — no diagnostic test. Collateral history crucial. Treatment: antipsychotics (second-generation: risperidone, olanzapine, quetiapine, aripiprazole — fewer EPS than first-gen like haloperidol). Clozapine for treatment-resistant. Monitor for metabolic syndrome (weight, glucose, lipids). Long-acting injectables for non-adherence. Psychosocial interventions: CBT, family therapy, supported employment. Safety assessment for self-harm/aggression.

patient_voice.pain: Unresponsive, respiratory depression

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with unresponsive.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Neurologic exam focused on mental status and focal deficits.
Warm skin with fever; no purpura on initial survey.
109.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents unresponsive with respiratory depression, CNS depression, and hypotonia. Pupils may be normal or slightly constricted (unlike opioid pinpoint). History of diazepam use confirmed. Benzo overdose alone rarely causes death unless mixed with other sedatives (alcohol, opioids). Flumazenil is a competitive benzodiazepine antagonist — but use with EXTREME CAUTION. Flumazenil can precipitate acute withdrawal seizures, especially in chronic benzo users or mixed overdose with TCAs. Generally NOT recommended for routine use. Treatment: supportive care — airway protection (intubate if needed), respiratory support, IV fluids, observation. Decontamination with activated charcoal if recent ingestion (<1h) and airway protected. Full recovery expected with supportive care alone for isolated benzo overdose. Toxicology screen to rule out co-ingestants. Psychiatry consult for intentional overdose.

History of diazepam use confirmed. Benzo overdose alone rarely causes death unless mixed with other sedatives (alcohol, opioids). Flumazenil is a competitive benzodiazepine antagonist — but use with EXTREME CAUTION. Flumazenil can precipitate acute withdrawal seizures, especially in chronic benzo users or mixed overdose with TCAs. Generally NOT recommended for routine use. Treatment: supportive care — airway protection (intubate if needed), respiratory support, IV fluids, observation. Decontamination with activated charcoal if recent ingestion (<1h) and airway protected. Full recovery expected with supportive care alone for isolated benzo overdose. 110.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with rash, lymphadenopathy, and possible genital lesion history. Secondary syphilis: diffuse maculopapular rash (INCLUDING palms and soles — key differentiating feature), condyloma lata (wart-like lesions in moist areas), lymphadenopathy, flu-like symptoms. Primary syphilis: painless indurated chancre at inoculation site (resolves spontaneously). Caused by Treponema pallidum (spirochete). Diagnosis: screening with RPR or VDRL (non-treponemal — titer correlates with disease activity). Confirm with treponemal-specific test (FTA-ABS, TP-PA). Darkfield microscopy of chancre fluid can directly visualize spirochetes. HIV testing (high co-infection). Treatment: benzathine penicillin G 2.4M units IM once (primary/secondary/early latent). Doxycycline if penicillin-allergic. Jarisch-Herxheimer reaction may occur (fever, myalgias, headache within 24h). Report to public health. Partner notification. Follow RPR titers to confirm cure (4-fold decline).
110.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Syphilis.

111.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset dyspnea, tachypnea, hypoxemia, petechial rash (chest, axillae, conjunctivae), and CNS changes (confusion, AMS) 24-72 hours after a long bone fracture (femur, tibia) or pelvic fracture. Fat embolism syndrome is caused by fat globules from bone marrow entering venous circulation → lodged in pulmonary and cerebral capillaries → mechanical obstruction + inflammatory cascade. Triad: respiratory distress + petechial rash + CNS dysfunction. Diagnosis is clinical (no gold standard test). CXR may show diffuse bilateral infiltrates (ARDS pattern). ABG: hypoxemia, A-a gradient elevated. UA may show fat globules in urine. Treatment: SUPPORTIVE — oxygen, respiratory support (may require mechanical ventilation). Early surgical fixation of long bone fractures reduces risk. Maintain adequate oxygenation and hemodynamics.

112.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents found unconscious with signs of physical struggle (bruises, abrasions, torn clothing). Management requires a multidisciplinary, trauma-informed approach. Priorities: medical stabilization first (ABCs), then forensic examination. Obtain consent before any exam. Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner (SANE) if available. Forensic evidence collection (rape kit): clothing, swabs, fingernail scrapings, hair samples — ideally within 72h. Document injuries with photographs. Labs: STI testing (chlamydia, gonorrhea, HIV, syphilis, hepatitis), pregnancy test, toxicology screen (drug-facilitated assault —GHB, benzodiazepines, ketamine). Empiric treatment: ceftriaxone + doxycycline + metronidazole for STI prophylaxis. Emergency contraception (levonorgestrel 1.5mg PO once). HIV PEP if within 72h. Report to law enforcement (with consent). Arrange safe discharge and follow-up. Psychiatry/crisis counseling referral.

115.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute agitation, aggression, psychomotor activation, and possible threatening behavior. Priority: ensure safety of patient and staff. Determine etiology: psychiatric (schizophrenia, bipolar mania, psychosis) vs substance-induced (stimulants, PCP, alcohol withdrawal) vs medical (hypoglycemia, hypoxia, head injury, sepsis, encephalopathy). Rapid assessment: vital signs, fingerstick glucose, pulse oximetry, brief neuro exam. Verbal de-escalation first-line. If pharmacologic needed: PO preferred over IM if patient willing — lorazepam (benzo) or olanzapine (antipsychotic). If IM required: midazolam + haloperidol or olanzapine IM. Avoid physical restraints unless absolutely necessary — can worsen agitation and cause rhabdomyolysis. If restraints used: 1:1 observation, frequent monitoring. Once stabilized → workup for underlying cause (tox screen, CT head, labs). Psychiatry consult.

116.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Headache
History of present Illness:
A 55-year-old female with a past medical history of hypertension presents to your office with a an occipital headache, mild vertigo, and a tendency to fall when walking for 6 days. She states that she never had any problems walking or being off-balance. Eight days ago, she stated that she had a pink rash on her arms and torso and felt feverish. The rash improved after a couple days, but the headache and tendency to fall persisted. She had nausea, but she denied any vomiting. She feels weak and "under the weather."  She denies travel, but went hiking 2 weeks ago nearby her house which she routinely does every summer. She denies any history of migraines. She will occasionally get a tension headache which she will treat with Ibuprofen. She has never had a headache that has lasted this long. She denies any trauma to her head. She denies any sick contacts. She denies any recent antibiotic use.  She is very concerned about her symptoms.

PMH:
Past Medical History: Hypertension. The patient recently had a colonoscopy screening which was normal. 
Current medications: HCTZ 25mg PO daily
Allergies: None
Vaccinations: Received Childhood vaccinations.
Women's health: The patient cannot remember when her last pap smear was done.
Family History:
Her father has a history of Hypertension and died of a stroke. Her mother has no health problems and is still living.

Social History:
Marital/Family: She is married with one child. She lives in Gaithersburg, Maryland.
Personal habits: The patient denies smoking. She lives an active lifestyle. She drinks alcohol socially. She denies use of illegal drugs or misuse of medications.
Occupation/educational: She works as a public relations specialist. She is a college graduate with a BS in communication.
Recreational: The patient enjoys to bike and hike. She loves the outdoors and spends as much time as she is able.

Review of systems:
General: See HPI
Skin: See HPI
HEENT: Negative
Cardiorespiratory: Negative
Gastrointestinal: See HPI
Genitourinary: Negative
Neuropsychiatric: See HPI

117.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Chest pain; respiratory distress
History of present Illness:
The patient, a 65-year-old accountant, is brought to the emergency department by ambulance from the trucking company, where he works. Ten minutes prior to the ambulance’s arrival, the patient developed excruciating, sharp pain on the right side of his chest accompanied by marked respiratory distress. He rates the pain as an 8 on a 10-point scale. The pain increases on respiration, and he is unable to answer questions. A coworker who accompanied the patient to the hospital says that this has never happened to the patient in the past. Coworker mentions patient has a past medical history of emphysema and asthma. Oxygen was administered during transport.

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Diffuse muscle pain, dark urine, weakness
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with diffuse muscle pain, weakness, dark cola-colored urine (myoglobinuria), and fatigue following prolonged immobilization, crush injury, extreme exertion, or medication re…
patient_voice.pain: Diffuse muscle pain, dark urine, weakness

exam: presents with diffuse muscle pain, weakness, dark cola-colored urine (myoglobinuria), and fatigue following prolonged immobilization, crush injury, extreme exertion, or medication reaction.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Motor strength and reflexes tested for fatigability and focal deficits.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
118.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with diffuse muscle pain, weakness, dark cola-colored urine (myoglobinuria), and fatigue following prolonged immobilization, crush injury, extreme exertion, or medication reaction. Labs: markedly elevated CK (often >5,000, can be >100,000), elevated Cr (AKI from myoglobin), hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia. UA positive for blood on dipstick but no RBCs on microscopy (myoglobinuria). Rhabdomyolysis = skeletal muscle breakdown → release of intracellular contents (K, phosphate, myoglobin, CK) into bloodstream. Biggest risk: acute kidney injury from myoglobin pigment nephropathy. Management: AGGRESSIVE IV crystalloid resuscitation (NS or LR, 1-2L bolus then 200-300 mL/hr titrated to urine output >200-300 mL/hr). Monitor urine output, renal function, electrolytes (hyperkalemia → cardiac arrhythmia). Alkalinization with bicarb generally NOT recommended. Treat underlying cause.
118.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Rhabdomyolysis.

interventions.label: CK, serum
interventions.why: Markedly elevated >5,000.

interventions.label: BMP / UA / Ca / Phos
interventions.why: AKI, hyperK, hyperP, hypoCa. UA: blood+, no RBCs.

interventions.label: ECG
interventions.why: HyperK → peaked T, wide QRS.

interventions.label: Aggressive IV fluids
interventions.why: 1-2L bolus, then 200-300mL/h. Goal UOP 200-300mL/h.

interventions.label: Treat hyperkalemia
interventions.why: Calcium gluconate, insulin+glucose, bicarb if severe.

Labs: markedly elevated CK (often >5,000, can be >100,000), elevated Cr (AKI from myoglobin), hyperkalemia, hyperphosphatemia, hypocalcemia. UA positive for blood on dipstick but no RBCs on microscopy (myoglobinuria). Rhabdomyolysis = skeletal muscle breakdown → release of intracellular contents (K, phosphate, myoglobin, CK) into bloodstream. Biggest risk: acute kidney injury from myoglobin pigment nephropathy. Management: AGGRESSIVE IV crystalloid resuscitation (NS or LR, 1-2L bolus then 200-300 mL/hr titrated to urine output >200-300 mL/hr). Monitor urine output, renal function, electrolytes (hyperkalemia → cardiac arrhythmia). Alkalinization with bicarb generally NOT recommended. Treat underlying cause.

122.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset fever, widespread painful target-like lesions, bullae, epidermal detachment (<10% BSA = SJS, 10-30% = SJS/TEN overlap, >30% = TEN), and mucosal involvement (oral, ocular, genital). Nikolsky sign positive (epidermis sloughs with gentle pressure). Most commonly triggered by medications: sulfa antibiotics, anti-epileptics (lamotrigine, phenytoin, carbamazepine), allopurinol, NSAIDs, within 1-8 weeks of exposure. This is a medical emergency. Immediately discontinue offending drug. Admit to burn ICU. Supportive care: fluid/electrolyte management, wound care, infection prevention, nutritional support, ophthalmology consult. Systemic steroids controversial — not universally recommended. IVIG or cyclosporine may be considered. SCORTEN score for prognosis.

123.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with unilateral leg swelling, pain, warmth, and erythema. Risk factors: Virchow's triad — stasis (immobilization, long travel), hypercoagulability (malignancy, OCPs, pregnancy, thrombophilia), endothelial injury (surgery, trauma). Exam: Homan's sign unreliable. Measure leg circumference difference. Wells criteria determines pretest probability. If low probability → D-dimer. If D-dimer elevated or high probability → compression ultrasound (proximal DVT). Treatment: most DVT → anticoagulation with DOAC (rivaroxaban, apixaban) or LMWH bridge to warfarin. Duration: provoked = 3 months, unprovoked = 6-12 months or indefinite. NO routine thrombectomy or IVC filter unless anticoagulation contraindicated. Compression stockings for symptom relief and post-thrombotic syndrome prevention.

123.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Deep Venous Thrombosis (DVT).

125.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 16:00 Temperature: 37.0 C (98.6 degrees F) Pulse: 120 beats/min, Weak Respiratory rate: 34 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 100 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 60 mm Hg Height: 183cm (72.0 in) Weight: 97.5 kg (215 lb) Body Mass Index: 29.1 kg/m2
exam: presents with chest pain, hypotension, clear lung fields, elevated JVP, and Kussmaul's sign.
125.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chest pain, hypotension, clear lung fields, elevated JVP, and Kussmaul's sign. ECG shows ST elevation in inferior leads (II, III, aVF) with ST elevation in V1 > V3 and ST elevation in V4R (right-sided leads) — indicating RV involvement. RV infarction occurs in ~30% of inferior MIs (usually RCA occlusion). RV is preload-dependent — nitroglycerin and morphine can cause dangerous hypotension because they reduce preload. Treatment: AVOID nitrates and diuretics (reduce preload → worsen RV output). Give IV fluids aggressively to maintain RV preload. Aspirin, P2Y12 inhibitor, anticoagulation. REPERFUSION: emergent PCI (preferred) or fibrinolysis. If hypotensive despite fluids: dobutamine (inotrope). Atropine for bradycardia. Admit to CCU.

exam: Patient appears dyspneic and fatigued. Assess severity of illness and work of breathing.
Heart exam indicated for cardiac etiology. Assess for murmurs, rubs, gallops, JVD.
Chest and lung exam indicated for shortness of breath. Assess for crackles, wheezes, diminished breath sounds.
126.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is an elderly woman with a history of diabetes mellitus and hypertension who presents to the emergency department with progressive shortness of breath, fatigue, and dizziness. She denies chest pain. The dyspnea has been gradual in onset, associated with lightheadedness but no fever, cough, palpitations, or orthopnea. Given her cardiovascular risk factors and atypical presentation — ST depression in leads I, II, V4-V6 suggesting subendocardial ischemia — acute coronary syndrome must be ruled out urgently.
126.clinical_tip: Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) — follow CCS review orders.

interventions.why: The patient is complaining of shortness of breath, so this should be examined.

interventions.label: Electrocardiography, 12 lead
interventions.why: Shortness of breath and fatigue can be atypical symptoms for MI. This EKG will show NSTEMI which needs to be treated quickly.

interventions.label: Monitor, cardiac

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: CBC will be important to get to look at the hematocrit of the patient.

interventions.label: Basic metabolic profile

interventions.label: Intravenous access
interventions.why: Good practice to order IV access when administering IV fluids or medications, though not required for grade.

interventions.label: Aspirin, therapy
interventions.why: The patient should immediately be given Aspirin along with a beta blocker and atorvastatin for ACS.

interventions.label: Atorvastatin / Rosuvastatin
interventions.why: Guidelines recommend high-intensity statins (Rosuvastatin 20-40 mg or Atorvastatin 40-80 mg) for ACS. Simvastatin is not high-intensity even at max dose.

interventions.label: Beta-blocker (Metoprolol / Atenolol)
interventions.why: Metoprolol or atenolol are the preferred agents for treating MI. Oral preferred over IV.

interventions.label: Ticagrelor / Clopidogrel
interventions.why: Dual antiplatelet therapy is standard for NSTEMI patients without contraindications. Ticagrelor and Prasugrel preferred over Clopidogrel.

interventions.label: Consult, cardiology / Angioplasty with stent placement, coronary artery
interventions.why: Cardiology should be consulted. PCI with stent placement is the preferred reperfusion treatment for NSTEMI.

interventions.label: Heparin, therapy
interventions.why: For NSTEMI, unfractionated heparin, enoxaparin, bivalirudin, or fondaparinux help prevent ischemic events.

decoys.label: Chest X-ray, PA and lateral
decoys.why: Not first-line for NSTEMI diagnosis — ECG and troponin are priority.

decoys.label: Morphine sulfate
decoys.why: Patient denies chest pain — morphine not indicated without pain.

decoys.label: Nitroglycerin, sublingual
decoys.why: Patient denies chest pain — nitroglycerin not indicated without anginal symptoms.

decoys.label: D-dimer, serum
decoys.why: PE is in differential but ECG findings and atypical anginal presentation point to NSTEMI. Troponin and ECG first.

decoys.label: Simvastatin
decoys.why: Simvastatin is not a high-intensity statin. Atorvastatin 40-80 mg or Rosuvastatin 20-40 mg required for ACS.

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Petechiae, purpura, easy bruising in well child
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with sudden onset petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, and possibly mucosal bleeding in an otherwise well-appearing child. No lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly,…
patient_voice.pain: Petechiae, purpura, easy bruising in well child

exam: presents with sudden onset petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, and possibly mucosal bleeding in an otherwise well-appearing child.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Skin rash morphology and distribution documented.
127.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with sudden onset petechiae, purpura, epistaxis, gum bleeding, and possibly mucosal bleeding in an otherwise well-appearing child. No lymphadenopathy, no hepatosplenomegaly, no fever, no bone pain — distinguishes from leukemia. ITP is an autoimmune destruction of platelets (antibodies against GPIIb/IIIa). Often preceded by viral URI or vaccination 1-4 weeks prior. Labs: ISOLATED thrombocytopenia (platelets <100K, often <20K). Normal Hb, normal WBC, normal peripheral smear (except low platelets). Bone marrow biopsy NOT needed in typical childhood ITP. Treatment: most children (>80%) recover spontaneously within 6 months. If platelets >20K and no bleeding → observation only. If <10K or significant bleeding → prednisone 2-4 mg/kg/day or IVIG or anti-D (if Rh+). Avoid IM injections, contact sports, NSAIDs/aspirin.
127.clinical_tip: Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP) — follow CCS review orders.
127.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Immune Thrombocytopenia (ITP).

interventions.label: CBC + Peripheral smear
interventions.why: Isolated thrombocytopenia. Normal Hb, WBC.

interventions.label: Observation (if platelets >20K, no bleeding)
interventions.why: Most resolve spontaneously.

interventions.label: Prednisone / IVIG (if <10K or bleeding)
interventions.why: First-line treatment.

interventions.label: Avoid contact sports, NSAIDs, IM injections
interventions.why: Bleeding precautions.

128.title: Depression

patient_voice.chief_complaint: I've been depressed, tired, and gaining weight
patient_voice.history: I haven't had a period in six months. My face looks puffy and I've been feeling down for months.
patient_voice.pain: Fatigue and low mood — not focal pain

exam: presents with depression, fatigue, weight gain, moon facies, hirsutism, thinning hair, and amenorrhea for six months.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Neurologic exam focused on mental status and focal deficits.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
128.hpi_narrative:
{{patient_name}} presents with depression, fatigue, weight gain, moon facies, hirsutism, thinning hair, and amenorrhea for six months. This is Cushing disease from a pituitary adenoma — not primary major depressive disorder.

Workup: pregnancy test (amenorrhea); dexamethasone suppression test or 24-hour urine cortisol to confirm hypercortisolism; ACTH level — high ACTH (>20 pg/mL) indicates ACTH-dependent Cushing (pituitary vs ectopic); brain MRI for pituitary tumor when ACTH is elevated.

Definitive treatment is transsphenoidal resection (neurosurgery consult). SSRIs or psychiatry consult alone do not treat the underlying endocrine cause.

interventions.label: CT, head, with contrast / CT of head without contrast / MRI, head, with gadolinium / MRI, head, without gadolinium

129.title: Facial Pain

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Sudden severe electric shock-like facial pain
patient_voice.history: The pain comes in bursts — like a shock in my face. Brushing my teeth or a breeze can set it off.
patient_voice.pain: Sharp, electric facial pain lasting seconds — triggered by touch or chewing.

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with facial pain.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Warm skin with fever; no purpura on initial survey.
129.hpi_narrative:
{{patient_name}} presents with classic trigeminal neuralgia — recurrent episodes of severe, sharp, electric shock-like facial pain in one area of the trigeminal nerve distribution, lasting seconds to two minutes, often precipitated by innocuous stimuli (light touch, chewing, wind). The most common cause is compression of the trigeminal nerve root (80–90% of cases), typically by a vascular loop.

Differential: acute herpes zoster, painful post-traumatic trigeminal neuropathy, idiopathic painful trigeminal neuropathy, postherpetic trigeminal neuropathy.

Workup: neurologic exam including cranial nerves; CBC to exclude infection; BMP/CMP; MRI or CT head to exclude tumor or neurovascular compression.

First-line treatment is carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine; gabapentin/pregabalin are second line. Surgery is not indicated until medical therapy fails.
129.clinical_tip: Trigeminal Neuralgia — follow CCS review orders.
129.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Trigeminal Neuralgia.

130.title: Cough

patient_voice.chief_complaint: High fever, cough, GI symptoms, hyponatremia
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with high fever, cough (initially dry then productive), dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and extrapulmonary symptoms: GI (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain), hyponatr…
patient_voice.pain: High fever, cough, GI symptoms, hyponatremia

exam: Ill-appearing with frequent cough; speaks in short phrases between paroxysms.
RR 25, tachypneic; SpO₂ 92%; hypoxemic; focal crackles and dullness to percussion on affected side.
Abdominal tenderness pattern matches history; no rigid abdomen documented yet.
Altered mental status with attention and command-following documented.
No petechiae; mild diaphoresis with exertional cough
130.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with high fever, cough (initially dry then productive), dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, and extrapulmonary symptoms: GI (nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, abdominal pain), hyponatremia (classic lab finding), confusion/AMS, relative bradycardia. History: exposure to contaminated water sources (hot tubs, cooling towers, hotel, cruise ship). Legionella is an atypical pneumonia — intracellular pathogen not seen on Gram stain. Diagnosis: urinary antigen test (detects L. pneumophila serogroup 1 — most common, rapid), sputum culture on specialized media (BCYE agar), PCR. Severe cases require hospitalization. Treatment: macrolides (azithromycin) or respiratory fluoroquinolones (levofloxacin, moxifloxacin). Doxycycline as alternative. Treatment duration 7-14 days (longer if immunocompromised). Report to public health (Legionnaires disease is reportable).
130.clinical_tip: Legionella Pneumonia (Legionnaires Disease) — follow CCS review orders.
130.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Legionella Pneumonia (Legionnaires Disease).

131.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Abdominal Pain
History of present Illness:
A 22-year-old female presents to the emergency room with abdominal pain, lethargy, and vomiting x2 days. Her vomiting is non-bloody. Her abdominal pain is diffuse, which she rates as a 6/10. She also claims to have had an increased appetite prior to having these symptoms. She also claims that she’s been developing blurry vision, dizziness, and drowsiness. She also states that she is having increased urination

Past Medical History

Past Medical History: None
Current medications: Birth control
Allergies: None
Vaccinations: The patient received her childhood vaccinations. She has never received any HPV vaccines.
Women's health: The patient cannot remember when her last pap smear was done.
Family History: The patient has a brother with Diabetes. 

Social History:
Marital/Family: Single. She is an undergraduate student at a local university.
Personal habits: The patient denies smoking. She drinks socially. She smoked marijuana "a few times" with her friends. She denies other illicit drugs or misuse of medications. Occupation/educational: She is a student at a local university
Recreational: She plays the piano and sings in a band. 

Review of systems:
General: See HPI
Skin: Her skin is dry. 
HEENT: Her throat is dry.

exam: presents with chronic low back pain (>3 months), morning stiffness (>30 min) that IMPROVES with exercise and WORSENS with rest.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
133.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic low back pain (>3 months), morning stiffness (>30 min) that IMPROVES with exercise and WORSENS with rest. Inflammatory back pain pattern (vs mechanical — worsens with activity). Associated: sacroiliitis, limited spinal mobility (Schober test), enthesitis, peripheral arthritis, uveitis. Young male predominance. Strong association with HLA-B27. Diagnosis: X-ray/MRI of SI joints — sacroiliitis (bamboo spine in advanced disease). Elevated ESR/CRP. Treatment: NSAIDs first-line (excellent response — diagnostic feature). Physical therapy — maintain posture and mobility. If NSAIDs insufficient → TNF inhibitors (infliximab, adalimumab, etanercept). IL-17 inhibitors (secukinumab) also effective. Do NOT recommend bed rest — makes it worse. Exercise program essential.

exam: presents with unilateral scrotal pain of gradual onset, swelling, tenderness, and erythema.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Warm skin with fever; no purpura on initial survey.
134.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with unilateral scrotal pain of gradual onset, swelling, tenderness, and erythema. Pain may radiate to lower abdomen. Prehn's sign: pain improves with scrotal elevation (distinguishes from testicular torsion — no relief with elevation, acute onset). Caused by ascending infection: sexually active young men → Chlamydia trachomatis, Neisseria gonorrhoeae. Older men or post-instrumentation → E. coli, enteric organisms. Diagnosis: UA (pyuria), urine culture, CT/GC NAAT. Scrotal ultrasound with Doppler if torsion suspected (increased flow in epididymitis, decreased/absent in torsion). Treatment: CT/GC → ceftriaxone 250mg IM once + doxycycline 100mg PO BID x 10d. Enteric → levofloxacin x 10d. Scrotal elevation, NSAIDs, ice. Treat sexual partners.
134.clinical_tip: Acute Epididymitis — follow CCS review orders.
134.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Acute Epididymitis.

135.diagnosis: Hyperkalemic Emergency secondary to ACE Inhibitor + NSAID

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Muscle weakness, palpitations
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive muscle weakness, fatigue, and palpitations. ECG shows peaked T waves, loss of P waves, widened QRS. Labs reveal severe hyperkalemia (K+ >6.5). Medication hi…
patient_voice.pain: Muscle weakness, palpitations

exam: presents with progressive muscle weakness, fatigue, and palpitations.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Motor strength and reflexes tested for fatigability and focal deficits.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
135.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive muscle weakness, fatigue, and palpitations. ECG shows peaked T waves, loss of P waves, widened QRS. Labs reveal severe hyperkalemia (K+ >6.5). Medication history: on ACE inhibitor for HTN and recently started NSAIDs for joint pain. ACEI reduces aldosterone → decreased renal K+ excretion. NSAIDs reduce renal blood flow → further decrease K+ excretion. Combined → dangerous hyperkalemia. Management: IMMEDIATE cardiac membrane stabilization — IV calcium gluconate or calcium chloride (does NOT lower K+, PROTECTS the heart). Then shift K+ intracellularly: IV regular insulin + glucose, beta-agonist (albuterol nebulized), sodium bicarbonate if acidotic. Then eliminate K+: furosemide (if renal function adequate), sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate), patiromer, or hemodialysis if refractory. Discontinue ACEI and NSAIDs.

135.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Hyperkalemic Emergency secondary to ACE Inhibitor + NSAID.

136.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive dyspnea, dry cough, fatigue, and bilateral hilar lymphadenopathy on CXR. May have erythema nodosum (painful red nodules on shins), uveitis, parotid enlargement, lupus pernio (purplish facial plaques). Sarcoidosis is a multisystem granulomatous disease of unknown etiology — more common in African Americans. Non-caseating granulomas are the pathologic hallmark. CXR staging: I (BHL only), II (BHL + parenchymal infiltrates), III (parenchymal only), IV (fibrosis). Labs: elevated ACE level (supports but not diagnostic), hypercalcemia/hypercalciuria (increased 1,25-vitamin D from activated macrophages in granulomas). Diagnosis: biopsy showing non-caseating granulomas + exclusion of other causes (TB, fungal, berylliosis). PFTs: restrictive pattern. Treatment: many resolve spontaneously (stage I). If symptomatic or progressive → corticosteroids (prednisone 0.5 mg/kg/day). Methotrexate or azathioprine for steroid-sparing. Anti-TNF for refractory. Monitor for TB reactivation before immunosuppression.

137.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with symmetric polyarthritis involving small joints of hands (MCP, PIP), wrists, and ankles. Morning stiffness >1 hour. Joints are warm, swollen, tender. RA is a chronic autoimmune inflammatory arthritis. Key features: symmetric, polyarticular, involves hands/feet, spares DIP joints (distinguishes from osteoarthritis which involves DIP/PIP, Heberden/Bouchard nodes). Extra-articular: rheumatoid nodules, interstitial lung disease, pericarditis, vasculitis, Felty's syndrome. Labs: RF (rheumatoid factor — 80% sensitive), anti-CCP (anti-citrullinated peptide — very specific >95%), elevated ESR/CRP. X-ray: periarticular osteopenia, joint space narrowing, marginal erosions. Treatment: early aggressive DMARDs — methotrexate first-line. Plus short-term prednisone bridge. If MTX inadequate → add biologic (TNF inhibitor — etanercept, adalimumab). Refer to rheumatology. Physical and occupational therapy.
137.clinical_tip: Rheumatoid Arthritis — follow CCS review orders.

138.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive fatigue, weakness, anorexia, nausea, pruritus, edema, and oliguria. Labs: markedly elevated BUN/Cr, hyperkalemia, metabolic acidosis, anemia (low EPO), hypocalcemia, hyperphosphatemia, secondary hyperparathyroidism. ESRD is irreversible loss of renal function (GFR <15). Most common causes: diabetes, hypertension, glomerulonephritis. Management: renal replacement therapy — hemodialysis, peritoneal dialysis, or kidney transplant. Urgent indications for dialysis: AEIOU — Acidosis, Electrolytes (hyperkalemia), Intoxication (toxins), Overload (volume), Uremia (pericarditis, encephalopathy). Treat anemia (EPO), manage mineral bone disease (phosphate binders, vitamin D, calcimimetics). Refer for AV fistula creation. Nephrology referral.

The headaches are worse in the morning and when she bears down or strains. She describes brief episodes where her vision goes dark for a few seconds, a whooshing sound in her ears that pulses with her heartbeat, and occasional double vision when she looks to the side. LP: elevated opening pressure (>25 cm H2O) with normal CSF composition. Treatment: weight loss (most important), acetazolamide (carbonic anhydrase inhibitor — reduces CSF production). 142.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a neonate presenting with seizures, poor feeding, vomiting, lethargy, and urine/cerumen that smells like maple syrup (burnt sugar). MSUD is an autosomal recessive inborn error of metabolism — deficiency of branched-chain alpha-ketoacid dehydrogenase complex → accumulation of branched-chain amino acids (leucine, isoleucine, valine) and their ketoacids. Leucine is neurotoxic → encephalopathy, seizures. Newborn screening detects elevated leucine. Diagnosis: plasma amino acids — markedly elevated leucine, isoleucine, valine. Urine organic acids: branched-chain ketoacids. During acute decompensation: remove leucine (dialysis if severe), provide calories (glucose + insulin to promote anabolism), correct electrolyte abnormalities. Long-term: dietary restriction of BCAAs with special formula, liver transplant for severe cases.

patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is a neonate presenting with poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, lethargy, and failure to thrive after initiating breast milk or cow's milk formula feeds. Galactosemia is an autosomal …

143.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a neonate presenting with poor feeding, vomiting, jaundice, lethargy, and failure to thrive after initiating breast milk or cow's milk formula feeds. Galactosemia is an autosomal recessive deficiency of galactose-1-phosphate uridylyltransferase (GALT) → inability to metabolize galactose → accumulation of galactose-1-phosphate (toxic to liver, brain, kidneys, lens). Classic findings: jaundice (unconjugated progressing to conjugated), hepatomegaly, cataracts (galactitol accumulation in lens), E. coli sepsis (increased risk), renal tubular dysfunction. Newborn screening detects elevated galactose. Confirm: GALT enzyme activity in RBCs. Treatment: ELIMINATE galactose from diet — soy formula instead of milk. Lifelong. Even with treatment, some may have long-term complications (cognitive, ovarian failure).
143.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Galactosemia.

exam: Well-appearing 6-year-old girl; height 10th percentile, weight 90th percentile. Possible Turner stigmata: short stature, webbed neck, shield chest, widely spaced nipples.

Born at term (40 weeks) via uncomplicated vaginal delivery; APGAR scores 10 and 10. No hospitalizations or medical problems. Vaccinations up to date. Family history is unremarkable.

interventions.label: Consult, pediatric endocrinology

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Burning facial pain after shingles rash
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with persistent, severe, burning/shooting pain in the trigeminal nerve distribution (V1 most common) following a recent herpes zoster (shingles) outbreak with characteristic…
patient_voice.pain: Burning facial pain after shingles rash

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with facial pain.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.

145.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with persistent, severe, burning/shooting pain in the trigeminal nerve distribution (V1 most common) following a recent herpes zoster (shingles) outbreak with characteristic vesicular rash in the same distribution. Postherpetic neuralgia is the most common complication of HZ — pain persisting >90 days after rash resolution. Risk increases with age (>60). Caused by viral damage to sensory ganglia → neuropathic pain. Treatment: first-line — gabapentin or pregabalin, TCAs (amitriptyline, nortriptyline), lidocaine patch 5% (localized pain). Opioids NOT first-line. Prevention: recombinant zoster vaccine (Shingrix) for adults ≥50 — reduces HZ risk by >90% and PHN risk. VZV is reactivation of latent varicella virus in dorsal root ganglia.

145.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Postherpetic Neuralgia (Trigeminal Distribution).

148.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with pleuritic chest pain, fever, malaise, and pericardial friction rub 2-6 weeks after a myocardial infarction. Dressler syndrome is an autoimmune-mediated pericarditis occurring post-MI (or post-cardiac surgery) — immune response to exposed myocardial antigens. ECG: diffuse ST elevation, PR depression (pericarditis pattern). Echo: pericardial effusion (usually small). Differentiate from peri-infarct pericarditis (occurs within days of MI, localized ECG changes over infarct zone, more directly due to transmural necrosis). Treatment: high-dose aspirin (650mg q4-6h) or NSAIDs (ibuprofen). Colchicine added for symptom reduction and recurrence prevention. Avoid steroids unless refractory (impair myocardial healing). NOT heparin (risk of hemorrhagic pericardial effusion/tamponade).

exam: presents with severe, refractory peptic ulcer disease, chronic watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, and GI bleeding.
Abdominal tenderness pattern matches history; no rigid abdomen documented yet.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Warm skin with fever; no purpura on initial survey.
149.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with severe, refractory peptic ulcer disease, chronic watery diarrhea, abdominal pain, and GI bleeding. Multiple ulcers in atypical locations (distal duodenum, jejunum). ZES is caused by a gastrin-secreting neuroendocrine tumor (gastrinoma) — most commonly in the duodenum or pancreas → massive gastric acid hypersecretion → severe PUD and diarrhea (acid inactivates pancreatic enzymes + damages mucosa). Often associated with MEN1. Diagnosis: fasting serum gastrin level — markedly elevated (>1000 pg/mL or >10x normal). If borderline → secretin stimulation test (paradoxical increase in gastrin in ZES). Localize tumor: somatostatin receptor scintigraphy (Octreoscan), CT/MRI, EUS. Treatment: high-dose PPI (omeprazole, pantoprazole) to control acid hypersecretion. Surgical resection if localized. If metastatic or unresectable → long-term PPI + octreotide.
149.clinical_tip: Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (Gastrinoma) — follow CCS review orders.
149.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Zollinger-Ellison Syndrome (Gastrinoma).

150.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with persistent back pain (pathologic vertebral compression fractures), fatigue (normocytic anemia), and possibly hypercalcemia. Multiple myeloma is a malignant proliferation of plasma cells in bone marrow → monoclonal immunoglobulin (M protein) production. Classic CRAB criteria: hyperCalcemia, Renal insufficiency, Anemia, Bone lesions (lytic lesions on X-ray/skeletal survey). Labs: elevated total protein with globulin gap, M spike on SPEP, immunofixation confirms monoclonal Ig (IgG most common), elevated kappa/lambda free light chains with abnormal ratio, Bence Jones protein in urine (UPEP). Bone marrow biopsy: >10% clonal plasma cells. Skeletal survey: lytic punched-out lesions. Treatment: induction (bortezomib + lenalidomide + dexamethasone), +/- autologous stem cell transplant if eligible. Bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid) for bone disease.

151.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents found unconscious in an enclosed space with possible exposure (car exhaust, faulty heater, fire). Cherry-red skin, headache, confusion, nausea. CO binds hemoglobin with 240x affinity of O2 → carboxyhemoglobin (COHb) → impaired O2 delivery + cellular toxicity (binds cytochrome c oxidase). Pulse oximetry falsely NORMAL (cannot distinguish COHb from O2Hb). ABG: normal PaO2, elevated COHb (>3% nonsmokers, >10% smokers). Treatment: 100% oxygen via non-rebreather (reduces COHb half-life from 5h to 1h). Hyperbaric O2 if: COHb >25%, LOC, neurologic symptoms, cardiac ischemia, pregnancy. Monitor for delayed neurologic sequelae. Identify source — others at risk.
151.clinical_tip: Carbon Monoxide Poisoning — follow CCS review orders.
151.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Carbon Monoxide Poisoning.

153.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with fragile skin, blistering lesions on sun-exposed areas (hands, face, forearms), milia, hyperpigmentation, and hypertrichosis. PCT is the most common porphyria — caused by deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) → accumulation of uroporphyrins in skin → photosensitivity. Acquired form associated with: alcohol, hepatitis C, HIV, hemochromatosis, estrogen therapy. Diagnosis: elevated uroporphyrins and heptacarboxyl porphyrins in urine, plasma porphyrins (peak at 620nm), stool isocoproporphyrin. Treatment: phlebotomy (remove iron — goal ferritin low-normal) or low-dose hydroxychloroquine (mobilizes porphyrins). Avoid sun exposure, alcohol, and estrogens. Screen for HCV, HIV, hemochromatosis.

PCT is the most common porphyria — caused by deficiency of uroporphyrinogen decarboxylase (UROD) → accumulation of uroporphyrins in skin → photosensitivity. patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with profuse, frothy, yellow-green malodorous vaginal discharge, vulvar irritation, dysuria, and dyspareunia. Exam reveals strawberry cervix (punctate hemorrhages) and vagin…

154.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with profuse, frothy, yellow-green malodorous vaginal discharge, vulvar irritation, dysuria, and dyspareunia. Exam reveals strawberry cervix (punctate hemorrhages) and vaginal erythema. Caused by Trichomonas vaginalis — flagellated protozoan. Diagnosis: wet mount shows motile trichomonads (flagellated organisms). Vaginal pH >4.5. Whiff test may be positive. NAAT (PCR) is gold standard — more sensitive than wet mount. Treatment: metronidazole 2g PO once or tinidazole 2g PO once. Treat sexual partners (even if asymptomatic). Avoid alcohol during treatment and for 24h after metronidazole (disulfiram-like reaction). Screen for other STIs.

156.title: Generalized Swelling

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Generalized edema, frothy urine, weight gain
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is a child presenting with generalized edema (periorbital — worse in morning, then leg/scrotal), weight gain, frothy urine (proteinuria), and fatigue. Nephrotic syndrome: massive pro…
patient_voice.pain: Generalized edema, frothy urine, weight gain

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with generalized swelling.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
156.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a child presenting with generalized edema (periorbital — worse in morning, then leg/scrotal), weight gain, frothy urine (proteinuria), and fatigue. Nephrotic syndrome: massive proteinuria (>3.5g/day or >40mg/m2/hr in children), hypoalbuminemia (<2.5), edema, hyperlipidemia. Most common cause in children: minimal change disease (MCD) — 80-90%. Often preceded by viral URI. Diagnosis: UA — 3-4+ protein, oval fat bodies. 24h urine protein confirms nephrotic range. Renal biopsy NOT routinely needed in children (MCD most common and responds to steroids). Treatment: prednisone 2mg/kg/day (response = remission in 2-4 weeks confirms MCD). Salt/fluid restriction. Diuretics for severe edema. If steroid-resistant or frequently relapsing: consider biopsy, alternative immunosuppression (cyclophosphamide, cyclosporine). Vaccinate before immunosuppression (pneumococcal). Monitor for complications: infection (loss of immunoglobulins), thrombosis (loss of antithrombin III).
156.clinical_tip: Nephrotic Syndrome (Minimal Change Disease) — follow CCS review orders.
156.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Nephrotic Syndrome (Minimal Change Disease).

157.title: Frequency of Urination

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with polyuria (dilute urine), polydipsia (excessive thirst), nocturia, and hypernatremia. Central DI: deficiency of ADH (vasopressin) from posterior pituitary → inability to…
patient_voice.pain: Polyuria, polydipsia, nocturia

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with frequency of urination.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Warm skin with fever; no purpura on initial survey.
157.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with polyuria (dilute urine), polydipsia (excessive thirst), nocturia, and hypernatremia. Central DI: deficiency of ADH (vasopressin) from posterior pituitary → inability to concentrate urine. Nephrogenic DI: kidneys resistant to ADH (lithium, hypercalcemia, hypokalemia). Workup: 24h urine volume (>3L/day), urine osmolality (<300 despite hypernatremia), serum osmolality elevated, hypernatremia. Water deprivation test: cannot concentrate urine despite fluid restriction. After desmopressin (DDAVP): central DI = urine osmolality increases >50% (kidneys respond to exogenous ADH). Nephrogenic DI = no response. Treatment: central DI → desmopressin (DDAVP) intranasal or PO. Nephrogenic → treat underlying cause, thiazide diuretics (paradoxically reduce urine output), low-solute diet. Free water access essential.
157.clinical_tip: Diabetes Insipidus (Central) — follow CCS review orders.
157.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Diabetes Insipidus (Central).

Nephrogenic DI = no response. Treatment: central DI → desmopressin (DDAVP) intranasal or PO. interventions.label: Order X-rays to rule out fractures or other bony abnormalities

interventions.label: Consider ordering an MRI if symptoms persist or worsen, or in cases of severe trauma

161.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with episodic severe headaches, palpitations, diaphoresis (classic triad), and paroxysmal hypertension. Pheochromocytoma is a catecholamine-secreting tumor of the adrenal medulla chromaffin cells. Rule of 10's: 10% bilateral, 10% extra-adrenal (paraganglioma), 10% malignant, 10% familial (MEN2, VHL, NF1). Diagnosis: plasma free metanephrines or 24h urine fractionated metanephrines and catecholamines (elevated). CT/MRI abdomen — adrenal mass. Pre-operative alpha-blockade (phenoxybenzamine or doxazosin) BEFORE beta-blockade (beta-blockade alone → unopposed alpha agonism → hypertensive crisis). Adequate alpha blockade for 10-14 days before surgery. Then add beta-blocker if tachycardia. Surgical resection (adrenalectomy) is curative.
161.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Pheochromocytoma.

interventions.why: Adrenal mass.

interventions.why: Curative.

162.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with dysuria, urinary frequency, urgency, suprapubic pain, and no vaginal discharge or irritation. No systemic symptoms (fever, CVA tenderness → rules out pyelo). Uncomplicated UTI in healthy premenopausal non-pregnant woman. Most common: E. coli (80%). Diagnosis: UA — positive leukocyte esterase, nitrites, pyuria, bacteriuria. Urine culture not routinely needed for uncomplicated cystitis (treat empirically). Treatment: nitrofurantoin 100mg PO BID x 5d (first-line), TMP-SMX DS PO BID x 3d (if local resistance <20%), fosfomycin 3g PO once. Avoid fluoroquinolones for uncomplicated cystitis (FDA warnings). Counsel: void after intercourse, adequate hydration, cranberry products (limited evidence). If recurrent → postcoital or continuous prophylaxis.

exam: presents with acute ear pain, pulling at ear, fever, and recent URI.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
163.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute ear pain, pulling at ear, fever, and recent URI. Otoscopy reveals a bulging, erythematous, non-mobile tympanic membrane with loss of landmarks. AOM is the most common bacterial infection in children. Common organisms: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis. Diagnosis: acute onset + middle ear effusion (bulging TM, impaired mobility, otorrhea) + signs of inflammation (erythema, otalgia). Treatment: watchful waiting for 48-72h if >6mo, unilateral, non-severe. If <6mo, bilateral, or severe: amoxicillin 80-90mg/kg/day x 10d (first-line). Amoxicillin-clavulanate if recent amoxicillin use or treatment failure. NO decongestants or antihistamines — not effective. Pneumococcal conjugate vaccine (PCV13) for prevention.

164.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset severe unilateral pelvic pain, nausea, vomiting, and possibly low-grade fever. Pain is sudden, severe, and may have occurred intermittently before (partial torsion). Ovarian torsion is a GYNECOLOGIC EMERGENCY — the ovary twists on its vascular pedicle → venous and lymphatic outflow obstruction → arterial compromise → ovarian ischemia and necrosis if not detorsed within hours. Risk: ovarian mass/cyst, pregnancy, ovulation induction. Diagnosis: pelvic ultrasound with Doppler — enlarged ovary, decreased/absent arterial and venous flow. However, normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion (may be intermittent or only venous flow absent). Treatment: EMERGENCY surgical exploration with detorsion (preserve ovary if viable) ± oophoropexy. Do NOT delay surgery for imaging if high clinical suspicion.

Pain is sudden, severe, and may have occurred intermittently before (partial torsion). Ovarian torsion is a GYNECOLOGIC EMERGENCY — the ovary twists on its vascular pedicle → venous and lymphatic outflow obstruction → arterial compromise → ovarian ischemia and necrosis if not detorsed within hours. Risk: ovarian mass/cyst, pregnancy, ovulation induction. Diagnosis: pelvic ultrasound with Doppler — enlarged ovary, decreased/absent arterial and venous flow. However, normal Doppler does NOT exclude torsion (may be intermittent or only venous flow absent). Treatment: EMERGENCY surgical exploration with detorsion (preserve ovary if viable) ± oophoropexy. Do NOT delay surgery for imaging if high clinical suspicion.

patient_voice.pain: Postcoital bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding

exam: presents with postcoital (after intercourse) vaginal bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding, and possibly malodorous discharge.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
165.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with postcoital (after intercourse) vaginal bleeding, intermenstrual bleeding, and possibly malodorous discharge. Speculum exam reveals a friable, exophytic, or ulcerated cervical lesion. Cervical cancer is the most common GYN cancer worldwide — SCC most common. Caused by persistent high-risk HPV infection (16, 18 most common). Risk factors: multiple sexual partners, early sexual activity, immunosuppression, smoking, lack of Pap screening. Diagnosis: cervical biopsy (colposcopy-directed). Staging: clinical (FIGO). Treatment: early stage (IA-IB1) → radical hysterectomy or fertility-sparing cone biopsy. Locally advanced (IB2-IVA) → chemoradiation. Metastatic → systemic therapy. Prevention: HPV vaccination, routine Pap/HPV co-testing.
165.clinical_tip: Cervical Cancer (Squamous Cell Carcinoma) — follow CCS review orders.
165.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Cervical Cancer (Squamous Cell Carcinoma).

patient_voice.pain: Joint bleeding, easy bruising, prolonged PTT

exam: presents with excessive bleeding after minor trauma, easy bruising, hemarthrosis (bleeding into joints — knees, ankles, elbows), and prolonged PTT with normal PT and normal platelet count.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
166.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with excessive bleeding after minor trauma, easy bruising, hemarthrosis (bleeding into joints — knees, ankles, elbows), and prolonged PTT with normal PT and normal platelet count. Hemophilia A is X-linked recessive deficiency of Factor VIII. Severity: mild (5-40% FVIII), moderate (1-5%), severe (<1%). PTT is prolonged (intrinsic pathway), PT normal (extrinsic pathway intact), platelets normal. Mixing study: PTT corrects (rules out inhibitor). Factor VIII assay confirms low activity. Treatment: factor VIII concentrate (recombinant preferred) for bleeding episodes or prophylaxis. Desmopressin (DDAVP) for mild hemophilia A (releases stored VIII and vWF). Avoid aspirin, NSAIDs, IM injections. Genetic counseling (X-linked).
166.clinical_tip: Hemophilia A (Factor VIII Deficiency) — follow CCS review orders.
166.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Hemophilia A (Factor VIII Deficiency).

patient_voice.pain: Chronic nausea, vomiting undigested food hours later

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with nausea and vomiting.
Abdominal tenderness pattern matches history; no rigid abdomen documented yet.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
167.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a diabetic patient presenting with chronic nausea, vomiting of undigested food eaten hours earlier, early satiety, bloating, and erratic blood glucose control. Diabetic gastroparesis is delayed gastric emptying due to autonomic neuropathy — vagus nerve damage from chronic hyperglycemia. Diagnosis: gastric emptying study (scintigraphy) — delayed emptying of radiolabeled meal. Upper endoscopy to rule out obstruction. Treatment: glycemic control (most important). Dietary: small frequent meals, low-fiber, low-fat. Medications: prokinetics — metoclopramide (first-line, watch for EPS/tardive dyskinesia, limit to 12 weeks), erythromycin, domperidone. Antiemetics: ondansetron. Severe refractory: gastric electrical stimulator, jejunostomy tube.
167.clinical_tip: Diabetic Gastroparesis — follow CCS review orders.
167.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Diabetic Gastroparesis.

hard.intro: Chronic nausea, vomiting undigested food hours later
hard.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a diabetic patient presenting with chronic nausea, vomiting of undigested food eaten hours earlier, early satiety, bloating, and erratic blood glucose control. Diabetic gastroparesis is delayed gastric emptying due to autonomic neuropathy — vagus nerve damage from chronic hyperglycemia. Diagnosis: gastric emptying study (scintigraphy) — delayed emptying of radiolabeled meal. Upper endoscopy to rule out obstruction. Treatment: glycemic control (most important). Dietary: small frequent meals, low-fiber, low-fat. Medications: prokinetics — metoclopramide (first-line, watch for EPS/tardive dyskinesia, limit to 12 weeks), erythromycin, domperidone. Antiemetics: ondansetron. Severe refractory: gastric electrical stimulator, jejunostomy tube.

169.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive somnolence, confusion, fatigue, constipation, polyuria, polydipsia, and nausea. Labs: elevated calcium (>11), low PTH (rules out primary hyperparathyroidism), elevated PTHrP. Hypercalcemia of malignancy is the most common cause of hypercalcemia in hospitalized patients. Mechanisms: PTHrP secretion (squamous cell cancers — lung, head/neck), osteolytic bone metastases (breast, multiple myeloma), excess 1,25-vitamin D (lymphoma). Treatment: aggressive IV normal saline (3-4L/day) to promote calciuresis. Then IV bisphosphonates (zoledronic acid or pamidronate — inhibit osteoclast activity). Calcitonin for rapid short-term reduction. Denosumab if refractory. Treat underlying malignancy. Monitor for arrhythmias (shortened QT on ECG).
169.clinical_tip: Hypercalcemia Secondary to Malignancy — follow CCS review orders.
169.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Hypercalcemia Secondary to Malignancy.

170.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with recurrent falls, dizziness, lightheadedness, and near-syncope upon standing (within 3 min of standing). Orthostatic hypotension = drop in SBP ≥20mmHg or DBP ≥10mmHg within 3 min of standing. Causes: medications (antihypertensives — especially alpha-blockers, diuretics, nitrates, TCAs, dopaminergics), hypovolemia, autonomic neuropathy (DM, Parkinson's), prolonged bed rest. Workup: orthostatic vital signs, medication review, CBC (anemia), BMP (dehydration, electrolyte), EKG, consider autonomic testing. Treatment: review and adjust medications. Non-pharmacologic: increase fluid/salt intake (if no CHF), compression stockings, elevate head of bed, slow position changes, avoid prolonged standing. If needed: fludrocortisone (mineralocorticoid — expand volume) or midodrine (alpha-1 agonist).

172.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents after attempted hanging. Initial priorities: ABCs — airway management critical (laryngeal injury, edema, fracture). C-spine immobilization (associated cervical spine injury from hanging drop/jerk). Assess for: ligature marks on neck, stridor, dysphonia, subcutaneous emphysema. patient_voice.chief_complaint: I've been vomiting blood and my stools have been black. I'm terrified.

patient_voice.pain: My belly feels full and I'm weak and dizzy when I stand up.

exam: Ill-appearing; assess for shock, jaundice, cachexia, and stigmata of chronic liver disease.
Tachycardia; evaluate for hypotension indicating hypovolemia.
Evaluate for respiratory distress or aspiration.
Assess for ascites, splenomegaly, or tenderness suggesting portal hypertension.
Alert unless encephalopathy or perfusion compromise; watch for hepatic encephalopathy after bleed.

He is found to have severe anemia (Hct 24%, Hgb 8.0 g/dL), mild coagulopathy (INR 1.8), and thrombocytopenia (platelets 100,000). Evaluate for upper GI bleeding from portal hypertension — esophageal varices are the leading concern.
174.clinical_tip: Bleeding esophageal varices — follow CCS review orders.

175.title: Heavy Menstrual Bleeding

patient_voice.chief_complaint: My periods are extremely heavy — I'm soaking through pads every hour
patient_voice.history: This started around when my periods began. I've been tired and bruise easily. My gums bleed when I brush.
patient_voice.pain: Cramping with the heavy flow — I'm also dizzy when I stand up

exam: Assess pallor and signs of acute blood loss.
Look for mucosal bleeding — epistaxis, gum bleeding.
Bruising or petechiae suggesting bleeding disorder.
Tachycardia or hypotension from blood loss.
Rule out other causes of bleeding or pain.
Chief complaint — assess pelvic bleeding source.
175.hpi_narrative:
{{patient_name}} is a young woman presenting to the ED with heavy menstrual bleeding. Classic vWD at menarche: anemia on CBC with normal platelets; PT normal, mildly elevated PTT, normal fibrinogen; decreased ristocetin-induced platelet aggregation.

Workup: CBC/hemoglobin; PT/PTT; platelet aggregation; TSH (rule out hypothyroid menorrhagia); pelvic/genital exam; vWF activity or hematology consult (confirmatory labs take 3 days).

Acute treatment: IV fluids for hypovolemia (Hgb ~10 — not transfusion threshold); DDAVP and tranexamic acid together for mucosal bleeding; iron for anemia. Long-term: hormonal therapy or OB/GYN consult; avoid NSAIDs and contact sports until diagnosis confirmed.

Acute treatment: IV fluids for hypovolemia (Hgb ~10 — not transfusion threshold); DDAVP and tranexamic acid together for mucosal bleeding; iron for anemia. Long-term: hormonal therapy or OB/GYN consult; avoid NSAIDs and contact sports until diagnosis confirmed.

181.diagnosis: Severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea with Secondary Nocturnal Enuresis

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Nocturnal enuresis, loud snoring, daytime fatigue
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with primary or secondary nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting), loud snoring, restless sleep, daytime fatigue, and behavioral issues. Severe OSA causes nocturnal enuresis through…
patient_voice.pain: Nocturnal enuresis, loud snoring, daytime fatigue

exam: Decreased engagement and cognitive change compared with reported baseline.
Abdominal tenderness pattern matches history; no rigid abdomen documented yet.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Warm skin with fever; no purpura on initial survey.
181.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with primary or secondary nocturnal enuresis (bedwetting), loud snoring, restless sleep, daytime fatigue, and behavioral issues. Severe OSA causes nocturnal enuresis through: (1) increased intra-abdominal pressure during apnea → increased venous return → ANP/BNP release → increased nocturnal urine production; (2) disrupted sleep architecture → decreased arousal to bladder distention. Polysomnography confirms severe OSA (AHI >30). Treatment: CPAP or adenotonsillectomy if large tonsils/adenoids. Treating the OSA often resolves the enuresis. Do NOT treat enuresis in isolation without evaluating for sleep-disordered breathing.
181.clinical_tip: Severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea with Secondary Nocturnal Enuresis — follow CCS review orders.
181.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Severe Obstructive Sleep Apnea with Secondary Nocturnal Enuresis.

001.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents to the emergency department with acute onset chest pain and severe respiratory distress. The patient appears diaphoretic, tachypneic, and in extremis. Symptoms began suddenly with rapid progression. Exam reveals unilateral absence of breath sounds, tracheal deviation, and hyperresonance on percussion. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis made at the bedside — immediate intervention is critical and must not be delayed for imaging.

interventions.label: Electrocardiography, 12 lead
interventions.why: Initial EKG to rule out myocardial infarction.

interventions.label: Cardiac troponin I, serum
interventions.why: Troponins should be evaluated — patient has chest pain, MI must be ruled out.

interventions.label: Thoracentesis
interventions.why: Good diagnostic step to confirm tension pneumothorax. However, chest tube must follow to prevent recurrence.

interventions.label: Tube thoracostomy / Needle thoracostomy
interventions.why: Chest tube should be placed after needle thoracostomy and placed to suction.

interventions.label: Chest X-ray (post-procedure)
interventions.why: X-ray verifies chest tube placement AFTER insertion. Do NOT diagnose by X-ray — tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. Imaging before tube placement loses points.

decoys.label: Chest X-ray (before intervention)
decoys.why: Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis. Imaging before decompression causes dangerous delay.

decoys.label: CT chest with contrast
decoys.why: CT causes unacceptable delay in a life-threatening emergency.

decoys.label: Echocardiogram
decoys.why: Too time-consuming. Immediate decompression is the priority.

decoys.label: D-dimer, serum
decoys.why: While PE is on the differential, exam findings point to tension pneumothorax. Decompress first.

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Altered mental status following fall
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient with a history of chronic alcoholism who presents to the emergency department with altered mental status following a recent fall. The patient has had episodic c…
patient_voice.pain: Altered mental status following fall

002.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 11:00 Temperature: 36.8 C (98.2 degrees F) Pulse: 88 beats/min. Regular rhythm Respiratory rate: 18 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 115 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 85 mm Hg Height: 180cm (70.9 in) Weight: 91.0 kg (200.6 lb) Body Mass Index: 27.9 kg/m2
exam: Fluctuating level of consciousness. Assess for lateralizing signs, pupil asymmetry, and GCS. Focal deficits may indicate mass effect from expanding hematoma.
Assess for signs of head trauma or skull fracture.
Altered mental status — differentiate from psychiatric etiology.
002.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient with a history of chronic alcoholism who presents to the emergency department with altered mental status following a recent fall. The patient has had episodic confusion and fluctuating consciousness since the fall. The subdural hematoma risk is elevated due to advanced age and chronic alcohol use, both of which contribute to brain atrophy and increased tension on bridging veins. Time is critical — expanding hematoma may cause mass effect and progressive neurological deterioration.
002.clinical_tip: Subdural Hematoma — follow CCS review orders.
002.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Subdural Hematoma.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: The general examination is extremely useful to determine how sick the patient looks.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
interventions.why: It's important to look for lung pathology.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
interventions.why: It's important to look for abdominal pathology.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Neuro / Psych
interventions.why: This is the patient's chief complaint — neurologic exam is essential.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: CBC is always a good screening tool in nearly every patient.

interventions.label: TSH, serum
interventions.why: TSH screens for abnormal thyroid levels which could contribute to altered mental status.

interventions.label: CT of head without contrast
interventions.why: CT without contrast is the order of choice. With possible head trauma, rule out intracranial bleed. CT with contrast makes it difficult to distinguish contrast from hemorrhage. CT preferred for speed; MRI more sensitive but slower.

interventions.label: Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive metabolic profile / Liver function panel
interventions.why: Chemistries are an important screening tool to reach a diagnosis.

interventions.label: Consult, surgery, neurologic / Craniotomy
interventions.why: Neurosurgery should be consulted to evacuate the subdural hematoma. Craniotomy for evacuation.

decoys.label: CT, head, with contrast
decoys.why: CT with contrast makes it difficult to distinguish between contrast enhancement and intracranial hemorrhage. Non-contrast CT is the correct choice for suspected bleed.

decoys.label: CT head with contrast
decoys.why: Contrast makes it difficult to distinguish blood from enhancement. Non-contrast CT is required for suspected intracranial hemorrhage.

decoys.label: Lumbar puncture
decoys.why: LP is contraindicated with suspected mass effect from intracranial hemorrhage — risk of herniation.

decoys.label: EEG
decoys.why: While seizure is on the differential, CT head takes priority given history of fall and AMS.
