003.title: Pelvic Pain

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Severe pelvic pain, worse with intercourse
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is a reproductive-age woman who presents with severe pelvic pain that worsens with sexual activity. The pain is localized to the right adnexal region. Differential for a right adnexa…
patient_voice.pain: Severe pelvic pain, worse with intercourse

003.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 9:00 Temperature: 37.0 C (98.6 degrees F) Pulse: 110 beat/min, Tachycardic Respiratory rate: 22 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 140 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 92 mm Hg Height: 175.3 cm (69.0 in) Weight: 65.8 kg (145 lb) Body Mass Index: 21.4 kg/m2
exam: Patient in moderate distress from pelvic pain.
Lower abdominal tenderness. Pelvic pathology can present with abdominal symptoms.
Right adnexal mass. Pelvic exam indicated — source of pain is pelvic. Cervical motion tenderness assessment needed.
003.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a reproductive-age woman who presents with severe pelvic pain that worsens with sexual activity. The pain is localized to the right adnexal region. Differential for a right adnexal mass in a reproductive-age female is broad and includes ectopic pregnancy, tuboovarian abscess, inflammatory bowel disease, ovarian mass, endometrioma, theca lutein cysts, and germ cell neoplasms. Imaging and appropriate surgical consultation are required.
003.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Endometrioma.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: The general examination is extremely useful to determine how sick the patient looks.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
interventions.why: It's important to rule out any lung issues such as metastatic disease.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
interventions.why: Abdominal pathology can present as pelvic pain. Example: inflammatory bowel disease.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Genitalia
interventions.why: Important since the source of pain is coming from the pelvic area.

interventions.label: CT/MRI/US abdomen/pelvis
interventions.why: CT would give diagnosis of endometrioma. Pelvic US (transvaginal) is typically first-line.

interventions.label: Laparotomy / Laparoscopy / Consult OB/GYN
interventions.why: The endometrioma should be surgically removed. OB/GYN consult is appropriate.

interventions.label: Instruct patient, smoking cessation
interventions.why: One of the most important things patients can do for their health is to stop smoking.

interventions.label: Advise patient, no illegal drug use
interventions.why: Good opportunity to discuss the medical effects of cannabis use.

decoys.label: Appendectomy
decoys.why: While appendicitis can present with RLQ pain, imaging shows adnexal mass consistent with endometrioma. Gynecologic consult is correct.

decoys.label: Broad-spectrum antibiotics (without culture)
decoys.why: No evidence of infection. Tuboovarian abscess is on the differential but imaging should guide therapy.

decoys.label: Discharge home without follow-up
decoys.why: Patient has a surgical adnexal mass requiring OB/GYN consultation and likely operative management.

004.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a 22-year-old woman with no known past medical history who presents to the emergency department with diffuse abdominal pain, lethargy, and vomiting for two days. She reports increased appetite prior to symptom onset, along with blurry vision, dizziness, drowsiness, and polyuria. She is on oral contraceptives and has a family history of diabetes in a sibling. Exam reveals dry mucous membranes, decreased skin turgor, and tachycardia. Point-of-care glucose is markedly elevated in the 600s. The clinical picture is consistent with new-onset diabetic ketoacidosis — the abdominal pain is a common presenting feature of DKA, not a primary surgical abdomen.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: The general examination is extremely useful to determine how sick the patient looks.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
interventions.why: Patient in moderate distress — important to look for pulmonary problems.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
interventions.why: Patient in moderate distress — important to look for cardiovascular problems.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
interventions.why: This is the presenting chief complaint — abdominal exam is required.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Genitalia
interventions.why: Pelvic pain can present as abdominal pain — should be examined.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: HEENT / Neck
interventions.why: Will show dry mucous membranes — key finding in DKA.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Skin
interventions.why: Will show low skin turgor from dehydration.

interventions.label: HCG, beta, urine/serum qualitative
interventions.why: Every female patient of childbearing age should have a pregnancy test done.

interventions.label: Hemoglobin A1C, blood
interventions.why: Expected to be elevated with new-onset diabetes. Not required for acute management.

interventions.label: Arterial blood gases
interventions.why: ABGs are not required in DKA. Bicarbonate levels and anion gap are sufficient to monitor correction. Best way to monitor DKA resolution is disappearance of elevated anion gap.

interventions.label: Urinalysis
interventions.why: Important to see extent of chronic diabetes. Patient spilling protein into urine with normal creatinine.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: Important to rule out infection. Leukocyte count is high — DKA patients often have elevated counts from catecholamine release and dehydration.

interventions.label: Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive metabolic profile
interventions.why: Will find extremely high blood glucose. Important to monitor electrolytes — DKA can cause pseudohypercalcemia.

interventions.label: Insulin (regular / lispro / glargine / NPH)
interventions.why: Mainstay treatment for DKA is insulin. Patient will slowly improve once insulin treatment initiated.

interventions.label: Normal saline / Lactated Ringer / 0.45% saline
interventions.why: IV fluids should be given to every DKA patient. Normal saline or LR if sodium is normal.

interventions.label: Potassium replacement (KCl / K citrate / K phosphate)
interventions.why: Potassium must be checked prior to insulin therapy — insulin worsens pre-existing hypokalemia, risking fatal cardiac arrhythmias. Start replacement if K < 5.3. KCl is preferred as patients are chloride-depleted.

interventions.label: Intravenous access
interventions.why: Good practice to order IV access when administering IV fluids/medications.

interventions.label: Papanicolaou smear / HPV DNA test
interventions.why: Patient has not had a recent pap smear — this should be done.

interventions.label: Tdap vaccine
interventions.why: Tdap should be given every 10 years. No history given — should be administered.

interventions.label: HPV vaccine
interventions.why: HPV vaccine should be given to females ages 11-26.

interventions.label: Advise patient, no illegal drug use
interventions.why: If patient admits to illicit drug use, it is important to advise against use.

interventions.label: Instruct patient, diabetes
interventions.why: Patient needs diabetes education about proper glucose management after discharge.

decoys.label: Dextrose solutions
decoys.why: Patient is already hyperglycemic in the 600s — additional glucose is not warranted. Glucose can be added once levels reach 250 range, but should not be used during initial treatment.

decoys.label: CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast
decoys.why: While abdominal pain warrants investigation, markedly elevated glucose (600s) with anion gap acidosis is diagnostic of DKA. Treat the DKA first — the pain resolves with insulin and fluids.

decoys.label: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
decoys.why: Leukocytosis in DKA is caused by catecholamine release and dehydration, not infection. No evidence of infectious source.

decoys.label: Surgical consult for acute abdomen
decoys.why: Abdominal pain in DKA can mimic acute abdomen but resolves with metabolic correction. Surgery is not indicated.

decoys.label: Dextrose-containing fluids initially
decoys.why: Patient has glucose in the 600s. Dextrose would worsen hyperglycemia. Only add dextrose once glucose reaches ~250 mg/dL.

005.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a 55-year-old woman who presents with fever, headache, and progressive ataxia. She has developed pink macular lesions on the left thigh. interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: The general examination is extremely useful to determine how sick the patient looks.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
interventions.why: Important to look for lung pathology in a febrile patient.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
interventions.why: Important to look for abdominal pathology in a febrile patient.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Neuro / Psych
interventions.why: This is the patient's chief complaint — neurologic exam is essential.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Skin
interventions.why: This will reveal pink macular lesions on the left thigh — characteristic rash.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: Important to order a CBC with differential in a patient with fever.

interventions.label: Chest X-ray
interventions.why: Important to get a chest X-ray to rule out pneumonia and other causes of fever.

interventions.label: Urinalysis
interventions.why: Important to get urinalysis to rule out bacterial infection and other causes of fever.

interventions.label: Toxicology screen, urine
interventions.why: Urine tox screen is important as illicit drugs can cause fever.

interventions.label: Bacterial culture, blood
interventions.why: Blood culture will aid in localizing the source of infection.

interventions.label: MRI/CT head
interventions.why: Ataxia should lead to consideration of neurological infection or stroke. Brain imaging to rule out stroke or tumor. MRI preferred (more sensitive for West Nile abnormalities) but CT acceptable.

interventions.label: Lumbar puncture
interventions.why: Lumbar puncture is essential for evaluation of patient with ataxia and fever.

interventions.label: Protein, cerebrospinal fluid
interventions.why: CSF analysis is important in patient with fever and neurological signs.

interventions.label: Fungal culture, cerebrospinal fluid
interventions.why: Important to culture CSF for viral, bacterial, and fungal etiologies.

interventions.label: Viral culture, cerebrospinal fluid
interventions.why: Important to culture CSF. Note: West Nile virus is frequently negative in viral culture.

interventions.label: Bacterial culture, cerebrospinal fluid
interventions.why: Important to culture CSF for bacterial etiologies.

interventions.label: Glucose, cerebrospinal fluid
interventions.why: CSF glucose points toward fungal, viral, or bacterial picture. Normal glucose suggests viral (not bacterial) etiology.

interventions.label: Cell count, cerebrospinal fluid
interventions.why: CSF cell count consistent with aseptic meningitis. Lymphocytic predominance suggests viral etiology.

interventions.label: West Nile virus antibody, CSF/serum
interventions.why: Confirms aseptic meningitis is from West Nile virus.

interventions.label: HSV PCR, CSF/serum
interventions.why: Aseptic meningitis workup should include herpes simplex screening.

interventions.label: Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive metabolic profile / Liver function panel
interventions.why: Chemistries are an important screening tool and should be done in nearly every non-emergent patient.

interventions.label: Tdap vaccine
interventions.why: Tdap should be given every 10 years. No history given — should be administered.

interventions.label: Papanicolaou smear
interventions.why: HPV DNA test every 3 years for women ≥30 with normal cytology. No history given — should be scheduled.

interventions.label: Mammography
interventions.why: USPSTF recommends mammogram screening every 2 years for patients ages 50-69.

decoys.label: Empiric antibiotics without LP
decoys.why: Bacterial meningitis is on the differential and requires CSF culture before antibiotics. But this is viral encephalitis — LP is diagnostic, not empiric.

decoys.label: Corticosteroids
decoys.why: No evidence for steroids in West Nile encephalitis. Supportive care is the mainstay.

decoys.label: Discharge from office
decoys.why: Patient with encephalitis requires inpatient monitoring. West Nile can progress to flaccid paralysis and respiratory failure.

006.title: Rash and Lethargy

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Fever, rash, and lethargy
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is a 6-year-old child who presents with fever, sore throat, malaise, and generalized rash. Exam reveals posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, palatal petechiae, and splenomegaly. The c…
patient_voice.pain: Fever, rash, and lethargy

exam: Febrile, lethargic child. Sore throat, malaise.
Splenomegaly — classic finding in mononucleosis. Palpable spleen tip.
Maculopapular rash — characteristic of EBV infection.
Posterior cervical lymphadenopathy. Palatal petechiae. Pharyngeal erythema with tonsillar exudates.
006.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a 6-year-old child who presents with fever, sore throat, malaise, and generalized rash. Exam reveals posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, palatal petechiae, and splenomegaly. The combination of pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, fever, and the characteristic maculopapular rash is classic for infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus. The differential includes other viral infections (CMV, acute HIV), streptococcal pharyngitis, and toxoplasmosis. Key management considerations: avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin (causes characteristic EBV rash), avoid aspirin (Reye syndrome risk in febrile children), and in older patients, restrict contact sports to prevent splenic rupture.
006.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Mononucleosis.

interventions.why: Always important to verify oxygenation in a febrile patient.

interventions.label: Sedimentation rate, erythrocyte
interventions.why: Not required, but ESR would be elevated in EBV.

interventions.label: Mononucleosis screening / EBV serology
interventions.why: Heterophil antibody (Monospot) or EBV-specific serology confirms the diagnosis.

interventions.label: Basic metabolic profile / LFTs
interventions.why: BMPs are excellent screening tools. LFTs may show elevated transaminases in EBV hepatitis.

interventions.label: Acetaminophen / Ibuprofen
interventions.why: Tylenol or ibuprofen for fever reduction. Symptomatic management.

interventions.label: Advise patient, no aspirin
interventions.why: Important to tell caregiver not to give aspirin to the febrile child.

decoys.label: Aspirin, therapy
decoys.why: Administering aspirin to a febrile child is associated with Reye's syndrome. Contraindicated.

decoys.label: Amoxicillin / Ampicillin
decoys.why: In EBV, amoxicillin and ampicillin cause a characteristic morbilliform rash. Viral infection — antibiotics ineffective. Especially avoid these two.

decoys.label: Aspirin
decoys.why: Associated with Reye's syndrome in febrile children. Use acetaminophen or ibuprofen instead.

decoys.label: CT abdomen
decoys.why: Splenomegaly diagnosis is clinical. CT not indicated unless splenic rupture suspected.

easy.intro: Case Introduction Day 1 @ 9:00 Office A 6-year-old boy presents to your office with complaints of 3 days of lethargy and a rash.
easy.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a 6-year-old child who presents with fever, sore throat, malaise, and generalized rash. Exam reveals posterior cervical lymphadenopathy, palatal petechiae, and splenomegaly. The combination of pharyngitis, lymphadenopathy, fever, and the characteristic maculopapular rash is classic for infectious mononucleosis caused by Epstein-Barr virus. The differential includes other viral infections (CMV, acute HIV), streptococcal pharyngitis, and toxoplasmosis. Key management considerations: avoid amoxicillin/ampicillin (causes characteristic EBV rash), avoid aspirin (Reye syndrome risk in febrile children), and in older patients, restrict contact sports to prevent splenic rupture.

007.title: Generalized Weakness

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Progressive weakness, ptosis, dysphagia, dysarthria
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is a woman of childbearing age who presents with progressive generalized weakness that worsens with continued muscle use and improves with rest. She has developed ptosis, dysarthria,…
patient_voice.pain: Progressive weakness, ptosis, dysphagia, dysarthria

007.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 9:00 Temperature: 37.0 C (98.6 degrees F) Pulse: 110 beat/min, Regular rhythm; bounding Respiratory rate: 18 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 122 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 74 mm Hg Height: 175.3 cm (69.0 in) Weight: 65.8 kg (145 lb) Body Mass Index: 21.4 kg/m2
exam: Generalized fatigable weakness. Worsens with continued use, improves with rest.
Hypoventilation from respiratory muscle weakness. Decreased oxygen saturation. Monitor for myasthenic crisis.

Ptosis (eyelid drooping). Dysarthria. Dysphagia. Proximal asymmetric limb weakness. Fatigable weakness — repeat muscle testing worsens performance. Sensation and reflexes preserved. Differentiates from Lambert-Eaton and neuropathy.
Mild ptosis. Facial muscle weakness may affect chewing and speech.
007.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a woman of childbearing age who presents with progressive generalized weakness that worsens with continued muscle use and improves with rest. She has developed ptosis, dysarthria, and dysphagia. Respiratory muscle involvement is present with mild hypoxemia from hypoventilation. Exam reveals fatigable weakness with preservation of sensation and reflexes — the hallmark of myasthenia gravis. The underlying pathophysiology is autoimmune antibody-mediated destruction of postsynaptic acetylcholine receptors at the neuromuscular junction. CT chest is essential to evaluate for thymoma, which is present in 10-15% of MG patients and whose resection can lead to remission in ~85%.
007.clinical_tip: Myasthenia Gravis with Thymoma — follow CCS review orders.
007.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Myasthenia Gravis with Thymoma.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: Determine how sick the patient looks.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
interventions.why: Investigate for lung pathology — respiratory muscle weakness can cause hypoventilation.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
interventions.why: Investigate for cardiac pathology.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
interventions.why: Quick abdominal exam.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Genitalia
interventions.why: Pelvic pain can present as abdominal pain — should be examined.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: HEENT / Neck
interventions.why: Will show mild ptosis — key finding in MG.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Skin
interventions.why: Look for rashes suggestive of autoimmune disease.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Extremities / Spine
interventions.why: Look for edema or abnormalities given weakness symptoms.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Neuro / Psych
interventions.why: Neurological symptoms guide testing — fatigable weakness with preserved sensation and reflexes.

interventions.label: Chest X-ray
interventions.why: Not required, but would be abnormal. May show anterior mediastinal mass.

interventions.label: CT chest with contrast / MRI chest
interventions.why: CT chest is essential to rule out thymoma, seen in 10-15% of MG patients. Thymoma appears as anterior mediastinal mass.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: Good screening tool in nearly every patient.

interventions.label: ECG, 12 lead
interventions.why: Generalized weakness can be cardiac. ECG rules out cardiac etiologies.

interventions.label: Pulse oximetry
interventions.why: Oxygenation is lower than usual — likely from hypoventilation due to respiratory muscle weakness.

interventions.label: Sedimentation rate, erythrocyte
interventions.why: Not required but would be abnormal in autoimmune disease.

interventions.label: HCG, beta (pregnancy test)
interventions.why: All female patients of childbearing age should have pregnancy test before imaging and treatment.

interventions.label: TSH, serum
interventions.why: Hypothyroidism is associated with generalized weakness — important to screen.

interventions.label: Acetylcholine receptor antibody, serum
interventions.why: Positive detection strongly supports MG diagnosis. ~80% positive in generalized MG.

interventions.label: Electromyography
interventions.why: EMG with repetitive stimulation shows decremental response — decreased signal with each stimulation. Differentiates from Lambert-Eaton (which shows incremental response).

interventions.label: Tensilon test
interventions.why: Not required but would be positive in MG. Edrophonium temporarily improves muscle strength.

interventions.label: PT/PTT / INR
interventions.why: Patient is likely to have surgery (thymectomy) — pre-surgical labs needed.

interventions.label: Type and screen / Type and Rh
interventions.why: Pre-surgical labs for potential thymectomy.

interventions.label: Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive metabolic profile / LFTs
interventions.why: BMPs are excellent screening tools in any differential.

interventions.label: Methylprednisolone / Prednisone / Azathioprine
interventions.why: Corticosteroids and azathioprine are first-line immunosuppressive treatments for MG.

interventions.label: Pyridostigmine / Neostigmine
interventions.why: Pyridostigmine is for symptomatic treatment only — acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases ACh at neuromuscular junction. Does NOT treat underlying disease. Use in conjunction with immunosuppressants.

interventions.label: Consult surgery / Thymectomy
interventions.why: Thymoma should be surgically removed. Thymectomy can lead to complete remission in ~85% of patients without further medication.

interventions.label: IVIG / Plasmapheresis
interventions.why: Can be used pre-thymectomy for severe symptoms. However, expensive — conservative trial of steroids + pyridostigmine first is reasonable if patient is stable.

interventions.label: Instruct patient, smoking cessation
interventions.why: One of the most important things for health — address smoking.

interventions.label: Advise patient, safe sex techniques
interventions.why: Patient has history of STIs — review safe sex practices.

interventions.label: Reassure patient
interventions.why: New chronic diagnosis causes anxiety — reassure and inform.

interventions.label: Papanicolaou smear
interventions.why: HPV DNA test every 3 years for women ≥30. No history given — should be scheduled.

interventions.label: Tdap vaccine
interventions.why: Tdap every 10 years. No history given — should be administered.

decoys.label: Intubation / mechanical ventilation (too early)
decoys.why: Patient has respiratory muscle weakness but intubation is invasive and can often be avoided with medical management of MG first.

decoys.label: Pyridostigmine as monotherapy
decoys.why: Pyridostigmine only treats symptoms. In a patient with respiratory involvement, immunosuppression (steroids/azathioprine) is needed to treat the underlying autoimmune process. Pyridostigmine also increases airway secretions.

008.title: Burning During Urination

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Dysuria, fevers, chills
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is a 19-year-old sexually active man who presents with dysuria, fevers, and chills. Rectal exam reveals an edematous, tender prostate — the key finding that localizes the infection t…
patient_voice.pain: Dysuria, fevers, chills

008.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 9:00 Temperature: 38.3 C (101.0 degrees F) Pulse: 89 beat/min, Regular rhythm Respiratory rate: 20 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 122 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 74 mm Hg Height: 183cm (72.0 in) Weight: 97.5 kg (215 lb) Body Mass Index: 29.1 kg/m2
exam: Suprapubic tenderness may be present. No CVA tenderness (rules out pyelonephritis).
Dysuria. Urethral discharge absent. Testicular exam normal.
Edematous, tender prostate on digital rectal exam — pathognomonic for prostatitis. CAUTION: do not perform vigorous prostate massage — risk of bacteremia.
008.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a 19-year-old sexually active man who presents with dysuria, fevers, and chills. Rectal exam reveals an edematous, tender prostate — the key finding that localizes the infection to the prostate rather than the bladder or urethra alone. He denies flank pain or CVA tenderness (making pyelonephritis less likely). The differential includes cystitis, urethritis, pyelonephritis, and sexually transmitted infections (Chlamydia, gonorrhea). E. coli accounts for approximately one-third of prostatitis cases. Fluoroquinolones are the treatment of choice due to their ability to penetrate the inflamed prostate.
008.clinical_tip: Prostatitis (E. coli) — follow CCS review orders.
008.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Prostatitis (E. coli).

interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: Determine how sick the patient looks.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
interventions.why: Investigate for lung pathology.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
interventions.why: Investigate for cardiac pathology.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
interventions.why: Urinary problems could be caused by abdominal pathology.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Genitalia
interventions.why: Chief complaint — genital exam essential.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Rectal
interventions.why: Edematous, tender prostate on DRE — key finding that localizes infection to prostate.

interventions.label: Urinalysis
interventions.why: Quick diagnostic tool. Shows pyuria, bacteriuria.

interventions.label: Gram stain, urine, unspun
interventions.why: Guides antibiotic treatment by identifying organism class (gram-negative rods = E. coli).

interventions.label: Chlamydia testing (DNA probe / DFA / culture)
interventions.why: In any suspected prostatitis, rule out STIs — Chlamydia must be excluded.

interventions.label: Gonorrhea testing (DNA probe / culture)
interventions.why: In any suspected urethritis/prostatitis, rule out gonorrhea.

interventions.label: Bacterial culture, urine
interventions.why: Before antibiotic treatment, always get urine culture. Confirms organism and sensitivities.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: CBC important in febrile patient. Leukocytosis expected.

interventions.label: Pulse oximetry
interventions.why: In any febrile patient, know oxygenation status.

interventions.label: Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive metabolic profile
interventions.why: BMPs are excellent screening tools.

interventions.label: Ciprofloxacin / TMP-SMX / Levofloxacin
interventions.why: Fluoroquinolones are first-line for prostatitis — excellent penetration of inflamed prostate. TMP-SMX is alternative. Treat 14-28 days for chronic bacterial prostatitis.

interventions.label: Advise patient, drive with seat belt
interventions.why: Emphasize seat belt use — common cause of death in young adults.

interventions.label: Advise patient, safe sex techniques
interventions.why: Patient has history of risky sexual practices — review safe sex to prevent future STIs.

interventions.label: Reassure patient
interventions.why: Reassuring the patient is good medicine.

interventions.label: Tdap vaccine
interventions.why: Tdap every 10 years. No history given — should be administered.

interventions.label: Meningococcal vaccine
interventions.why: College-age patient should receive meningitis vaccine.

decoys.label: Blood culture
decoys.why: Patient does not meet SIRS criteria. Blood cultures not necessary for uncomplicated prostatitis without sepsis.

decoys.label: Vigorous prostate massage
decoys.why: Can cause bacteremia. Gentle DRE is sufficient for diagnosis.

decoys.label: Ceftriaxone as sole therapy
decoys.why: Ceftriaxone does not adequately penetrate the prostate. Fluoroquinolones are the treatment of choice.

exam: RLQ tenderness. Assess for rebound, guarding. Post-surgical setting — concern for abscess.
009.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a young woman with recent appendectomy who presents to the inpatient unit with RLQ abdominal pain, fever, tachycardia, nausea, and vomiting. interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: Determine how sick the patient looks.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
interventions.why: Investigate for lung pathology — sometimes presents as abdominal pain.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
interventions.why: Investigate for cardiac pathology. Tachycardia noted.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
interventions.why: Chief complaint — RLQ tenderness, assess for peritoneal signs.

interventions.label: Bacterial culture, blood
interventions.why: Fever + tachycardia after abdominal surgery is concerning — blood culture warranted prior to antibiotics.

interventions.label: Bacterial culture, urine
interventions.why: Abdominal pain — urine culture to rule out GU pathology prior to antibiotics.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: Important in febrile patient. Leukocytosis supports infection.

interventions.label: Chest X-ray
interventions.why: Lung pathology can present as abdominal pain — rule out.

interventions.label: Urinalysis
interventions.why: Rule out bacterial infection and other causes of fever.

interventions.label: Bacterial culture, abscess
interventions.why: Culture of drained abscess confirms organism and guides antibiotic therapy.

interventions.label: Gram stain, abscess
interventions.why: Gram stain provides early guidance for antibiotic selection before culture results.

interventions.label: Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive metabolic profile / LFTs
interventions.why: Chemistries are important screening tool.

interventions.label: CT abdomen/pelvis with contrast
interventions.why: CT with IV contrast is preferred for abdominal pathology — will reveal intra-abdominal abscess.

interventions.label: Normal saline / Lactated Ringer
interventions.why: Low sodium, nausea/vomiting — IV fluids indicated for resuscitation.

interventions.label: Analgesia (Hydromorphone / Fentanyl / Morphine / Ketorolac)
interventions.why: Patient is in pain — treat. Nauseous, so IV route appropriate.

interventions.label: Broad-spectrum antibiotics (Meropenem / Pip-Tazo / Cipro + Metronidazole / Cefepime + Metronidazole)
interventions.why: Empiric antimicrobials with broad-spectrum activity against gram-negatives, anaerobes, and enterococci for high-severity community-acquired intra-abdominal infection.

interventions.label: Antiemetic (Ondansetron / Metoclopramide / Promethazine)
interventions.why: Patient is nauseous — treat symptomatically.

interventions.label: Acetaminophen
interventions.why: Patient is febrile. Ibuprofen/NSAIDs not ideal after recent surgery and upcoming procedure.

interventions.label: Needle drainage, abscess, imaging guided
interventions.why: First step: percutaneous image-guided drainage. Avoids difficult laparotomy, anesthesia, wound complications, and reduces hospitalization length. Open laparotomy is excessive — less invasive first.

interventions.label: Intravenous access
interventions.why: Good practice for IV fluids/medications.

interventions.label: Advise patient, safe sex techniques
interventions.why: Patient is sexually active — review safe sex practices.

interventions.label: Instruct patient, smoking cessation
interventions.why: One of the most important health interventions — excellent opportunity.

interventions.label: Papanicolaou smear / HPV DNA test
interventions.why: Patient has not had recent pap smear — should be scheduled.

decoys.label: Open laparotomy (first-line)
decoys.why: Percutaneous drainage is preferred — less invasive, avoids laparotomy morbidity, reduces hospitalization. Open only if percutaneous approach fails or necrotic tissue present.

decoys.label: NSAIDs (ibuprofen/ketorolac)
decoys.why: Patient recently had surgery and needs another procedure — increased bleeding risk. Acetaminophen preferred for fever.

decoys.label: Discharge from ED
decoys.why: Intra-abdominal abscess requires inpatient monitoring. Percutaneous drainage + IV antibiotics + observation.

010.title: Pain in Legs

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Bilateral leg pain on exertion, relieved by rest
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is a middle-aged man with multiple cardiovascular risk factors — hypertension, hyperlipidemia, newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, and smoking — who presents with bilateral leg pain on …
patient_voice.pain: Bilateral leg pain on exertion, relieved by rest

exam: Diminished peripheral pulses. Assess for bruits (carotid, femoral). Hypertension.

Rule out neurogenic claudication (spinal stenosis) vs vascular claudication. Vascular: pain with exertion, relieved quickly by rest. Neurogenic: pain with standing/walking, relieved by sitting/leaning forward.
010.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a middle-aged man with multiple cardiovascular risk factors — hypertension, hyperlipidemia, newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes, and smoking — who presents with bilateral leg pain on exertion that is relieved by rest (intermittent claudication). He has diminished peripheral pulses and cool extremities. The ankle-brachial index is less than 0.7, consistent with moderate PAD (normal ≥ 1.0, claudication < 0.7, rest pain < 0.4). Importantly, he has intermittent claudication rather than rest pain, which means conservative management is appropriate rather than invasive intervention. The 6 P's of peripheral artery disease are: Pulselessness, Pain, Pallor, Poikilothermia, Paresthesia, and Paralysis.
010.clinical_tip: Intermittent Claudication (Peripheral Artery Disease) — follow CCS review orders.
010.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Intermittent Claudication (Peripheral Artery Disease).

interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: Determine how sick the patient looks.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
interventions.why: Investigate for lung pathology.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
interventions.why: Cardiac pathology could cause leg pain — cardiovascular exam essential.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Extremities / Spine
interventions.why: Chief complaint — examine extremities for pulses, skin changes, temperature.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Neuro / Psych
interventions.why: Neurological issues on differential for leg pain — neuro exam needed.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: Good screening tool.

interventions.label: ECG, 12 lead
interventions.why: Rule out cardiac causes of leg pain. PAD patients often have concomitant CAD.

interventions.label: Hemoglobin A1C, blood
interventions.why: All patients with possible PVD should be evaluated for diabetes.

interventions.label: Lipid profile
interventions.why: Lipids contribute to atherosclerosis — check and treat if abnormal. Goal LDL < 100 in PAD.

interventions.label: Microalbumin, urine (24-hour or spot)
interventions.why: Newly diagnosed type 2 diabetes — screen for early glomerular disease.

interventions.label: Basic metabolic profile / Comprehensive metabolic profile / LFTs
interventions.why: Chemistries are important screening tool.

interventions.label: Ankle-brachial index / Arterial Doppler, lower extremities
interventions.why: ABI is the main diagnostic tool. ABI < 0.7 = claudication. Normal ≥ 1.0. Non-invasive, first-line.

interventions.label: Metformin
interventions.why: First-line therapy for type 2 diabetes. Start at diagnosis.

interventions.label: ACE inhibitor (Lisinopril / Enalapril / Ramipril) or ARB
interventions.why: ACE inhibitors are first-line for hypertensive diabetics — nephroprotective. ARB if ACEI intolerant.

interventions.label: Statin (Atorvastatin / Rosuvastatin / Simvastatin)
interventions.why: Statin for hyperlipidemia — prevents worsening of PVD. Goal LDL < 100 mg/dL.

interventions.label: Aspirin, therapy
interventions.why: Antiplatelet therapy indicated for PAD. Aspirin is most common and most tested. Reduces cardiovascular events.

interventions.label: Instruct patient, smoking cessation
interventions.why: One of the most important interventions — smoking accelerates PVD.

interventions.label: Diet modification (calorie-restricted / diabetic / DASH)
interventions.why: Weight loss to control diabetes and hypertension. DASH diet for hypertension.

interventions.label: Instruct patient, diabetes
interventions.why: Diabetes education increases compliance and improves outcomes.

interventions.label: Advise patient, exercise program
interventions.why: Exercise is excellent for weight loss, glucose control, and collateral circulation development. Supervised walking programs improve claudication symptoms.

decoys.label: Angiography, lower extremity
decoys.why: Invasive test with contrast risks. Conservative management first for intermittent claudication, not rest pain.

decoys.label: Angiography / Arteriography
decoys.why: Invasive, uses contrast (nephrotoxic, allergic reactions), expensive. Conservative management with risk factor modification is first-line for intermittent claudication. Only for rest pain or failed medical therapy.

decoys.label: Surgical bypass / Angioplasty
decoys.why: Not indicated for intermittent claudication. Reserved for rest pain, tissue loss, or disabling symptoms refractory to conservative therapy.

decoys.label: CT angiography
decoys.why: Radiation + iodinated contrast exposure. Duplex ultrasound or ABI is preferred non-invasive screening.

011.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a man who recently returned from a cruise ship and presents with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and shortness of breath. He has RUQ tenderness on exam. LFTs are markedly elevated in the 2000-3000 range. The cruise ship travel and profoundly elevated transaminases are highly suspicious for acute viral hepatitis A (fecal-oral transmission). His episodes of vomiting led to aspiration pneumonia. Acetaminophen level should be checked to rule out overdose as a cause of acute liver injury. Management is supportive: IV fluids, antiemetics, oxygen for hypoxia, and antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia per ATS/IDSA guidelines (treat as community-acquired pneumonia; no anaerobic coverage needed without abscess/empyema). Acetaminophen is contraindicated with hepatic injury. Admit to inpatient unit.
011.clinical_tip: Hepatitis A with Aspiration Pneumonia — follow CCS review orders.
011.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Hepatitis A with Aspiration Pneumonia.

interventions.why: Patient has chest pain — examine heart.

interventions.why: Good screening tool.

interventions.why: Rule out cardiac causes of chest pain.

interventions.label: Chest imaging (X-ray / CT)
interventions.why: Chest imaging will show aspiration pneumonia from vomiting episodes.

interventions.label: Abdominal imaging (US / CT / MRI)
interventions.why: RUQ tenderness — abdominal imaging for further clarification.

interventions.label: Acetaminophen level / Toxicology screen
interventions.why: With very high LFTs, must rule out acetaminophen overdose.

interventions.label: Pulse oximetry
interventions.why: Patient having trouble breathing — check SpO2.

interventions.label: Bacterial culture, sputum
interventions.why: Aspiration pneumonia — sputum culture to guide antibiotics. May be negative (anaerobes); treat empirically.

interventions.label: BMP / CMP / LFTs
interventions.why: LFTs show markedly elevated transaminases (2000-3000). Key diagnostic clue.

interventions.label: Hepatitis panel / HAV IgM & IgG
interventions.why: Cruise ship travel + very high LFTs = high suspicion for viral hepatitis. HAV IgM confirms.

interventions.label: IV fluids (NS / LR)
interventions.why: Low sodium, nausea/vomiting — IV fluids indicated.

interventions.label: Antiemetic (Ondansetron / Metoclopramide)
interventions.why: Patient is nauseous — treat symptomatically.

interventions.label: Oxygen
interventions.why: Low oxygen — supplemental O2.

interventions.label: Analgesia (Hydromorphone / Fentanyl / Morphine)
interventions.why: Treat patient's pain.

interventions.label: Levofloxacin / Moxifloxacin / Penicillin G / Ceftriaxone + Azithromycin
interventions.why: ATS/IDSA guidelines: treat aspiration pneumonia as CAP. Anaerobic coverage NOT needed without abscess/empyema.

interventions.label: Advise patient, no alcohol
interventions.why: Avoid alcohol to prevent further liver damage during recovery.

interventions.label: Follow-up LFTs in 1-4 weeks
interventions.why: Schedule follow-up to monitor downward trajectory of liver enzymes.

decoys.label: Acetaminophen
decoys.why: Acetaminophen with hepatitis and high LFTs is CONTRAINDICATED.

decoys.label: Acetaminophen for pain/fever
decoys.why: Contraindicated with acute hepatitis and elevated LFTs — hepatotoxic.

decoys.label: Tube thoracostomy
decoys.why: Invasive and not indicated for aspiration pneumonia without empyema.

decoys.label: Anaerobic antibiotic coverage (clindamycin / metronidazole)
decoys.why: ATS/IDSA guidelines: treat aspiration pneumonia as CAP without anaerobic coverage unless abscess or empyema present.

012.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a sexually active young adult who presents with dysuria, purulent urethral discharge, and scrotal swelling. The patient admits to illicit drug use and risky sexual practices. Chlamydia trachomatis is the most common bacterial STI — an obligate intracellular pathogen. Co-infection with gonorrhea is common (40% of women, 20% of men), so empiric treatment for both is recommended even if only chlamydia is confirmed. Most cases are asymptomatic (80% women, 50% men), making the presence of overt urethritis clinically useful. First-line diagnosis is NAAT (DNA probe) on first-catch urine. Treatment: azithromycin 1g PO single dose OR doxycycline 100mg PO BID x 7 days. Sexual partners must be treated. Screen for all STIs (gonorrhea, HIV, hepatitis B/C, syphilis, HSV).
012.clinical_tip: Chlamydia Urethritis — follow CCS review orders.
012.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Chlamydia Urethritis.

013.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 18:00 Temperature: 37.2 C (98.9 degrees F) Pulse: 106 beat/min, Tachycardic Respiratory rate: 20 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 114 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 79 mm Hg Height: 160.0 cm (63.0 in) Weight: 80.5 kg (177.4 lb) Body Mass Index: 31.4 kg/m2
exam: Epigastric tenderness. No peritoneal signs. No rebound/guarding.
Osteoarthritic knee changes — source of chronic NSAID use.
013.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is an older man with chronic osteoarthritis who presents with epigastric abdominal pain of one week's duration. History reveals extensive, prolonged use of oral ibuprofen for knee pain. NSAIDs block both COX-1 and COX-2, impairing gastric prostaglandin production and disrupting mucosal defense — this is classic NSAID-induced gastropathy. Symptoms began one week ago and the patient is medically stable. Conservative management is key: discontinue NSAIDs, start a proton-pump inhibitor, and follow up in 2-4 weeks. If no improvement with conservative therapy, then EGD would be indicated, but ordering it now loses points — the USMLE tests restraint from invasive testing. H. pylori should be ruled out. For his osteoarthritis, switch to acetaminophen and/or topical diclofenac gel rather than oral NSAIDs. Address modifiable risk factors: smoking cessation and alcohol avoidance.
013.clinical_tip: Acute Gastritis (NSAID-induced) — follow CCS review orders.
013.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Acute Gastritis (NSAID-induced).

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
interventions.why: Investigate for lung pathology.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
interventions.why: Investigate for cardiac pathology.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
interventions.why: Chief complaint — epigastric tenderness.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Rectal
interventions.why: May contribute to current symptoms.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: Good screening tool.

interventions.label: H. pylori testing (antibody / urea breath test / stool antigen)
interventions.why: H. pylori should be ruled out as cause of gastritis.

interventions.label: Occult blood, stool
interventions.why: Rule out GI bleed. Negative in this case. Not required — could be gathered from physical exam.

interventions.label: BMP / CMP / LFTs
interventions.why: Screening labs.

interventions.label: Endoscopy, upper gastrointestinal (EGD)
interventions.why: EGD should ONLY be done after conservative treatment has failed for 2-4 weeks. Ordering now loses points — tests restraint from invasive testing.

interventions.label: PPI (Omeprazole / Lansoprazole / Pantoprazole / Esomeprazole) or H2 blocker
interventions.why: Decrease stomach acid to treat NSAID-induced gastritis. PPIs preferred over H2 blockers.

interventions.label: Acetaminophen / Topical diclofenac
interventions.why: For osteoarthritis pain: Tylenol first-line. If ineffective, topical diclofenac gel is preferred initial pharmacologic therapy. Avoid oral NSAIDs and opioids.

interventions.label: Consult, orthopedic surgery
interventions.why: Long-term solution for osteoarthritis — surgical evaluation.

interventions.label: Advise patient, no NSAIDs
interventions.why: Extensive NSAID use caused this gastritis. Must discontinue oral NSAIDs.

interventions.label: Advise patient, no alcohol
interventions.why: Alcohol exacerbates acute gastritis — avoid until symptoms resolve.

interventions.label: Instruct patient, smoking cessation
interventions.why: Smoking contributes to gastritis and peptic ulcer disease.

interventions.label: Tdap vaccine
interventions.why: Tdap every 10 years. No history given.

decoys.label: EGD / Upper endoscopy
decoys.why: Should only be ordered after 2-4 weeks of failed conservative therapy. The USMLE tests your ability to restrain from ordering invasive tests in stable patients.

decoys.label: Opioids for chronic OA pain
decoys.why: Opioids are not first-line for chronic osteoarthritis. Acetaminophen and topical NSAIDs are preferred. Avoid long-term opioid prescribing.

decoys.label: Broad-spectrum antibiotics
decoys.why: No evidence of infection. H. pylori negative. Gastritis is chemical (NSAID-induced), not infectious.

easy.intro: Case Introduction Day 1 @ 18:00 Emergency Department A 22-year-old female presents to the emergency room complaining of abdominal pain
easy.hpi: {{patient_name}} is an older man with chronic osteoarthritis who presents with epigastric abdominal pain of one week's duration. History reveals extensive, prolonged use of oral ibuprofen for knee pain. NSAIDs block both COX-1 and COX-2, impairing gastric prostaglandin production and disrupting mucosal defense — this is classic NSAID-induced gastropathy. Symptoms began one week ago and the patient is medically stable. Conservative management is key: discontinue NSAIDs, start a proton-pump inhibitor, and follow up in 2-4 weeks. If no improvement with conservative therapy, then EGD would be indicated, but ordering it now loses points — the USMLE tests restraint from invasive testing. H. pylori should be ruled out. For his osteoarthritis, switch to acetaminophen and/or topical diclofenac gel rather than oral NSAIDs. Address modifiable risk factors: smoking cessation and alcohol avoidance.

014.title: Facial and Upper Extremity Edema

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Facial/upper extremity edema, severe hypertension, headache, blurry vision at 33 weeks
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is a pregnant woman at 33 weeks gestation who presents with facial and upper extremity edema, severe hypertension (189/99), new-onset headaches, and blurry vision — signs of end-orga…
patient_voice.pain: Facial/upper extremity edema, severe hypertension, headache, blurry vision at 33 weeks

exam: Severe hypertension (189/99). Assess for pulmonary edema.
Headache, blurry vision — signs of cerebral end-organ damage. Hyperreflexia may be present.
014.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a pregnant woman at 33 weeks gestation who presents with facial and upper extremity edema, severe hypertension (189/99), new-onset headaches, and blurry vision — signs of end-organ damage. Pre-eclampsia is defined as SBP > 140 or DBP > 90 developing after 20 weeks gestation WITH end-organ dysfunction (proteinuria, visual/cerebral disturbances, pulmonary edema, creatinine > 1.1, elevated LFTs, or thrombocytopenia < 100,000). With SBP > 160, she meets criteria for pre-eclampsia with severe features. Management triad: (1) Magnesium sulfate for seizure prophylaxis to prevent progression to eclampsia, (2) IV labetalol or hydralazine for blood pressure control (labetalol is superior with fewer side effects), (3) Betamethasone for fetal lung maturity if delivering < 34 weeks. Definitive treatment is delivery — with severe features, deliver at ≥ 34 weeks. OB/GYN consult for cesarean section. Admit to ICU or inpatient unit — this is an emergency.
014.clinical_tip: Pre-Eclampsia with Severe Features — follow CCS review orders.
014.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Pre-Eclampsia with Severe Features.

interventions.label: Cardiac monitor / ECG
interventions.why: Monitor heart in pre-eclamptic patient.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: Screening. Assess for thrombocytopenia (<100K = severe feature).

interventions.label: Type and screen / Type and Rh
interventions.why: Baby may need delivery — pre-operative labs essential.

interventions.label: PT/PTT / INR
interventions.why: Pre-operative labs for potential cesarean.

interventions.label: Urinalysis
interventions.why: Screen for proteinuria — positive in pre-eclampsia. Leads to 24-hour quantitative protein.

interventions.label: US pelvis (transabdominal, then transvaginal)
interventions.why: Monitor fetus: amniotic fluid volume, EFW. Risk of oligohydramnios and IUGR. TA before TV for placenta previa screening.

interventions.label: Fetal heart rate monitoring / Doppler
interventions.why: Monitor fetal well-being.

interventions.label: Protein, 24-hour urine, quantitative
interventions.why: ≥300mg in 24h = proteinuria supporting pre-eclampsia diagnosis. May not return before intervention but must be started.

interventions.label: BMP / CMP / LFTs
interventions.why: Elevated creatinine, LFTs, and uric acid. Screen for HELLP syndrome.

interventions.label: Betamethasone / Dexamethasone
interventions.why: Antenatal corticosteroids for fetal lung maturity if < 34 weeks. Patient likely to deliver at 33 weeks.

interventions.label: Magnesium sulfate
interventions.why: Seizure prophylaxis to prevent progression to eclampsia. Standard of care for pre-eclampsia with severe features.

interventions.label: Labetalol / Hydralazine (IV)
interventions.why: IV labetalol is first-line for pre-eclampsia hypertension — superior efficacy with fewer side effects than hydralazine. Nifedipine has fetal effects.

interventions.label: Consult OB/GYN / Cesarean section
interventions.why: Delivery is definitive treatment. With severe features, deliver ≥ 34 weeks. OB/GYN for cesarean.

interventions.label: Intravenous access
interventions.why: Good practice for IV fluids/medications.

decoys.label: Nifedipine
decoys.why: Can cause reflexive tachycardia and has fetal effects. Not mentioned in ACOG recommendations for pre-eclampsia. Labetalol and hydralazine are preferred.

decoys.label: Expectant management / discharge home
decoys.why: Pre-eclampsia with severe features is an emergency. Requires ICU/inpatient management. Delivery is definitive treatment.

015.title: Chest Pain

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Pleuritic chest pain, relieved by leaning forward
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is a man with no significant past medical history who presents with acute chest pain that is pleuritic (worse with inspiration) and positional (relieved by leaning forward). He has n…
patient_voice.pain: Pleuritic chest pain, relieved by leaning forward

015.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 16:00 Temperature: 37.0 C (98.6 degrees F) Pulse: 120 beats/min, Weak Respiratory rate: 34 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 100 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 60 mm Hg Height: 183cm (72.0 in) Weight: 97.5 kg (215 lb) Body Mass Index: 29.1 kg/m2
exam: Pericardial friction rub may be present (pathognomonic but not always). No muffled heart sounds (no tamponade).
Pleuritic component — pain worse with inspiration.
015.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a man with no significant past medical history who presents with acute chest pain that is pleuritic (worse with inspiration) and positional (relieved by leaning forward). He has no history of recent viral infection, making this likely idiopathic pericarditis. ECG shows diffuse ST elevation. Echocardiogram reveals a small pericardial effusion — no tamponade physiology. Troponin is negative, ruling out MI. First-line treatment: NSAIDs (ibuprofen/naproxen) PLUS colchicine — colchicine reduces symptoms and decreases rate of recurrent pericarditis. Add a PPI/H2 blocker for GI protection with high-dose NSAID therapy. Rest until symptoms resolve — activity can trigger recurrence. Pericardiocentesis is NOT indicated for small, asymptomatic effusions (only for moderate/large effusions > 2 cm or tamponade). Transesophageal echo is unnecessary — transthoracic echo is sufficient.
015.clinical_tip: Acute Pericarditis (Idiopathic) — follow CCS review orders.
015.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Acute Pericarditis (Idiopathic).

interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: Gauge how sick the patient may be.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
interventions.why: Investigate for lung pathology. Pleuritic pain may have pulmonary origin.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
interventions.why: Cardiac pathology often causes chest pain — must examine. Listen for pericardial friction rub.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
interventions.why: Pain radiating to back — abdominal exam needed.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Extremities / Spine
interventions.why: Look for edema or pathology guiding workup.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: HEENT / Neck
interventions.why: GERD or esophageal pathology could cause symptoms.

interventions.label: Pulse oximetry
interventions.why: Check oxygenation if concerned about circulation.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: Good screening tool.

interventions.label: ECG, 12 lead
interventions.why: ECG on every chest pain patient. Will show diffuse ST elevation in pericarditis (not territorial like MI).

interventions.label: Cardiac troponin I, serum
interventions.why: Must rule out MI in chest pain. Negative in pericarditis.

interventions.label: Echocardiography (transthoracic)
interventions.why: TTE shows small pericardial effusion. Transthoracic is sufficient — TEE is unnecessary and invasive.

interventions.label: TSH, serum
interventions.why: Hypothyroidism can cause pericardial effusion.

interventions.label: Chest X-ray
interventions.why: Rule out other causes of chest pain.

interventions.label: ANA, serum
interventions.why: Autoimmune etiology is one cause of pericarditis.

interventions.label: Rheumatoid factor
interventions.why: Autoimmune screening for pericarditis etiology.

interventions.label: BMP / CMP / LFTs
interventions.why: Screening labs.

interventions.label: NSAIDs (Ibuprofen / Naproxen / Aspirin)
interventions.why: NSAIDs are treatment of choice for acute pericarditis.

interventions.label: Colchicine
interventions.why: Added to NSAID therapy — reduces symptoms AND decreases rate of recurrent pericarditis. Well tolerated. Should be added for first-episode acute pericarditis.

interventions.label: PPI / H2 blocker (Omeprazole / Famotidine)
interventions.why: High-dose NSAID therapy requires GI protection with PPI or H2 blocker.

interventions.label: Advise patient, rest at home
interventions.why: Activity may trigger recurrence. Rest until symptoms resolve.

decoys.label: Echocardiography, transesophageal
decoys.why: TTE is more than sufficient. TEE is invasive and unnecessary for small pericardial effusion — points lost for ordering.

decoys.label: Pericardiocentesis
decoys.why: Only small effusion — will resolve on its own. Pericardiocentesis only for moderate/large effusions (>2 cm) or tamponade.

decoys.label: Transesophageal echocardiography
decoys.why: Invasive and unnecessary. TTE is sufficient to evaluate pericardial effusion. Ordering TEE loses points.

decoys.label: NSAIDs alone (without colchicine)
decoys.why: Colchicine should be added to NSAID therapy for first-episode acute pericarditis — it reduces recurrence rate and improves symptom resolution.

decoys.label: Glucocorticoids as first-line
decoys.why: Steroids are reserved for refractory pericarditis unresponsive to NSAIDs/colchicine, or autoimmune-associated pericarditis.

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Cough, dyspnea, hypoxemia with HIV
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is an HIV-positive woman with unknown CD4 count who presents with cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia. She has concurrent candida vulvovaginitis from poorly controlled HIV. CD4 is likely <…
patient_voice.pain: Cough, dyspnea, hypoxemia with HIV

exam: Assess for oral thrush (common in HIV).
016.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is an HIV-positive woman with unknown CD4 count who presents with cough, dyspnea, and hypoxemia. She has concurrent candida vulvovaginitis from poorly controlled HIV. CD4 is likely <200 given the presentation with Pneumocystis jirovecii pneumonia — the most common respiratory infection in HIV patients not on prophylaxis. CXR shows classic diffuse bilateral perihilar interstitial infiltrates. Elevated LDH supports the diagnosis (though not specific). ABG shows hypoxemia with PaO2 >70, so oral TMP-SMX is first-line. Screen for TB, bacterial pneumonia, and other OIs. Start ART based on viral load and CD4. Admit to inpatient/ICU. PCP prophylaxis indicated when CD4 <200.
016.clinical_tip: PCP Pneumonia (HIV/AIDS) — follow CCS review orders.
016.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for PCP Pneumonia (HIV/AIDS).

017.title: Weight Loss and Night Sweats

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Painless cervical lymphadenopathy, weight loss, night sweats
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and constitutional B-symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fever). Hodgkin's lymphoma is a B-cell malignancy defined by Reed-Sternberg …
patient_voice.pain: Painless cervical lymphadenopathy, weight loss, night sweats

exam: Weight loss, night sweats — constitutional B-symptoms.
Painless cervical lymphadenopathy — firm, rubbery, non-tender.
017.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with painless cervical lymphadenopathy and constitutional B-symptoms (weight loss, night sweats, fever). Hodgkin's lymphoma is a B-cell malignancy defined by Reed-Sternberg cells — 'owl-eyed' nucleoli with clear cytoplasm, CD15+ and CD30+. Excisional lymph node biopsy (NOT FNA) is required for diagnosis to preserve architecture for immunophenotyping and cytogenetics. CXR is initial screening. PET/CT for staging: Stage I (single node), II (≥2 nodes same side of diaphragm), III (both sides), IV (extranodal). Treatment: ABVD chemotherapy (Adriamycin, Bleomycin, Vinblastine, Dacarbazine) ± radiation for early stage. Check albumin as prognostic indicator. Screen for HIV and EBV, which can mimic lymphoma.
017.clinical_tip: Hodgkin's Lymphoma — follow CCS review orders.
017.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Hodgkin's Lymphoma.

019.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with the classic triad of diverticulitis: LLQ pain, low-grade fever, and leukocytosis. He has changes in bowel habits with nausea and vomiting. He meets SIRS criteria (fever >100.4°F, WBC >12,000). CT abdomen/pelvis with IV and oral contrast is the gold standard — findings include bowel wall thickening, pericolic fat stranding, and a 2 cm abscess (complicated diverticulitis). Abscesses <3-4 cm can be managed conservatively with antibiotics alone without percutaneous drainage. Colonoscopy and barium enema are CONTRAINDICATED in acute diverticulitis due to risk of perforation. Treatment: NPO for bowel rest, IV fluids, IV antibiotics (cefazolin + metronidazole, cefuroxime + metronidazole, ceftriaxone + metronidazole, or ampicillin/sulbactam). 020.title: Palpitations

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Palpitations, syncope, dizziness, hypotension
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is an older woman with hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide who presents with palpitations, syncope, dizziness, and hypotension. ECG demonstrates complete heart block (3rd degree AV b…
patient_voice.pain: Palpitations, syncope, dizziness, hypotension

exam: Bradycardic rhythm. Regular but slow. No relationship between atrial and ventricular contractions. Cannon A waves may be present in JVP.
020.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is an older woman with hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide who presents with palpitations, syncope, dizziness, and hypotension. ECG demonstrates complete heart block (3rd degree AV block) — complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes with no relationship. This is a bradycardic rhythm. Third-degree AV block has an extensive differential: coronary ischemia (most common), fibrosis/sclerosis of conduction system (Lenegre/Lev disease — likely in this patient given age and HTN), Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, hyperkalemia, thyroid disorders, iatrogenic (AV nodal blockers), and congenital (unlikely — 90% symptomatic by age 30). TSH normal, troponin negative, chemistries normal, ESR normal, CBC normal — infectious and inflammatory causes unlikely. Most likely: fibrous degeneration of conduction system from aging + hypertension. Management: temporary transcutaneous/transvenous pacemaker, then permanent pacemaker placement.
020.clinical_tip: Complete (3rd Degree) AV Heart Block — follow CCS review orders.
020.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Complete (3rd Degree) AV Heart Block.

easy.intro: Palpitations, syncope, dizziness, hypotension
easy.hpi: {{patient_name}} is an older woman with hypertension on hydrochlorothiazide who presents with palpitations, syncope, dizziness, and hypotension. ECG demonstrates complete heart block (3rd degree AV block) — complete dissociation between P waves and QRS complexes with no relationship. This is a bradycardic rhythm. Third-degree AV block has an extensive differential: coronary ischemia (most common), fibrosis/sclerosis of conduction system (Lenegre/Lev disease — likely in this patient given age and HTN), Lyme disease, sarcoidosis, hyperkalemia, thyroid disorders, iatrogenic (AV nodal blockers), and congenital (unlikely — 90% symptomatic by age 30). TSH normal, troponin negative, chemistries normal, ESR normal, CBC normal — infectious and inflammatory causes unlikely. Most likely: fibrous degeneration of conduction system from aging + hypertension. Management: temporary transcutaneous/transvenous pacemaker, then permanent pacemaker placement.

022.title: Found Unconscious

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Found unconscious, respiratory depression, suspected overdose
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is a young woman found unconscious with respiratory depression, hypotension, and altered mental status. ECG shows widened QRS, prolonged QT — classic TCA cardiotoxicity. The 'Three C…
patient_voice.pain: Found unconscious, respiratory depression, suspected overdose

exam: Widened QRS, prolonged QT on ECG. Tachycardia (anticholinergic). Hypotension (alpha-1 blockade).
Depressed — requires intubation and mechanical ventilation.
Obtunded, GCS depressed. Coma — one of the 'Three C's'.
Suicide attempt — psychiatry consult after stabilization.
022.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a young woman found unconscious with respiratory depression, hypotension, and altered mental status. ECG shows widened QRS, prolonged QT — classic TCA cardiotoxicity. The 'Three C's' of TCA poisoning: Coma, Convulsions, Cardiac arrhythmias. Management priorities: ABCs — intubate for airway protection (GCS depressed), mechanical ventilation. IV fluids for hypotension (TCA blocks alpha-1 receptors → vasodilation). Sodium bicarbonate for cardiac toxicity (QRS >100ms or ventricular arrhythmia) — alkalinization to pH 7.45-7.55 favors non-ionized TCA, reducing sodium channel blockade. Activated charcoal via NG tube if within 2 hours of ingestion (airway must be secured first). 'Coma cocktail': check glucose, give thiamine before D50. Naloxone for possible opioid co-ingestion. CT head to rule out trauma (unwitnessed). Aspirin and acetaminophen levels for common co-ingestants. Psychiatry consult after stabilization for suicide attempt.
022.clinical_tip: Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA) Overdose — follow CCS review orders.
022.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Tricyclic Antidepressant (TCA) Overdose.

interventions.label: Pulse oximetry

interventions.label: Glucose, blood, random by glucometer

interventions.label: CBC with differential

interventions.label: Cardiac monitor

interventions.label: TSH
interventions.why: Hypothyroidism may present similarly — rule out.

interventions.label: Urinalysis
interventions.why: Good screening tool.

interventions.label: Acetaminophen level / Toxicology screen
interventions.why: Overdose presentation — check acetaminophen (common co-ingestant).

interventions.label: Arterial blood gases
interventions.why: Decreased RR — ABG essential.

interventions.label: CT head without contrast
interventions.why: Unwitnessed — rule out head trauma causing obtundation.

interventions.label: CPK, serum
interventions.why: Unknown down time — rhabdomyolysis risk. Prevent AKI.

interventions.label: HCG, beta (pregnancy test)
interventions.why: Child-bearing woman — pregnancy test before radiation. Ectopic can cause this presentation.

interventions.label: BMP / CMP / LFTs
interventions.why: Screening labs.

interventions.label: Toxicology screen, urine / serum
interventions.why: Drug screen in any overdose.

interventions.label: Ethanol / Toxic alcohol panel
interventions.why: History suggests ethanol abuse — common co-ingestant.

interventions.label: Salicylate level
interventions.why: Aspirin is common co-ingestant in overdose.

interventions.label: TCA level, serum
interventions.why: Urine/serum positive for TCA — quantify level.

interventions.label: Oxygen
interventions.why: Low SpO2 — supplemental O2 before intubation.

interventions.label: Thiamine (Vitamin B1)
interventions.why: Coma cocktail — thiamine before D50 to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff.

interventions.label: Dextrose 50%
interventions.why: Coma cocktail — if hypoglycemic. Give thiamine first.

interventions.label: Naloxone
interventions.why: Give in any overdose to rule out reversible opioid overdose.

interventions.label: IV fluids (NS / LR)
interventions.why: TCA overdose → hypotension from alpha-1 blockade. IV fluids for BP.

interventions.label: Nasogastric tube with suction
interventions.why: Prevent aspiration (intubated). Required for GI decontamination and activated charcoal.

interventions.label: Activated charcoal
interventions.why: GI decontamination if within 2 hours of ingestion. Only after airway secured. Via NG tube.

interventions.label: Intubation, endotracheal
interventions.why: Respiratory depression — airway protection required.

interventions.label: Mechanical ventilation
interventions.why: Respiratory depression — ventilatory support.

interventions.label: Sodium bicarbonate
interventions.why: For TCA cardiac toxicity (QRS >100ms, ventricular arrhythmia). Alkalinize to pH 7.45-7.55. Increases extracellular Na+ and favors non-ionized TCA.

interventions.label: Consult, psychiatry
interventions.why: Potential suicide attempt — psychiatry consult after medical stabilization.

interventions.label: IV access
interventions.why: Good practice for IV fluids/meds.

decoys.label: Activated charcoal WITHOUT securing airway
decoys.why: NEVER give charcoal without secure airway (ETT). Risk of aspiration pneumonitis. Intubate first, then charcoal via NG.

decoys.label: Flumazenil
decoys.why: Flumazenil is contraindicated in overdose of unknown etiology — can precipitate seizures, especially with TCA co-ingestion.

exam: S3 gallop. JVD present. Prior MI history.

023.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is an older man with history of prior myocardial infarction and hypertension on lisinopril who presents with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea, PND, and bilateral lower extremity pitting edema. Exam reveals JVD, S3 gallop, pulmonary crackles, and expiratory wheezing. CXR shows pulmonary edema and cardiomegaly. Echo confirms reduced ejection fraction — systolic dysfunction. BNP is elevated. The most common cause of systolic HF is ischemic heart disease. NYHA Class III-IV (symptoms with minimal activity). Treatment: IV loop diuretic (furosemide) for volume overload, continue ACEI, add nitroglycerin for afterload reduction. Once acute exacerbation resolves and patient is euvolemic, start beta-blocker (carvedilol preferred per COMET trial — 17% survival benefit over metoprolol, though bisoprolol and metoprolol succinate also accepted). Digoxin for symptom control if needed. No stress tests until recovered. Admit to inpatient unit. Discharge: low-sodium diet, smoking cessation, alcohol avoidance, pneumococcal and zoster vaccines, Tdap.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: Determine severity.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
interventions.why: Dyspnea — lung exam for crackles/wheezes.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
interventions.why: Dyspnea + cardiac history — S3 gallop, JVD.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Extremities / Spine
interventions.why: Pitting edema — hallmark of R-sided HF.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: HEENT / Neck
interventions.why: JVD — elevated filling pressures.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: Screening.

interventions.label: TSH
interventions.why: Thyroid pathology associated with arrhythmias precipitating HF.

interventions.label: Pulse oximetry
interventions.why: Dyspnea — check oxygenation.

interventions.label: ECG, 12 lead
interventions.why: Arrhythmias associated with HF development.

interventions.label: Cardiac troponin
interventions.why: Superimposed ischemia/infarction is common cause of HF exacerbation.

interventions.label: BNP, serum
interventions.why: Elevated in CHF — supports diagnosis.

interventions.label: Chest X-ray
interventions.why: Pulmonary edema + cardiomegaly. Rule out other causes of dyspnea.

interventions.label: Echocardiography
interventions.why: Confirms CHF — reduced ejection fraction (systolic dysfunction).

interventions.label: HbA1c / Glucose
interventions.why: Uncontrolled DM precipitates HF.

interventions.label: Foley catheter
interventions.why: Monitor I/Os during diuresis.

interventions.label: BMP / CMP / LFTs
interventions.why: Screening labs.

interventions.label: Furosemide (Lasix) / Bumetanide / Torsemide
interventions.why: Volume overloaded — loop diuretic for rapid symptom improvement.

interventions.label: Digoxin
interventions.why: Helps symptoms, not outcomes. For moderate-severe CHF (NYHA III-IV) as adjunct.

interventions.label: Input and output monitoring
interventions.why: Monitor fluid status during diuresis.

interventions.label: Nitroglycerin
interventions.why: Dilates coronary arteries — reduces afterload and improves coronary flow.

interventions.label: Beta-blocker (Carvedilol / Metoprolol / Bisoprolol)
interventions.why: Start after diuresis, prior to discharge. Carvedilol preferred (COMET trial: 17% survival benefit over metoprolol). All 3 accepted.

interventions.label: Low sodium diet
interventions.why: Lifestyle modification — limit Na intake.

interventions.label: Smoking cessation
interventions.why: Precipitating factor for CHF.

interventions.label: Limit alcohol
interventions.why: Alcohol precipitates CHF.

interventions.label: Pneumococcal vaccine
interventions.why: CHF + smoker — indication for PPSV23.

interventions.label: Tdap vaccine
interventions.why: Tdap every 10 years.

interventions.label: Herpes zoster vaccine
interventions.why: Age >50 — Shingrix (recombinant zoster vaccine) recommended.

decoys.label: Stress test / Stress echo
decoys.why: NO stress tests until patient recovers from acute HF exacerbation.

decoys.label: Stress test during acute exacerbation
decoys.why: Stress tests contraindicated until acute CHF exacerbation resolves. Risk of decompensation.

decoys.label: Beta-blocker BEFORE diuresis
decoys.why: Beta-blocker should be started after patient is euvolemic (post-diuresis), before discharge. Starting during acute volume overload can worsen hemodynamics.

025.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a 6-year-old boy with previously undiagnosed sickle cell disease (HbSS) who presents with generalized body pain, fever, and respiratory distress consistent with acute vaso-occlusive crisis complicated by acute chest syndrome and lobar pneumonia (H. influenzae B). Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive: single amino acid substitution (valine for glutamic acid) on beta-globin chain → HbS. Does not present before 6 months due to protective HbF. Patients are functionally asplenic by age 8 from repeated splenic infarction → susceptible to encapsulated organisms (S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae B, Salmonella). Management: IV fluids (dehydration precipitates sickling), IV opioids (morphine) for severe pain, oxygen for hypoxia, IV ceftriaxone (CAP treatment), blood transfusion if acute chest syndrome with hypoxia unresponsive to O2. interventions.label: Penicillin V prophylaxis

026.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a child presenting with chronic cough, recurrent respiratory infections, shortness of breath, and failure to thrive. Exam reveals nasal polyps, clubbing, and diffuse crackles. Cystic fibrosis is an autosomal recessive disorder caused by a mutation in the CFTR gene on chromosome 7. The defect in chloride transport leads to thick, viscous secretions affecting the lungs, pancreas, GI tract, and reproductive system. Diagnosis is made by elevated sweat chloride test (>60 mEq/L). CXR shows hyperinflation and bronchiectasis. Management includes pancreatic enzyme replacement, fat-soluble vitamin supplementation, airway clearance techniques, and aggressive treatment of pulmonary infections.
026.clinical_tip: Cystic Fibrosis — follow CCS review orders.

028.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a sexually active young woman presenting with bilateral lower abdominal/pelvic pain, cervical motion tenderness, adnexal tenderness, purulent cervical discharge, fever, and leukocytosis. Pelvic inflammatory disease is an ascending infection from the lower genital tract — commonly Chlamydia trachomatis and Neisseria gonorrhoeae, though polymicrobial. 029.title: Vaginal Bleeding

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Irregular heavy vaginal bleeding
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is a reproductive-age woman presenting with irregular, heavy vaginal bleeding without identifiable structural or systemic cause. This is dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB), most co…
patient_voice.pain: Irregular heavy vaginal bleeding

exam: Vaginal bleeding on speculum. No cervical lesions. Bimanual: normal uterus, no adnexal masses.
029.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a reproductive-age woman presenting with irregular, heavy vaginal bleeding without identifiable structural or systemic cause. This is dysfunctional uterine bleeding (DUB), most commonly anovulatory — unopposed estrogen stimulation leads to endometrial hyperplasia and irregular shedding. Diagnosis of exclusion after ruling out pregnancy, structural lesions (fibroids, polyps), thyroid dysfunction, coagulopathy, and malignancy. Workup: HCG (rule out pregnancy/complications), CBC (assess anemia from blood loss), TSH/prolactin, pelvic ultrasound (rule out structural causes), endometrial biopsy if age >45 or risk factors. Treatment depends on severity and fertility goals: hormonal regulation with combined OCPs or cyclic progestins. If acute heavy bleeding: high-dose estrogen or IV conjugated estrogens. Iron supplementation for anemia.
029.clinical_tip: Dysfunctional Uterine Bleeding (Anovulatory) — follow CCS review orders.
029.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Dysfunctional Uterine Bleeding (Anovulatory).

interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: Assess for pallor, hemodynamic stability.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
interventions.why: Assess for pelvic mass or tenderness.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Genitalia / Pelvic / Speculum
interventions.why: Visualize source of bleeding. Bimanual exam for uterine size, adnexal masses.

interventions.label: HCG, beta (pregnancy test)
interventions.why: MUST rule out pregnancy — ectopic, miscarriage, molar pregnancy can all present with vaginal bleeding.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: Assess degree of anemia from blood loss. Platelet count.

interventions.label: TSH / Prolactin
interventions.why: Thyroid dysfunction and hyperprolactinemia cause anovulatory bleeding.

interventions.label: PT/PTT / INR
interventions.why: Screen for coagulopathy (von Willebrand disease can present with menorrhagia).

interventions.label: Pelvic ultrasound (transvaginal)
interventions.why: Rule out fibroids, polyps, adenomyosis, ovarian masses. Assess endometrial thickness.

interventions.label: Endometrial biopsy
interventions.why: Indicated if age >45, unopposed estrogen exposure, or risk factors for endometrial hyperplasia/cancer.

interventions.label: BMP / CMP / LFTs
interventions.why: Screening labs. Iron studies if anemic.

interventions.label: Combined oral contraceptives
interventions.why: Hormonal regulation. Estrogen-progestin combination stabilizes endometrium and regulates cycles.

interventions.label: Iron supplementation
interventions.why: Treat iron deficiency anemia from chronic blood loss.

decoys.label: Hysterectomy as first-line
decoys.why: DUB responds to medical management (OCPs, cyclic progestins). Surgery reserved for failed medical therapy or completed childbearing.
