patient_voice.pain: Right wrist pain, swelling, and deformity after fall

exam: Assess for distress, fearfulness, withdrawn behavior.
Inspect for bruises in various stages of healing — concern for ongoing abuse.
Right wrist: dorsal angulation (dinner fork deformity), swelling, tenderness, limited ROM.
Screen for domestic violence privately and sensitively.
030.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with right wrist pain, swelling, and deformity after a reported fall. X-ray reveals a Colles' fracture — distal radius fracture with dorsal angulation (dinner fork deformity). However, the mechanism of injury and clinical presentation raise concern for domestic abuse. The physician must recognize red flags: inconsistent history, delay in seeking care, pattern of injuries in various stages of healing, and accompanying fearfulness or avoidance. Management: closed reduction and casting/splinting for the fracture. But equally important: a safety assessment, documentation of injuries, and referral to social work or appropriate support services. Domestic violence screening should be done privately and sensitively.

interventions.label: Iron supplementation

interventions.label: Discontinue NSAIDs / Aspirin

032.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 18:00 Temperature: 37.2 C (98.9 degrees F) Pulse: 106 beat/min, Tachycardic Respiratory rate: 20 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 114 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 79 mm Hg Height: 160.0 cm (63.0 in) Weight: 80.5 kg (177.4 lb) Body Mass Index: 31.4 kg/m2
exam: RUQ tenderness. Murphy's sign: inspiratory arrest on RUQ palpation — pathognomonic. No peritoneal signs.
032.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute RUQ abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, and fever. Pain may radiate to right shoulder or scapula. Exam reveals RUQ tenderness and positive Murphy's sign (arrest of inspiration with deep palpation of RUQ — pathognomonic). Risk factors: female, forty, fertile, fat (the 4 F's). Most commonly caused by gallstone impaction in the cystic duct. RUQ ultrasound is first-line imaging — shows gallstones, gallbladder wall thickening >4mm, pericholecystic fluid, and sonographic Murphy's sign. HIDA scan if US equivocal. Labs: leukocytosis, mildly elevated LFTs, possible elevated amylase/lipase if concurrent pancreatitis. Treatment: NPO, IV fluids, IV antibiotics (cover enteric gram-negatives + anaerobes — ceftriaxone + metronidazole or pip-tazo), analgesics. Definitive: laparoscopic cholecystectomy (within 24-72 hours).
032.clinical_tip: Acute Cholecystitis — follow CCS review orders.
032.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Acute Cholecystitis.

interventions.label: Lipase / Amylase
interventions.why: Rule out concurrent pancreatitis (gallstone pancreatitis).

interventions.label: RUQ Ultrasound
interventions.why: First-line imaging. Gallstones, wall thickening >4mm, pericholecystic fluid, sonographic Murphy's sign.

interventions.label: HIDA scan
interventions.why: If US equivocal. Non-filling of gallbladder = cystic duct obstruction.

interventions.label: IV fluids (NS / LR)
interventions.why: Nausea/vomiting — IV hydration. NPO.

interventions.label: Diet, NPO
interventions.why: Bowel rest — patient will need surgery.

interventions.label: IV antibiotics (Ceftriaxone + Metronidazole / Pip-Tazo)
interventions.why: Cover enteric gram-negatives + anaerobes.

interventions.label: Analgesia (Ketorolac / Morphine / Hydromorphone)
interventions.why: Pain management.

interventions.label: Surgery consult / Laparoscopic cholecystectomy
interventions.why: Definitive treatment within 24-72 hours.

decoys.label: ER discharge without surgery consult
decoys.why: Acute cholecystitis requires surgical admission and cholecystectomy within 24-72 hours. Discharge risks complications: gangrenous cholecystitis, perforation, sepsis.

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, cognitive decline
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient presenting with the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus: (1) gait disturbance ('magnetic gait' — feet feel stuck to floor), (2) urinary incontinence,…
patient_voice.pain: Gait disturbance, urinary incontinence, cognitive decline

033.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 11:00 Temperature: 36.8 C (98.2 degrees F) Pulse: 88 beats/min. Regular rhythm Respiratory rate: 18 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 115 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 85 mm Hg Height: 180cm (70.9 in) Weight: 91.0 kg (200.6 lb) Body Mass Index: 27.9 kg/m2
exam: Triad: magnetic gait (shuffling, feet stuck to floor) + urinary incontinence + cognitive decline. MMSE decreased. No focal deficits. Reflexes normal.
033.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient presenting with the classic triad of normal pressure hydrocephalus: (1) gait disturbance ('magnetic gait' — feet feel stuck to floor), (2) urinary incontinence, and (3) progressive cognitive decline/dementia. NPH is one of the few reversible causes of dementia and must be recognized early. CT/MRI shows ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy, without obstruction. LP opening pressure is NORMAL (<18 cm H2O) — this distinguishes NPH from obstructive hydrocephalus. High-volume LP (30-50 mL CSF removal) with pre- and post- gait assessment is diagnostic: improvement in gait after CSF removal supports the diagnosis and predicts response to VP shunting. Definitive treatment: ventriculoperitoneal shunt.
033.clinical_tip: Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus — follow CCS review orders.
033.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: Assess general condition.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Neuro / Psych
interventions.why: Gait assessment — magnetic gait, wide-based, shuffling. Cognitive: MMSE for baseline.

interventions.label: CT head without contrast / MRI brain
interventions.why: Ventriculomegaly out of proportion to sulcal atrophy. No obstruction. Evans' index >0.3.

interventions.label: Lumbar puncture (high-volume, 30-50 mL)
interventions.why: Normal opening pressure (<18 cm H2O). CSF analysis to rule out other causes. Post-LP gait assessment — improvement supports NPH diagnosis.

interventions.label: CBC
interventions.why: Screening.

interventions.label: TSH, B12, RPR
interventions.why: Rule out reversible causes of dementia (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, neurosyphilis).

interventions.label: BMP / CMP
interventions.why: Screening.

interventions.label: Neurosurgery consult / VP shunt
interventions.why: Definitive treatment: ventriculoperitoneal shunt. Best results if early intervention before irreversible damage.

decoys.label: Alzheimer's diagnosis without NPH workup
decoys.why: NPH is one of the FEW reversible causes of dementia. Classic triad + ventriculomegaly on imaging must prompt LP and consideration of VP shunting. Missing this condemns patient to irreversible decline.

035.title: Seizure

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Seizure, confusion, visual hallucinations, tremors
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with new-onset seizure, altered mental status, autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, hyperthermia), tremors, and visual/tactile hallucinations (fo…
patient_voice.pain: Seizure, confusion, visual hallucinations, tremors

exam: Generalized tremor. Hyperreflexia. Visual hallucinations (formication). Seizure. AMS. CIWA-Ar high.
Visual and tactile hallucinations. Agitation. Paranoia.
035.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with new-onset seizure, altered mental status, autonomic hyperactivity (tachycardia, hypertension, diaphoresis, hyperthermia), tremors, and visual/tactile hallucinations (formication). History reveals chronic heavy alcohol use with abrupt cessation 24-72 hours prior. This is alcohol withdrawal progressing to delirium tremens — a medical emergency with 5-15% mortality if untreated. Pathophysiology: chronic alcohol enhances GABA inhibition and suppresses NMDA glutamate excitation. Abrupt withdrawal → loss of GABA tone + rebound glutamate hyperactivity → CNS hyperexcitability. The CIWA-Ar score quantifies severity and guides treatment. Management: benzodiazepines (diazepam, lorazepam, chlordiazepoxide) — symptom-triggered or fixed-schedule dosing until sedated but arousable. Thiamine before glucose (prevent Wernicke's). IV fluids for dehydration. Correct electrolytes (hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia common). Admit to ICU for severe DTs. Rule out other causes of seizure: CT head, EEG, tox screen, metabolic panel.
035.clinical_tip: Alcohol Withdrawal / Delirium Tremens — follow CCS review orders.
035.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Alcohol Withdrawal / Delirium Tremens.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: Assess severity — tremulous, diaphoretic, agitated.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Neuro / Psych
interventions.why: AMS, hallucinations, tremors, hyperreflexia. Seizure activity.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
interventions.why: Tachycardia, hypertension — autonomic hyperactivity.

interventions.label: CIWA-Ar scoring
interventions.why: Quantifies withdrawal severity. Guides benzodiazepine dosing. Score >15 = severe withdrawal.

interventions.label: CBC
interventions.why: Screening. Anemia, thrombocytopenia common in AUD.

interventions.label: BMP / CMP
interventions.why: Electrolyte abnormalities — hypomagnesemia, hypokalemia. Check Mg, Phos, K.

interventions.label: LFTs
interventions.why: Alcoholic hepatitis? Elevated AST>ALT (2:1 ratio).

interventions.label: Toxicology screen (urine/serum)
interventions.why: Confirm co-ingestants. Rule out other toxidromes.

interventions.label: CT head without contrast
interventions.why: New-onset seizure — rule out intracranial hemorrhage, trauma, mass.

interventions.label: EEG
interventions.why: If seizure vs DT tremor unclear. Rule out non-convulsive status epilepticus.

interventions.label: Thiamine (IV/IM)
interventions.why: Thiamine BEFORE glucose to prevent Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome.

interventions.label: Benzodiazepine (Diazepam / Lorazepam / Chlordiazepoxide)
interventions.why: First-line for alcohol withdrawal. Symptom-triggered per CIWA or fixed-schedule. Titrate to sedation but arousable.

interventions.label: IV fluids (NS / LR with electrolytes)
interventions.why: Dehydration from diaphoresis, poor intake. Correct electrolytes.

interventions.label: Magnesium / Potassium replacement
interventions.why: Hypomagnesemia and hypokalemia common in AUD — correct.

interventions.label: Admit to ICU
interventions.why: Delirium tremens requires ICU for continuous CIWA monitoring, IV benzodiazepines, and management of autonomic instability.

decoys.label: Glucose without thiamine first
decoys.why: Giving glucose before thiamine in alcoholic/malnourished patients can PRECIPITATE Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome. Always give thiamine first.

decoys.label: Antipsychotics (haloperidol) as monotherapy
decoys.why: Antipsychotics lower seizure threshold — dangerous in alcohol withdrawal. Benzodiazepines are first-line. Antipsychotics only as adjunct for severe hallucination/agitation.

Petechial rash — non-blanching purple spots suggesting meningococcemia.
036.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with severe headache, fever, photophobia, nuchal rigidity, and altered mental status. Exam reveals positive Kernig's sign (pain with knee extension when hip flexed 90°) and Brudzinski's sign (involuntary hip/knee flexion with passive neck flexion). Petechial/purpuric rash is present — meningococcemia causes DIC and purpura fulminans. This is a medical emergency. Do NOT delay antibiotics for CT or LP. Blood cultures + LP with CSF analysis (opening pressure, cell count with differential, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture). CSF: neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose (<40 or <2/3 serum), elevated protein, Gram-negative diplococci. Empiric antibiotics: ceftriaxone 2g IV + vancomycin + dexamethasone (before or with first dose). Add ampicillin if Listeria risk (age >50, immunocompromised). Droplet precautions for meningococcal. Chemoprophylaxis for close contacts (rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone).
036.clinical_tip: Bacterial Meningitis (Meningococcal) — follow CCS review orders.
036.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Bacterial Meningitis (Meningococcal).

interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: Assess severity — ill-appearing, febrile, altered.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
interventions.why: Investigate for lung pathology.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
interventions.why: Tachycardia from fever/sepsis.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Skin
interventions.why: Petechiae in >50% of meningococcemia — non-blanching purple spots. Purpura fulminans.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Neuro / Psych
interventions.why: Kernig's and Brudzinski's signs. Nuchal rigidity. AMS. Focal deficits?

interventions.label: Blood cultures x2
interventions.why: Before antibiotics. Positive in 50-90% of bacterial meningitis.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: Leukocytosis. Thrombocytopenia in meningococcemia (DIC).

interventions.label: Lumbar puncture + CSF analysis
interventions.why: Opening pressure, cell count, glucose, protein, Gram stain, culture. Neutrophilic pleocytosis, low glucose, high protein.

interventions.label: CT head (if indicated before LP)
interventions.why: If papilledema, focal neuro deficit, AMS, seizure, immunocompromised — CT before LP to rule out mass effect.

interventions.label: BMP / CMP
interventions.why: Screening. Hyponatremia in SIADH from meningitis.

interventions.label: PT/PTT / INR
interventions.why: Assess for DIC — meningococcemia can trigger DIC.

interventions.label: Ceftriaxone 2g IV + Vancomycin IV
interventions.why: Empiric: ceftriaxone (covers N. meningitidis) + vancomycin (covers resistant S. pneumoniae). Add ampicillin if Listeria risk.

interventions.label: Dexamethasone IV
interventions.why: Before or with first antibiotics. Reduces hearing loss and neurologic sequelae in S. pneumoniae and H. influenzae meningitis.

interventions.label: Droplet precautions
interventions.why: Meningococcal meningitis requires droplet isolation until 24h of effective antibiotics.

interventions.label: Admit to ICU
interventions.why: Bacterial meningitis requires ICU for close monitoring and IV antibiotics.

decoys.label: Delay antibiotics for CT/LP results
decoys.why: NEVER delay antibiotics in suspected bacterial meningitis. Blood cultures first, then immediate empiric antibiotics. LP after stabilization. Mortality increases with each hour of delay.

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Painless jaundice, weight loss, dark urine, clay-colored stools
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with painless jaundice, dark urine, clay-colored stools, pruritus, and weight loss — classic for malignant biliary obstruction. Courvoisier's sign: palpable, non-tender gall…
patient_voice.pain: Painless jaundice, weight loss, dark urine, clay-colored stools

exam: Courvoisier's sign: palpable, non-tender gallbladder. Epigastric mass possible. Hepatomegaly from biliary obstruction.
038.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with painless jaundice, dark urine, clay-colored stools, pruritus, and weight loss — classic for malignant biliary obstruction. Courvoisier's sign: palpable, non-tender gallbladder in a jaundiced patient = malignancy until proven otherwise (most commonly pancreatic head adenocarcinoma). Pancreatic cancer most commonly arises in the head of the pancreas (70%), causing early obstructive jaundice. Late presentation is the rule — most are unresectable at diagnosis. Workup: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (pancreatic protocol — dual-phase) for staging. CA 19-9 tumor marker (not diagnostic but prognostic and monitors recurrence). ERCP/MRCP for biliary drainage if needed. Biopsy via EUS-FNA. If resectable (localized, no vascular involvement, no mets): pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure). If unresectable: palliative biliary stenting, chemotherapy (gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel or FOLFIRINOX). Poor prognosis — 5-year survival <10%.
038.clinical_tip: Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma — follow CCS review orders.
038.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma.

interventions.why: Anemia of chronic disease.

interventions.why: Obstructive pattern: elevated ALP, GGT, direct bilirubin. AST/ALT mildly elevated.

interventions.label: CA 19-9
interventions.why: Tumor marker. Prognostic + monitors treatment response. Not diagnostic (false positives in cholangitis, pancreatitis).

interventions.label: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (pancreatic protocol)
interventions.why: Dual-phase CT for pancreatic mass, vascular involvement, liver mets. Most important staging study.

interventions.label: EUS with FNA
interventions.why: Tissue diagnosis. Endoscopic ultrasound with fine needle aspiration of pancreatic mass.

interventions.label: ERCP / MRCP
interventions.why: Imaging of biliary tree. Therapeutic: biliary stent if obstruction.

interventions.label: Consult, oncology / Surgical oncology
interventions.why: Multidisciplinary decision: resectable (Whipple) vs palliative chemotherapy.

interventions.label: Refer to palliative care
interventions.why: Pancreatic cancer has poor prognosis — early palliative care improves QOL.

decoys.label: MRI as first-line for pancreatic mass
decoys.why: CT with pancreatic protocol (dual-phase, IV contrast) is first-line. MRI is second-line when CT is equivocal or patient cannot receive contrast.

Pancreatic cancer most commonly arises in the head of the pancreas (70%), causing early obstructive jaundice. Late presentation is the rule — most are unresectable at diagnosis. Workup: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast (pancreatic protocol — dual-phase) for staging. CA 19-9 tumor marker (not diagnostic but prognostic and monitors recurrence). ERCP/MRCP for biliary drainage if needed. Biopsy via EUS-FNA. If resectable (localized, no vascular involvement, no mets): pancreaticoduodenectomy (Whipple procedure). If unresectable: palliative biliary stenting, chemotherapy (gemcitabine + nab-paclitaxel or FOLFIRINOX). Poor prognosis — 5-year survival <10%.

hard.objective: High-acuity workup: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Pancreatic Adenocarcinoma.

039.title: Epigastric pain

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Severe epigastric pain radiating to back, nausea, vomiting

exam: May have decreased breath sounds (pleural effusion).
Epigastric tenderness with guarding. Assess for Grey Turner (flank ecchymosis) and Cullen (periumbilical ecchymosis) — retroperitoneal hemorrhage.
039.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute severe epigastric pain radiating to the back, nausea, vomiting, and low-grade fever. Exam reveals epigastric tenderness with guarding, jaundiced sclera, and possibly Grey Turner/Cullen signs in severe cases. Most common causes: gallstones (GET SMASHED mnemonic — Gallstones, Ethanol, Trauma, Steroids, Mumps, Autoimmune, Scorpion stings, Hypercalcemia/Hypertriglyceridemia, ERCP, Drugs). Diagnosis requires 2 of 3: (1) characteristic epigastric pain, (2) lipase/amylase >3x upper limit, (3) CT findings. Lipase is more sensitive and specific than amylase (especially in delayed presentation). Ranson criteria and BISAP score for severity. Management: aggressive IV fluid resuscitation (LR preferred over NS), NPO initially, IV analgesics (morphine OK), antiemetics. Early enteral nutrition within 24-48h (NG or NJ feeds). ERCP within 24h if gallstone pancreatitis with cholangitis or obstruction. CT with contrast at 48-72h if not improving to assess for necrosis/complications.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: General Appearance
interventions.why: Assess severity — may appear very ill.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Chest / Lungs
interventions.why: Pleural effusion possible (sympathetic).

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Heart / Cardiovascular
interventions.why: Tachycardia from pain, hypovolemia.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
interventions.why: Epigastric tenderness + guarding. Grey Turner (flank) / Cullen (periumbilical) in severe hemorrhagic pancreatitis.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: HEENT / Neck
interventions.why: Jaundiced sclera — suggests gallstone etiology.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: Leukocytosis. Hemoconcentration (high Hct = poor prognosis).

interventions.label: BMP / CMP / LFTs
interventions.why: Elevated AST/ALT/ALP/bilirubin if gallstone etiology. Elevated BUN ≥20 at 48h = poor prognosis.

interventions.label: Lipase
interventions.why: >3x ULN = diagnostic. More sensitive and specific than amylase.

interventions.label: RUQ ultrasound
interventions.why: Check for gallstones — most common cause.

interventions.label: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast
interventions.why: At 48-72h if not improving. Assess for necrosis, pseudocyst, abscess.

interventions.label: IV fluids (Lactated Ringer preferred)
interventions.why: Aggressive resuscitation. LR preferred over NS — reduces systemic inflammation. 250-500 mL/hr initially.

interventions.label: Diet, NPO
interventions.why: Initially NPO for bowel rest. Advance to clear liquids as pain improves.

interventions.label: IV analgesics (Morphine / Hydromorphone)
interventions.why: Pain management. Morphine is acceptable — does NOT worsen pancreatitis (old teaching was incorrect).

interventions.label: Antiemetic (Ondansetron / Metoclopramide)
interventions.why: Nausea/vomiting management.

decoys.label: Prophylactic antibiotics in all pancreatitis
decoys.why: Antibiotics NOT indicated for sterile pancreatic necrosis. Only for confirmed infected necrosis or concurrent infection. Prophylaxis does not improve outcomes.

040.title: Chest Pain

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Acute chest pain, palpitations, SOB, sense of impending doom
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, diaphoresis, nausea, and sense of impending doom. Symptoms peak within minutes and occur in discrete episodes…
patient_voice.pain: Acute chest pain, palpitations, SOB, sense of impending doom

040.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 16:00 Temperature: 37.0 C (98.6 degrees F) Pulse: 120 beats/min, Weak Respiratory rate: 34 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 100 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 60 mm Hg Height: 183cm (72.0 in) Weight: 97.5 kg (215 lb) Body Mass Index: 29.1 kg/m2
exam: Sense of impending doom. Fear of dying, losing control. Anticipatory anxiety about future attacks.
040.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset chest pain, palpitations, shortness of breath, diaphoresis, nausea, and sense of impending doom. Symptoms peak within minutes and occur in discrete episodes. The patient has a history of similar episodes and significant anxiety about future attacks (anticipatory anxiety). This is a panic attack — a psychiatric diagnosis but one that requires thorough medical evaluation because patients often present to the ED with cardiac concerns. Key: rule out MI, PE, arrhythmia, hyperthyroidism, pheochromocytoma, and substance-induced anxiety. ECG, troponin, CXR, TSH, and toxicology screen are appropriate. If negative and history consistent, panic disorder is the diagnosis. Treatment: SSRIs (first-line: sertraline, paroxetine, escitalopram) + CBT. Benzodiazepines for short-term acute management only (risk of dependence). Reassurance and psychoeducation are therapeutic.
040.clinical_tip: Panic Attack / Panic Disorder — follow CCS review orders.
040.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Panic Attack / Panic Disorder.

interventions.why: Shortness of breath — assess lungs.

interventions.why: Chest pain — assess cardiac. Tachycardia common in panic.

interventions.why: Nausea — examine.

interventions.why: Clues to etiology.

interventions.why: Rule out MI/arrhythmia — may show sinus tachycardia only.

interventions.label: Cardiac troponin
interventions.why: Rule out MI — must be negative to differentiate from ACS.

interventions.label: Chest X-ray
interventions.why: Rule out pulmonary causes.

interventions.label: CBC
interventions.why: Screening.

interventions.label: TSH
interventions.why: Hyperthyroidism can mimic panic attacks.

interventions.label: Toxicology screen, urine
interventions.why: Rule out substance-induced anxiety (cocaine, amphetamines, PCP).

interventions.label: BMP / CMP
interventions.why: Screening.

interventions.label: Reassure patient / Psychoeducation
interventions.why: Explain diagnosis — panic attacks are real physiological events but not dangerous. Education is therapeutic.

interventions.label: SSRI (Sertraline / Paroxetine / Escitalopram)
interventions.why: First-line for panic disorder. Start low, titrate slow.

interventions.label: Refer to psychiatry / CBT
interventions.why: CBT is gold standard psychotherapy for panic disorder. Psychiatry follow-up for medication management.

decoys.label: Benzodiazepines as sole long-term treatment
decoys.why: Benzos are for short-term acute management only (risk of dependence, tolerance, withdrawal). SSRIs are first-line for long-term panic disorder. CBT is essential.

decoys.label: Discharge without cardiac workup
decoys.why: Must rule out MI, PE, arrhythmia, hyperthyroidism, and substance-induced anxiety. Panic attack is a diagnosis of exclusion in the ED.

041.title: Weakness

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Generalized weakness, cola-colored urine, periorbital/ankle edema
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is a child who presents with generalized weakness, oliguria, cola-colored (dark brown) urine, periorbital and ankle edema (2+ pitting), and hypertension 1-4 weeks after a streptococc…
patient_voice.pain: Generalized weakness, cola-colored urine, periorbital/ankle edema

exam: Assess for pulmonary edema from fluid overload.
041.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a child who presents with generalized weakness, oliguria, cola-colored (dark brown) urine, periorbital and ankle edema (2+ pitting), and hypertension 1-4 weeks after a streptococcal pharyngitis or skin infection (impetigo). This is acute poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis — an immune complex-mediated (type III hypersensitivity) disease. Antigen-antibody complexes deposit in the glomerular basement membrane → complement activation → glomerular inflammation. Labs: UA shows hematuria (dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts — pathognomonic), proteinuria (<3.5g/day — nephritic, not nephrotic range). Low C3 complement (returns to normal in 6-8 weeks). Elevated ASO titer (pharyngitis) or anti-DNase B (skin infection). BMP shows elevated BUN/Cr (acute kidney injury). Diagnosis is clinical. Renal biopsy only if rapidly progressive GN or atypical course. Treatment: supportive — salt/fluid restriction, diuretics (furosemide) for hypertension and edema, antihypertensives if needed. Prognosis excellent in children (>95% complete recovery). Antibiotics if active strep infection. No immunosuppression needed.

041.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Poststreptococcal Glomerulonephritis.

interventions.why: Recent strep infection — assess for pneumonia signs.

interventions.why: Hypertension from fluid overload.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Abdomen
interventions.why: Assess for ascites.

interventions.label: Physical Exam: Extremities

interventions.label: Physical Exam: HEENT / Neck
interventions.why: Periorbital edema — classic nephritic finding.

interventions.label: Urinalysis with microscopy
interventions.why: Dysmorphic RBCs, RBC casts (pathognomonic), proteinuria (nephritic range <3.5g/day). Cola-colored urine from hematuria.

interventions.label: CBC with differential
interventions.why: Screening. Mild anemia from dilution/hematuria.

interventions.label: BMP / CMP
interventions.why: Elevated BUN/Cr — acute kidney injury. Hyperkalemia possible.

interventions.label: C3, C4 complement
interventions.why: Low C3 (returns to normal in 6-8 weeks). C4 normal — distinguishes PSGN from other GN.

interventions.label: ASO titer / Anti-DNase B
interventions.why: ASO elevated after strep pharyngitis. Anti-DNase B after skin infection.

interventions.label: 24-hour urine protein

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Acute severe knee pain, redness, swelling
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset severe monoarticular knee pain, erythema, warmth, and swelling. Pain began suddenly overnight — classic podagra (great toe) or knee involvement. History rev…

exam: Monoarticular: knee hot, swollen, erythematous, exquisitely tender.
042.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset severe monoarticular knee pain, erythema, warmth, and swelling. Pain began suddenly overnight — classic podagra (great toe) or knee involvement. History reveals dietary triggers (red meat, seafood, alcohol) or diuretic use. Gout is caused by monosodium urate crystal deposition in joints from chronic hyperuricemia. Definitive diagnosis: joint aspiration with synovial fluid analysis under polarized light microscopy — needle-shaped, negatively birefringent crystals. Do NOT give NSAIDs in renal impairment. First-line acute treatment: NSAIDs (indomethacin or naproxen), colchicine (within 36h of onset), or corticosteroids (oral prednisone or intra-articular injection). Colchicine: avoid in renal/hepatic impairment, CYP3A4 interactions. Long-term urate-lowering: allopurinol or febuxostat (start after acute flare resolves, with colchicine prophylaxis for 3-6 months). Target uric acid <6.0 mg/dL (or <5.0 for tophaceous gout).
042.clinical_tip: Acute Gout — follow CCS review orders.
042.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Acute Gout.

interventions.why: Start after flare resolves + colchicine prophylaxis. Target uric acid <6.0.

exam: Pustular/vesiculopustular lesions on extremities — DGI dermatitis.
Knee: hot, swollen, erythematous, exquisitely tender. Limited ROM. Tenosynovitis in hands/wrists.
Cervical motion tenderness. Purulent discharge possible. Often asymptomatic at primary site.
043.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute monoarticular knee pain, fever, and chills. The knee is warm, swollen, erythematous, and exquisitely tender with limited range of motion. Disseminated gonococcal infection (DGI) is the most common cause of septic arthritis in sexually active young adults. Classic triad: tenosynovitis, dermatitis (pustular or vesiculopustular lesions), and migratory polyarthralgia progressing to monoarticular septic arthritis. Most commonly affects knee. Diagnosis: arthrocentesis with synovial fluid analysis (WBC >50,000, Gram stain may show Gram-negative diplococci, culture positive in only 50%). Also culture cervix, urethra, rectum, pharynx for N. gonorrhoeae. NAAT on synovial fluid. Treatment: ceftriaxone 1g IV daily initially, then switch to oral cefixime or fluoroquinolone based on sensitivities. If chlamydia co-infection possible (common), add doxycycline or azithromycin. Joint drainage (serial aspiration or arthroscopy). Partner treatment essential.

044.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic foul-smelling, greasy diarrhea (steatorrhea), bloating, abdominal cramps, and weight loss. History reveals recent camping/hiking trip drinking untreated stream water. patient_voice.chief_complaint: Found unresponsive

patient_voice.pain: Found unresponsive

exam: Decreased bowel sounds — classic opioid effect.
045.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is found unresponsive with pinpoint pupils, respiratory depression (RR <12), and decreased bowel sounds — the classic opioid toxidrome. There may be needle track marks. Immediate management: airway protection, bag-valve-mask ventilation, naloxone 0.4-2mg IV/IM/IN (repeat q2-3min, up to 10mg if no response). Naloxone is a pure opioid antagonist — rapidly reverses respiratory depression but can precipitate acute withdrawal (agitation, vomiting, diarrhea, piloerection). Short half-life (30-90 min) compared to many opioids → patient may become re-sedated → need for observation or naloxone infusion. Check glucose (coma cocktail). ECG (QT prolongation with methadone). Acetaminophen and salicylate levels if polysubstance ingestion suspected. After stabilization: screen for other substances, assess for aspiration pneumonitis, evaluate for rhabdomyolysis (prolonged down time). Offer substance use disorder resources and naloxone prescription for harm reduction. Psychiatry/addiction medicine consult.
045.clinical_tip: Opioid Overdose — follow CCS review orders.
045.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Opioid Overdose.

046.title: Weakness in Extremities

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Progressive symmetric ascending weakness, areflexia
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with rapidly progressive symmetric ascending weakness beginning in the lower extremities, areflexia, and possible paresthesias. History often reveals antecedent infection (C…
patient_voice.pain: Progressive symmetric ascending weakness, areflexia

exam: Weak, may appear anxious about breathing.
Tachycardia/bradycardia from autonomic instability. Labile BP.
Assess diaphragmatic weakness — paradoxical abdominal breathing. Check FVC, NIF.
Symmetric ascending weakness (legs→arms). Areflexia. Paresthesias. Facial diplegia possible. GBS = motor >> sensory.
046.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with rapidly progressive symmetric ascending weakness beginning in the lower extremities, areflexia, and possible paresthesias. History often reveals antecedent infection (Campylobacter jejuni most common, also viral URI, EBV, CMV) or vaccination within 1-4 weeks. GBS is an acute inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (AIDP) caused by molecular mimicry — antibodies against infectious agents cross-react with peripheral nerve antigens. Classic: ascending symmetric weakness + areflexia + albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF (elevated protein with normal WBC count). EMG/NCS shows demyelinating pattern. Critical complication: respiratory failure from diaphragm involvement — monitor FVC and NIF (negative inspiratory force). FVC <20 mL/kg or NIF <-30 cm H2O = elective intubation. Autonomic instability common (labile BP, arrhythmias). Treatment: IVIG (0.4g/kg/day x 5 days) or plasmapheresis — both equally effective. Do NOT give steroids (ineffective in GBS, unlike CIDP). ICU admission for monitoring. Prognosis: 85% recover, 3-5% mortality.
046.clinical_tip: Guillain-Barre Syndrome — follow CCS review orders.
046.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Guillain-Barre Syndrome.

interventions.why: First-line treatment. Equally effective. Start early — best within 2 weeks of symptoms.

047.title: Chest Pain
047.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 16:00 Temperature: 37.0 C (98.6 degrees F) Pulse: 120 beats/min, Weak Respiratory rate: 34 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 100 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 60 mm Hg Height: 183cm (72.0 in) Weight: 97.5 kg (215 lb) Body Mass Index: 29.1 kg/m2
exam: Chest Pain — exam tailored to chief complaint on arrival.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
047.hpi_narrative:
Initial History

Reason(s) for visit: Chest pain; respiratory distress
History of present Illness:
The patient, a 65-year-old accountant, is brought to the emergency department by ambulance from the trucking company, where he works. Ten minutes prior to the ambulance’s arrival, the patient developed excruciating, sharp pain on the right side of his chest accompanied by marked respiratory distress. He rates the pain as an 8 on a 10-point scale. The pain increases on respiration, and he is unable to answer questions. A coworker who accompanied the patient to the hospital says that this has never happened to the patient in the past. Coworker mentions patient has a past medical history of emphysema and asthma. Oxygen was administered during transport.
047.clinical_tip: Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS) — follow CCS review orders.
047.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS).

interventions.label: Obtain electrocardiogram (ECG)
interventions.why: Appropriate CCS order for Acute Coronary Syndrome (ACS): Obtain electrocardiogram (ECG).

interventions.label: Obtain cardiac enzymes (troponin and CK-MB)
interventions.why: Cardiovascular exam is part of the ED survey; rule out cardiopulmonary contributors to chest pain.

interventions.label: Oxygen
interventions.why: Chest pain could indicate a variety of conditions, including cardiac issues that may require immediate oxygen therapy.

patient_voice.pain: Cough, fever, dyspnea, pleuritic pain

exam: Ill-appearing with frequent cough; speaks in short phrases between paroxysms.
RR 27, tachypneic; SpO₂ 94%; focal crackles and dullness to percussion on affected side.
048.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute productive cough, fever, dyspnea, and pleuritic chest pain. Exam reveals crackles and bronchial breath sounds over the affected lobe. CXR shows lobar consolidation. CAP severity assessed by CURB-65 or PORT score to determine outpatient vs inpatient treatment. Most common pathogens: S. pneumoniae (most common), H. influenzae, M. catarrhalis, atypical bacteria (Mycoplasma, Chlamydia, Legionella). Outpatient treatment (no comorbidities): amoxicillin or doxycycline or macrolide (azithromycin). Outpatient with comorbidities: respiratory fluoroquinolone (levofloxacin) or beta-lactam + macrolide. Inpatient non-ICU: beta-lactam (ceftriaxone) + macrolide. Inpatient ICU: beta-lactam + macrolide OR beta-lactam + fluoroquinolone. Add vancomycin if MRSA risk. Blood cultures and sputum cultures BEFORE antibiotics if inpatient. Smoking cessation counseling. Pneumococcal vaccine if indicated.
048.clinical_tip: Community Acquired Pneumonia — follow CCS review orders.
048.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Community Acquired Pneumonia.

050.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with severe unilateral orbital/supraorbital/temporal headache lasting 15-180 minutes, occurring in clusters (multiple times per day for weeks-months then remission). Associated ipsilateral autonomic features: lacrimation, conjunctival injection, nasal congestion, rhinorrhea, eyelid edema, miosis/ptosis (Horner's). Patient is restless/agitated during attacks (unlike migraine where patient lies still). Triggers: alcohol during cluster period. More common in men. First-line acute treatment: high-flow 100% oxygen 12-15 L/min via non-rebreather (aborts attack within 15 min) AND/OR subcutaneous sumatriptan 6mg. Bridge therapy: verapamil (first-line prophylaxis), prednisone taper for rapid suppression. Avoid triggers during cluster period. Refer to neurology.

051.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with transient focal neurological deficit (unilateral weakness, aphasia, visual field defect) resolving completely within 24 hours (typically <1 hour). Exam reveals carotid bruit on the right. TIA is a neurological emergency — 10-15% risk of stroke within 90 days, highest in first 48 hours. ABCD2 score predicts stroke risk. Workup: non-contrast head CT (rule out hemorrhage), carotid duplex ultrasound (identify stenosis — this patient has right carotid bruit), ECG (atrial fibrillation is common cause), echocardiogram (cardioembolic source), MRI brain (DWI for ischemia). Labs: CBC, BMP, lipids, HbA1c, PT/PTT. Treatment: antiplatelet therapy — aspirin 81-325mg + clopidogrel (dual antiplatelet for 21 days then single agent), or aspirin + dipyridamole. If carotid stenosis >70%: CEA (carotid endarterectomy). If atrial fibrillation: anticoagulation (DOAC or warfarin). Aggressive risk factor management: statin, BP control, diabetes control, smoking cessation. Admit for expedited workup.

052.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with new-onset chest pain at rest lasting >20 minutes, or accelerating pattern of previously stable exertional angina. ECG shows ischemic ST depression or T-wave inversion — no ST elevation (distinguishes from STEMI). Troponin is negative or minimally elevated (distinguishes from NSTEMI). UA is part of the acute coronary syndrome spectrum: USA = ischemia without infarction. Pathophysiology: atherosclerotic plaque rupture → subtotal thrombus → decreased coronary flow but not complete occlusion. Management: anti-ischemic therapy (oxygen if hypoxic, nitroglycerin, morphine), antiplatelet (aspirin 325mg chew + P2Y12 inhibitor — ticagrelor or clopidogrel), anticoagulation (UFH or LMWH or fondaparinux), beta-blocker (unless contraindicated), high-intensity statin, ACE inhibitor. Risk stratify: TIMI or GRACE score. Early invasive strategy (cardiac catheterization within 24h) for high-risk features. Admit to monitored bed.

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Jaundice in otherwise well-appearing term newborn
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} is a term newborn presenting with jaundice appearing after day 3-5 of life, clinically well-appearing, feeding well, gaining weight appropriately. Breastfeeding jaundice is the most …

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with yellow baby.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Warm skin with fever; no purpura on initial survey.
054.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a term newborn presenting with jaundice appearing after day 3-5 of life, clinically well-appearing, feeding well, gaining weight appropriately. Breastfeeding jaundice is the most common cause of prolonged neonatal unconjugated hyperbilirubinemia. Pathophysiology: inadequate breastfeeding intake → decreased stooling → increased enterohepatic circulation of bilirubin. Must distinguish from pathologic causes: hemolysis (ABO/Rh incompatibility, G6PD deficiency), sepsis, biliary atresia (conjugated), hypothyroidism. Key labs: total and direct bilirubin (unconjugated > conjugated by definition), CBC with reticulocyte count (anemia? hemolysis?), direct Coombs (immune hemolysis), G6PD screen. Plot on Bhutani nomogram for phototherapy threshold. Management: optimize breastfeeding (increase frequency, lactation consultation). Phototherapy if bilirubin exceeds threshold for gestational age and risk factors. Exchange transfusion if signs of bilirubin encephalopathy or failed phototherapy.
054.clinical_tip: Breastfeeding Neonatal Jaundice (Unconjugated Hyperbilirubinemia) — follow CCS review orders.
054.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Breastfeeding Neonatal Jaundice (Unconjugated Hyperbilirubinemia).

056.vitalsText: Initial Vital Signs Day 1 @ 18:00 Temperature: 37.2 C (98.9 degrees F) Pulse: 106 beat/min, Tachycardic Respiratory rate: 20 /minute Blood pressure, systolic: 114 mm Hg Blood pressure, diastolic: 79 mm Hg Height: 160.0 cm (63.0 in) Weight: 80.5 kg (177.4 lb) Body Mass Index: 31.4 kg/m2

056.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute abdominal/back pain, fatigue, jaundice, and dark urine (hemoglobinuria) following exposure to an oxidative stressor (fava beans, infection, certain drugs: sulfa, primaquine, dapsone, nitrofurantoin, rasburicase). Labs show acute hemolytic anemia (low Hb, elevated LDH, low haptoglobin, elevated reticulocyte count, indirect hyperbilirubinemia). Peripheral smear shows bite cells, blister cells, and Heinz bodies. G6PD deficiency is the most common enzymopathy worldwide — X-linked recessive. G6PD protects RBCs from oxidative stress. Trigger → oxidative damage → intravascular + extravascular hemolysis. Diagnosis: G6PD enzyme assay (do NOT check during acute hemolysis — reticulocytes have higher G6PD). Treatment: supportive — remove trigger, IV fluids, transfuse if severe anemia. Avoid oxidative drugs lifelong. Screen family members (X-linked).

057.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a child (commonly 6 months - 3 years) presenting with acute severe colicky abdominal pain occurring in episodes, with drawing up of knees, and currant jelly stools (blood and mucus). Between episodes the child may appear normal. A sausage-shaped mass may be palpable in the RLQ (intussusception of terminal ileum into cecum — most common type). Intussusception is the most common cause of intestinal obstruction in children <2 years. Peak incidence 6-12 months. Often preceded by viral illness (rotavirus, adenovirus). Diagnostic test of choice: abdominal ultrasound (target sign/doughnut sign on transverse view). Treatment: therapeutic air or contrast enema (reduces the intussusception in 80-90%). Do NOT attempt enema if perforation (free air on X-ray). Surgical reduction if enema fails or perforation present. NPO and NG tube for decompression. IV fluids for resuscitation.
057.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Intussusception.

exam: Ill-appearing with frequent cough; speaks in short phrases between paroxysms.
058.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a child (6 months - 3 years) presenting with acute onset barky cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, and respiratory distress, worse at night. Often preceded by viral URI (parainfluenza virus type 1 most common). Croup is inflammation of the larynx and subglottic airway. Westley croup score assesses severity based on stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, and level of consciousness. Classic CXR finding: steeple sign (subglottic narrowing on AP view). Treatment: mild (no stridor at rest) = supportive care, cool mist. Moderate to severe = dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO/IM once ± nebulized racemic epinephrine. Dexamethasone reduces airway edema. Racemic epinephrine is for temporary relief only — observe 2-4 hours after administration for rebound. Hospitalize if requiring racemic epinephrine, stridor at rest, hypoxia, or dehydration. Avoid unnecessary agitation — keep child calm.
058.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Croup (Laryngotracheitis).

standard.hpi: {{patient_name}} is a child (6 months - 3 years) presenting with acute onset barky cough, inspiratory stridor, hoarseness, and respiratory distress, worse at night. Often preceded by viral URI (parainfluenza virus type 1 most common). Croup is inflammation of the larynx and subglottic airway. Westley croup score assesses severity based on stridor, retractions, air entry, cyanosis, and level of consciousness. Classic CXR finding: steeple sign (subglottic narrowing on AP view). Treatment: mild (no stridor at rest) = supportive care, cool mist. Moderate to severe = dexamethasone 0.6 mg/kg PO/IM once ± nebulized racemic epinephrine. Dexamethasone reduces airway edema. Racemic epinephrine is for temporary relief only — observe 2-4 hours after administration for rebound. Hospitalize if requiring racemic epinephrine, stridor at rest, hypoxia, or dehydration. Avoid unnecessary agitation — keep child calm.

060.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute severe unilateral flank pain radiating to the groin, associated with nausea, vomiting, and hematuria. Pain is colicky — comes in waves as the stone passes. Non-contrast CT abdomen/pelvis is the gold standard for diagnosis. Ultrasound can be used in pregnancy/children. UA shows microscopic or gross hematuria. Most stones are calcium oxalate. Treatment depends on size and location: <5-10mm stones at UVJ or distal ureter → medical expulsive therapy (tamsulosin) + analgesia + IV fluids. Larger stones or proximal location → urology consult for lithotripsy or ureteroscopy. Strain urine and send stone for analysis. Metabolic workup if recurrent. Prevention: increase fluid intake (>2L/day), dietary modifications based on stone type.

061.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with bilateral, pressing/tightening (non-pulsating), mild to moderate intensity headache without nausea, vomiting, photophobia, or phonophobia. No aura. Not aggravated by routine physical activity. Duration 30 min to 7 days. Tension headache is the most common primary headache disorder — bilateral, band-like pressure. Distinguish from migraine (unilateral, pulsating, moderate-severe, nausea/photophobia, aggravated by activity) and cluster (unilateral with autonomic features). Tongue laceration and urinary incontinence are common. 063.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with vague abdominal/pelvic discomfort, early satiety, bloating, increased abdominal girth, urinary frequency, and unintentional weight loss — classic insidious presentation of ovarian cancer. Exam may reveal pelvic mass, ascites, omental cake. Ovarian cancer is the leading cause of gynecologic cancer death because it presents late. Workup: transvaginal ultrasound (first-line imaging — adnexal mass, complex cystic-solid, ascites), CA-125 tumor marker (elevated in 80% of advanced ovarian cancer, but not diagnostic — also elevated in endometriosis, PID, fibroids), CT abdomen/pelvis for staging. Definitive diagnosis: surgical exploration with staging laparotomy (TAH-BSO, omentectomy, lymph node sampling). Refer to gynecologic oncology. BRCA testing if family history (germline BRCA1/2 in ~15%).

064.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a child presenting with abdominal pain, constipation, irritability, lethargy, ataxia, and cognitive changes. History reveals exposure to lead-based paint in older home (built <1978). Lead intoxication causes microcytic anemia with basophilic stippling on peripheral smear. Elevated free erythrocyte protoporphyrin (FEP). Definitive diagnosis: blood lead level (BLL) >5 mcg/dL is elevated. >45 mcg/dL requires chelation. >70 mcg/dL is a medical emergency. Chronic lead exposure affects: nervous system (encephalopathy, developmental delay), kidneys (Fanconi syndrome), bone marrow (anemia), GI (colic). Treatment: remove source (lead abatement). Chelation therapy: succimer (DMSA) PO for BLL >45, or IV edetate calcium disodium (EDTA) + dimercaprol (BAL) for lead encephalopathy (BLL >70). Iron supplementation for anemia. Report to public health.

patient_voice.chief_complaint: I can't stop feeling anxious and my heart races. My hands are shaking.
patient_voice.history: I've been nervous, sweaty, and shaky. I thought it was just stress but it's not getting better.
patient_voice.pain: My chest feels fluttery when my heart races.

exam: Tachycardia; evaluate for arrhythmia contributing to palpitations.
Examine for pulmonary pathology that could contribute to anxiety symptoms.
Screen for abdominal pathology contributing to symptoms.
Tremor; psychiatric symptoms may reflect underlying hyperthyroidism.
065.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a young woman who presents with anxiety, palpitations, tremor, and sweating. She reports feeling nervous and on edge. Symptoms could be mistaken for a primary psychiatric disorder, but the presentation warrants evaluation for medical causes of anxiety — especially hyperthyroidism, substance use, arrhythmia, and withdrawal. She is of child-bearing age; pregnancy status affects choice of antithyroid therapy.

interventions.label: CBC with differential

interventions.label: Electrocardiography, 12 lead
interventions.why: Rule out cardiac causes of palpitations and anxiety.

interventions.label: HCG, beta, urine, qualitative
interventions.why: Pregnancy test required before antithyroid therapy — methimazole vs PTU choice depends on pregnancy status.

interventions.label: Toxicology screen, urine

interventions.label: Basic metabolic profile

interventions.label: Triiodothyronine, serum, free

interventions.label: Propranolol hydrochloride
interventions.why: First-line symptomatic treatment for hyperthyroidism; beta-blockade controls palpitations and tremor.

interventions.label: Consult, endocrinology

interventions.label: Methimazole
interventions.why: First-line antithyroid drug for Graves; use PTU instead in first trimester of pregnancy.

interventions.label: Vaccine, diphtheria/tetanus/pertussis
interventions.why: Tdap due every 10 years; no history documented.

interventions.label: Papanicolaou smear
interventions.why: Patient has not had a recent Pap smear.

decoys.why: Stable office presentation — not hypoxic respiratory failure.

decoys.why: Treat underlying hyperthyroidism; psychiatric meds alone miss the diagnosis.

066.title: Cough

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Chronic cough >3w, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic cough >3 weeks, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, fever, and fatigue. Risk factors: immigration from endemic area, HIV, homelessness, incarceration, health…
patient_voice.pain: Chronic cough >3w, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss

exam: Cachectic-appearing; weak with paroxysmal cough; reports weeks of symptoms and weight loss.
RR 24, tachypneic; SpO₂ 91%; hypoxemic; productive cough; decreased breath sounds with possible upper-lobe crackles.
No acute rash; night sweats and weight loss noted in history when obtained.
066.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic cough >3 weeks, hemoptysis, night sweats, weight loss, fever, and fatigue. Risk factors: immigration from endemic area, HIV, homelessness, incarceration, healthcare exposure. TB is caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis — acid-fast bacillus. CXR: apical infiltrates, cavitary lesions (reactivation TB), hilar lymphadenopathy, Ghon complex (primary). Diagnosis: sputum AFB smear (rapid, less sensitive), NAAT (PCR), mycobacterial culture (gold standard, results in weeks). IGRA (QuantiFERON) or PPD for latent TB screening — positive in active and latent. Airborne isolation (negative pressure room, N95). Treatment: RIPE therapy — Rifampin, Isoniazid, Pyrazinamide, Ethambutol for 2 months then INH + rifampin for 4 months. Directly observed therapy (DOT) preferred. Monitor LFTs (hepatotoxicity), vision (ethambutol → optic neuritis). Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine) with INH to prevent neuropathy. Report to public health.
066.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Tuberculosis.

interventions.why: Apical crackles.

interventions.label: Chest X-ray
interventions.why: Apical infiltrates ± cavitary lesions.

interventions.label: Sputum AFB smear + culture
interventions.why: AFB positive. Culture = gold standard.

interventions.label: NAAT (PCR) for TB
interventions.why: Rapid confirmation + rifampin resistance.

interventions.label: IGRA / PPD
interventions.why: Positive in active + latent TB.

interventions.label: CBC / BMP / LFTs
interventions.why: Baseline before RIPE.

interventions.label: Airborne isolation
interventions.why: Negative pressure, N95.

interventions.label: RIPE therapy
interventions.why: Rifampin + INH + PZA + EMB x 2mo, then INH + RIF x 4mo. DOT.

interventions.label: Vitamin B6 (pyridoxine)
interventions.why: Prevent INH-induced peripheral neuropathy.

interventions.label: Public health reporting
interventions.why: Reportable disease. Contact tracing.

067.title: Frequency of Urination

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia, weak stream
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia, weak stream, hesitancy, straining, and sensation of incomplete bladder emptying — classic LUTS (lower urinary tract symptoms) in a…
patient_voice.pain: Urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia, weak stream

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with frequency of urination.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Warm skin with fever; no purpura on initial survey.
067.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with urinary frequency, urgency, nocturia, weak stream, hesitancy, straining, and sensation of incomplete bladder emptying — classic LUTS (lower urinary tract symptoms) in an older man. DRE reveals enlarged, smooth, non-tender prostate. BPH is caused by benign proliferation of prostatic stromal and epithelial tissue, causing urethral compression. AUA symptom score quantifies severity. Labs: UA (rule out UTI), BMP (Cr — assess for obstructive nephropathy), PSA (age-appropriate screening). If mild: watchful waiting, lifestyle modifications. If moderate-severe: medical therapy — alpha-blockers (tamsulosin, alfuzosin — relax smooth muscle, rapid onset) ± 5-alpha reductase inhibitors (finasteride, dutasteride — shrink prostate, slow onset, reduce risk of urinary retention and surgery). Combination therapy for significant symptoms. Surgery (TURP) if refractory. Avoid anticholinergics and decongestants.
067.clinical_tip: Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia — follow CCS review orders.
067.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Benign Prostatic Hyperplasia.

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Progressive proximal muscle weakness, myalgias
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness, myalgias, and fatigue. History reveals concurrent use of simvastatin and gemfibrozil — a CONTRAINDICATED combination. Gemfibrozil …

exam: presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness, myalgias, and fatigue.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Motor strength and reflexes tested for fatigability and focal deficits.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
068.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive proximal muscle weakness, myalgias, and fatigue. History reveals concurrent use of simvastatin and gemfibrozil — a CONTRAINDICATED combination. Gemfibrozil inhibits CYP2C8 and OATP1B1, dramatically increasing simvastatin levels → myotoxicity. Labs show markedly elevated CK (often >10x ULN). UA shows myoglobinuria (risk of AKI). Differentiate from other causes: hypothyroidism, polymyositis, alcohol myopathy, steroid myopathy. Management: IMMEDIATELY discontinue simvastatin and gemfibrozil. Aggressive IV fluids to prevent pigment nephropathy from rhabdomyolysis. Monitor renal function and electrolytes (hyperkalemia risk from muscle breakdown). Alternative lipid management after recovery: atorvastatin or rosuvastatin (metabolized differently, less interaction risk), ezetimibe, PCSK9 inhibitor. Fenofibrate (not gemfibrozil) can be used with statins with caution.
068.clinical_tip: Statin-Induced Myopathy (Simvastatin + Gemfibrozil interaction) — follow CCS review orders.
068.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Statin-Induced Myopathy (Simvastatin + Gemfibrozil interaction).

069.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset unilateral leg pain, erythema, warmth, swelling, and fever. The affected area shows poorly demarcated erythema, warmth, and edema. Cellulitis is an infection of the deep dermis and subcutaneous tissue — most commonly caused by beta-hemolytic Streptococci (Group A Strep) and S. aureus. Differentiate from erysipelas (more superficial, well-demarcated, raised borders). Risk factors: skin breaks, tinea pedis, lymphedema, venous stasis, diabetes, immunocompromise. Portal of entry must be identified. Mark the borders of erythema to monitor progression. Treatment: oral antibiotics for mild-moderate (cephalexin, dicloxacillin, clindamycin if penicillin-allergic). IV antibiotics for severe/systemic symptoms (cefazolin, nafcillin, vancomycin if MRSA risk). Elevate affected limb. Treat underlying predisposing conditions.

073.title: Memory Loss

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Progressive memory loss, cognitive decline
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive episodic memory loss (recent > remote), difficulty with word finding, visuospatial deficits, apraxia, and decline in executive function, gradually worsening…

exam: Decreased engagement and cognitive change compared with reported baseline.

073.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with progressive episodic memory loss (recent > remote), difficulty with word finding, visuospatial deficits, apraxia, and decline in executive function, gradually worsening over months to years. Alzheimer's disease is the most common cause of dementia. Pathophysiology: accumulation of extracellular beta-amyloid plaques and intracellular neurofibrillary tangles (hyperphosphorylated tau protein) → neuronal death. Rule out reversible causes: B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism (TSH), neurosyphilis (RPR), normal pressure hydrocephalus, depression (pseudodementia). Imaging: CT/MRI brain shows diffuse cortical atrophy (especially medial temporal/hippocampal). Diagnosis is clinical — supportive features. MMSE or MOCA for cognitive screening. Treatment: cholinesterase inhibitors (donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine) for mild-mod AD. Memantine (NMDA antagonist) for mod-severe. Both provide modest symptomatic benefit — no disease-modifying therapy currently. Caregiver support, advance care planning, safety assessment.
073.clinical_tip: Alzheimer's Disease — follow CCS review orders.
073.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Alzheimer's Disease.

exam: Ill-appearing with chronic cough; fatigued and thinner than stated baseline.
RR 25, tachypneic; SpO₂ 92%; hypoxemic; productive cough with scattered rhonchi; increased work of breathing.

074.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with persistent cough >3 weeks, hemoptysis, weight loss, chest pain, dyspnea, and fatigue. History of smoking (most common risk factor). CXR shows a solitary pulmonary nodule or mass — may have spiculated borders, pleural effusion, hilar lymphadenopathy. CT chest with IV contrast for characterization. Tissue diagnosis: bronchoscopy with biopsy, CT-guided needle biopsy, or surgical biopsy. NSCLC (adenocarcinoma most common in non-smokers, also squamous, large cell) vs SCLC (almost exclusively smokers, aggressive, central). NSCLC staging: PET/CT, brain MRI. Treatment: NSCLC stage I-II: surgical resection (lobectomy). Stage III: chemoradiation. Stage IV: systemic therapy (targeted therapy if EGFR/ALK/ROS1/Pd-L1 positive; immunotherapy; chemo). SCLC: limited → chemoradiation; extensive → chemo + immunotherapy. Palliative care. Smoking cessation.

exam: presents with fever, sore throat, and a diffuse erythematous sandpaper-like rash that blanches with pressure.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
Skin rash morphology and distribution documented.
076.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with fever, sore throat, and a diffuse erythematous sandpaper-like rash that blanches with pressure. Exam reveals strawberry tongue (initially white-coated then red), pharyngeal erythema with exudates, and Pastia lines (linear petechiae in skin folds). Caused by Group A Streptococcus pyogenes producing erythrogenic exotoxin. Diagnosis: rapid strep test or throat culture. Treatment: penicillin VK PO x 10 days or amoxicillin (first-line). If penicillin-allergic: cephalexin or clindamycin. Complete full course to prevent acute rheumatic fever (not PSGN — which occurs after skin infection). Children can return to school 24h after starting antibiotics.

077.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with palpitations, irregularly irregular pulse, dizziness, fatigue, and chest discomfort. ECG shows no P waves, irregularly irregular R-R intervals with narrow QRS. May have rapid ventricular response (RVR). AFib is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia. Causes: HTN, CAD, valvular disease, CHF, hyperthyroidism, alcohol, PE, post-op, lone AFib. Classification: paroxysmal (<7d), persistent (>7d), long-standing persistent (>1yr), permanent. Management priorities: (1) Rate control: beta-blocker (metoprolol) or CCB (diltiazem/verapamil), target HR <110. (2) Anticoagulation: CHA2DS2-VASc score — if ≥2 in men or ≥3 in women → anticoagulation (DOAC preferred over warfarin). If <2, no anticoagulation. (3) Rhythm control if symptomatic despite rate control: cardioversion (electrical or pharmacological — flecainide, amiodarone). If AFib <48h → safe to cardiovert. If >48h or unknown → TEE to rule out LAA thrombus first, or anticoagulate x3 weeks before cardioversion. Anticoagulate x4 weeks post-cardioversion.

077.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Atrial Fibrillation.

078.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with generalized weakness, fatigue, weight loss, fever, and flank pain. Classic triad of RCC: flank pain + palpable flank mass + hematuria. However, triad present only in 10% — most present with incidental finding or paraneoplastic syndromes. RCC is an adenocarcinoma of the renal cortex, most common type: clear cell carcinoma. Paraneoplastic syndromes: hypercalcemia (PTHrP), polycythemia (EPO), hypertension (renin), Stauffer syndrome (hepatic dysfunction without liver mets). Diagnosis: CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast — enhancing renal mass. Renal US differentiates solid vs cystic. No biopsy needed before surgery if resectable. Treatment: localized → partial or radical nephrectomy. Metastatic → systemic therapy (immunotherapy — checkpoint inhibitors, targeted therapy — VEGF/TKI inhibitors). Cytoreductive nephrectomy in select metastatic patients. Refer urology/oncology.

exam: presents with fever, chills, unilateral flank pain/CVA tenderness, nausea, vomiting, and lower urinary tract symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency).
Tenderness with guarding; peritoneal signs assessed.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.

079.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with fever, chills, unilateral flank pain/CVA tenderness, nausea, vomiting, and lower urinary tract symptoms (dysuria, frequency, urgency). Acute pyelonephritis is an ascending bacterial infection of the renal parenchyma — most commonly E. coli (80%). Risk factors: female, sexual activity, pregnancy, urinary tract obstruction, catheterization, DM, immunosuppression. UA shows pyuria, leukocyte esterase, nitrites, WBC casts. Urine culture for confirmation + sensitivities. Blood cultures if severe/septic. CT abdomen/pelvis if complicated (abscess, obstruction, stone) or not responding to 48-72h of antibiotics. Treatment: outpatient (mild, stable): PO fluoroquinolone (ciprofloxacin) or TMP-SMX. Inpatient (severe, vomiting, pregnant, immunocompromised): IV ceftriaxone or fluoroquinolone. Switch to PO after clinical improvement. Total course 7-14 days. Repeat urine culture after treatment to confirm clearance.

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with vomiting.
Abdominal tenderness pattern matches history; no rigid abdomen documented yet.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.

080.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a neonate/infant presenting with bilious (green) vomiting — a surgical emergency until proven otherwise. Bilious vomiting in a newborn = malrotation with volvulus. Malrotation occurs when the midgut fails to complete its normal 270° counterclockwise rotation during fetal development, resulting in a narrow mesenteric base. This predisposes to volvulus — twisting of the midgut around the superior mesenteric artery → intestinal ischemia and necrosis. Diagnosis: upper GI series (gold standard) showing DJJ (duodenojejunal junction) to the RIGHT of midline and spiral/corkscrew duodenum. Abdominal X-ray may show double bubble sign or gasless abdomen. Treatment: EMERGENCY surgical exploration (Ladd procedure). NPO, NG tube decompression, IV fluids. Time-critical — delay leads to bowel necrosis and short gut syndrome.
080.clinical_tip: Malrotation with Midgut Volvulus — follow CCS review orders.
080.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Malrotation with Midgut Volvulus.

081.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic diarrhea (often non-bloody), RLQ abdominal pain, weight loss, fatigue, and fever. Crohn's disease is a transmural granulomatous inflammatory bowel disease that can affect any part of the GI tract from mouth to anus — most commonly terminal ileum. Skip lesions (areas of inflammation between normal mucosa), cobblestoning, creeping fat, strictures, and fistulas are characteristic. Extraintestinal manifestations: arthritis, uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum, PSC. Diagnosis: colonoscopy with terminal ileum intubation and biopsy (transmural inflammation, non-caseating granulomas). CT/MR enterography for small bowel evaluation. Labs: anemia, elevated CRP/ESR, fecal calprotectin. Treatment: mild-mod → budesonide (terminal ileal/right colon) or prednisone for induction. Maintenance: immunomodulators (azathioprine, MTX), biologics (anti-TNF — infliximab, adalimumab). Surgery for complications (strictures, fistulas, abscess) — NOT curative (disease recurs).

081.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Crohn's Disease.

082.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute onset nausea, vomiting, diffuse abdominal cramping, watery diarrhea, and low-grade fever. History reveals recent consumption of undercooked food or potential contaminated source. Most common causes: S. aureus (preformed toxin, 1-6h onset), B. cereus, C. perfringens, Salmonella, Campylobacter, Shigella, E. coli. Most cases are self-limited (viral or toxin-mediated). Key: assess hydration status. Stool culture if: bloody diarrhea, severe illness, immunocompromised, >3 days, recent antibiotics or hospitalization. Treatment: supportive — oral rehydration (or IV fluids if severe). Antiemetics (ondansetron), loperamide if non-bloody diarrhea and no fever (avoid in dysentery — can prolong illness). Empiric antibiotics only for severe cases, bloody diarrhea, immunocompromised (fluoroquinolone or azithromycin).

084.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is an elderly patient with cardiovascular risk factors who presents with acute LLQ abdominal pain and bloody diarrhea following a meal (postprandial pain). Ischemic colitis is the most common form of GI ischemia — caused by non-occlusive hypoperfusion of the watershed areas (splenic flexure = Griffith's point, rectosigmoid = Sudeck's point). Differentiate from acute mesenteric ischemia (small bowel — embolic, more severe, pain out of proportion). CT abdomen/pelvis with IV contrast shows segmental colonic wall thickening, thumbprinting (submucosal edema/hemorrhage). Colonoscopy confirms with segmental erythema, ulceration. Most cases are self-limited and resolve with supportive care: bowel rest (NPO), IV fluids, broad-spectrum antibiotics (cover gram-neg + anaerobes if severe). Surgery only if transmural infarction, perforation, peritonitis, or stricture.

085.title: Amenorrhea

patient_voice.chief_complaint: Irregular periods, hirsutism, acne, difficulty conceiving
patient_voice.history: {{patient_name}} presents with oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, obesity, and infertility. PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in reproductive-age women. Rotterdam criteria (need 2 o…
patient_voice.pain: Irregular periods, hirsutism, acne, difficulty conceiving

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with amenorrhea.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Alert and oriented unless perfusion or metabolic derangement present.
No acute rash; night sweats and weight loss noted in history when obtained.
085.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with oligomenorrhea/amenorrhea, hirsutism, acne, obesity, and infertility. PCOS is the most common endocrine disorder in reproductive-age women. Rotterdam criteria (need 2 of 3): (1) oligo/anovulation, (2) clinical or biochemical hyperandrogenism (hirsutism, acne, elevated free testosterone), (3) polycystic ovaries on ultrasound (≥12 follicles 2-9mm per ovary or ovarian volume >10mL). Other causes of hyperandrogenism must be ruled out: late-onset CAH (check 17-OH progesterone), androgen-secreting tumor (rapid virilization, very high testosterone), Cushing's, hyperprolactinemia. Labs: LH:FSH ratio >2:1 is classic but not diagnostic. Associated with insulin resistance → screen for diabetes (glucose, HbA1c, OGTT). Treatment: weight loss (first-line, improves all parameters), combined OCPs (regulate cycles, reduce hyperandrogenism), metformin (insulin sensitizer, improves ovulation), spironolactone (anti-androgen for hirsutism). Clomiphene or letrozole for ovulation induction if fertility desired.

085.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Polycystic Ovary Syndrome (PCOS).

interventions.why: LH:FSH >2:1 supports PCOS.

interventions.why: Elevated androgens.

interventions.label: 17-OH progesterone
interventions.why: Rule out late-onset CAH.

interventions.label: TSH / Prolactin
interventions.why: Rule out thyroid, prolactin causes.

interventions.label: Pelvic US
interventions.why: Polycystic ovaries — ≥12 follicles.

interventions.label: Glucose / HbA1c / OGTT
interventions.why: Screen for insulin resistance/DM.

interventions.label: Weight loss + lifestyle
interventions.why: First-line. Improves all parameters.

interventions.label: Combined OCPs
interventions.why: Regulate cycles, reduce hyperandrogenism.

interventions.label: Metformin
interventions.why: Insulin sensitizer.

086.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with hematuria, flank pain, hypertension, and palpable bilateral flank masses. Family history of ADPKD (autosomal dominant — 50% of children inherit). ADPKD is the most common inherited kidney disease — mutations in PKD1 (85%, chromosome 16) or PKD2 (15%, chromosome 4). Cysts develop in kidneys (and liver, pancreas) over decades, eventually causing renal failure by age 50-60. Diagnosis: renal ultrasound — multiple bilateral cysts in enlarged kidneys (usually by age 30 for PKD1). CT/MRI for more detail. Labs: elevated Cr (declining renal function), UA shows hematuria. Screen for cerebral aneurysms (berry aneurysms — 5-10% of ADPKD patients, higher if family history) with MRA/CTA brain. Management: BP control with ACEI/ARB (nephroprotective), treat UTIs aggressively, avoid contact sports (cyst rupture risk). Tolvaptan (vasopressin antagonist) slows cyst growth. Genetic counseling.
086.clinical_tip: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease — follow CCS review orders.
086.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease.

087.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with chronic bloody diarrhea, LLQ abdominal cramping, tenesmus, urgency, and weight loss. UC is an inflammatory bowel disease limited to the colon and rectum — inflammation is continuous from the rectum proximally (unlike Crohn's skip lesions), limited to mucosa/submucosa (unlike Crohn's transmural). Extraintestinal manifestations: PSC (most specific), arthritis (axial/peripheral), uveitis, erythema nodosum, pyoderma gangrenosum. Diagnosis: colonoscopy with biopsy — continuous inflammation from rectum, friable mucosa, loss of haustra (lead pipe colon on barium enema), crypt abscesses, crypt distortion. Labs: anemia, elevated CRP/ESR, fecal calprotectin, p-ANCA positive. Severity determines treatment: mild → 5-ASA (mesalamine) topical or PO. Moderate → 5-ASA + steroids (prednisone or budesonide MMX). Severe → IV steroids, if refractory → biologics (anti-TNF — infliximab) or JAK inhibitor (tofacitinib). Fulminant/toxic megacolon → cyclosporine or colectomy. Increased colon cancer risk → surveillance colonoscopy starting 8 years after diagnosis.
087.clinical_tip: Ulcerative Colitis — follow CCS review orders.
087.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Ulcerative Colitis.

090.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a pregnant woman >20 weeks gestation with elevated BP (>140/90 on two occasions at least 4 hours apart) and no proteinuria and no end-organ damage. This is gestational hypertension (PIH) — distinguished from pre-eclampsia by absence of proteinuria and end-organ dysfunction. Risk factors: nulliparity, advanced maternal age, obesity, family history, multiple gestation. Must monitor closely for progression to pre-eclampsia (up to 25% progress). Management: if BP >160/110 → antihypertensive treatment (labetalol, nifedipine ER, methyldopa). If BP 140-159/90-109 → conservative monitoring, no medication needed but close surveillance. ACEI/ARBs CONTRAINDICATED in pregnancy. Serial monitoring: BP checks, UA for protein, fetal growth US, NST/BPP starting at 32 weeks. Delivery at 37 weeks (no later than term). If develops pre-eclampsia features → manage as pre-eclampsia. Low-dose aspirin 81mg for pre-eclampsia prevention in high-risk women (started at 12-28 weeks).

091.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with a firm, non-tender, immobile breast lump with irregular borders, possible skin dimpling (peau d'orange), nipple retraction, or axillary lymphadenopathy. Breast cancer is the most common cancer in women. Most are invasive ductal carcinoma (IDC). Workup: diagnostic mammogram + breast ultrasound. If suspicious (BIRADS 4-5) → core needle biopsy for tissue diagnosis. Hormone receptor status: ER, PR, HER2/neu — guides treatment. Genetic testing: BRCA1/2 if family history, triple-negative, bilateral, or young age. Staging: CT chest/abdomen/pelvis, bone scan, PET/CT if advanced. Treatment: surgery (lumpectomy + radiation vs mastectomy) + sentinel lymph node biopsy. Adjuvant therapy per receptor status: endocrine therapy (tamoxifen/AI) if ER+, HER2-directed therapy (trastuzumab) if HER2+, chemotherapy per Oncotype DX or stage.

093.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with altered mental status, fever (or hypothermia), tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypotension unresponsive to fluid resuscitation — requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP ≥65. Lactate is elevated (>2 mmol/L) indicating tissue hypoperfusion. Sepsis = SIRS + infection. Septic shock = sepsis + persistent hypotension despite fluids + lactate >2. Source must be identified: blood cultures x2, urine culture, CXR, and cultures from any suspected site (sputum, wound, CSF). Empiric broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 HOUR of recognition — every hour delay increases mortality 7-8%. Initial resuscitation: 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid bolus. If still hypotensive → start vasopressors (norepinephrine first-line). Monitor lactate clearance (goal >20% decrease). Measure ScvO2. Admit to ICU. 094.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with malar (butterfly) rash across cheeks (sparing nasolabial folds), photosensitivity, polyarthritis, fatigue, and fever. SLE is a multisystem autoimmune disease with autoantibodies against nuclear antigens. Diagnosis per ACR/EULAR criteria: ANA positivity is required (sensitive but not specific). Anti-dsDNA and anti-Smith are specific for SLE. Other features: oral ulcers, serositis (pleuritis/pericarditis), nephritis (proteinuria, RBC casts), neurologic (seizures/psychosis), hematologic (anemia, leukopenia, lymphopenia, thrombocytopenia). Monitor: CBC, BMP, UA (proteinuria), complement C3/C4 (low = active disease), anti-dsDNA titers (correlates with disease activity). Treatment: mild (skin/joints) → hydroxychloroquine (ALL SLE patients) + NSAIDs. Moderate: add steroids (prednisone). Severe (nephritis, CNS) → high-dose steroids + immunosuppression (mycophenolate mofetil or cyclophosphamide). Sun protection.

097.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with vaginal dryness, dyspareunia, hot flashes, night sweats, mood changes, and irregular menses/amenorrhea. FSH is elevated (>40), estradiol is low. Menopause = 12 months of amenorrhea. Genitourinary syndrome of menopause (atrophic vaginitis): thinning and drying of vaginal mucosa from estrogen loss → dyspareunia, pruritus, increased UTIs. Treatment: for vasomotor symptoms (hot flashes) — systemic HRT (estrogen ± progestin) for shortest duration at lowest dose. Contraindications: breast cancer, VTE, stroke. For GU symptoms only — vaginal estrogen (cream, ring, tablet). Non-hormonal: lubricants, moisturizers, SSRIs/SNRIs for hot flashes. Osteoporosis prevention: calcium, vitamin D, weight-bearing exercise, screening DEXA.

098.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with acute low back pain radiating down the leg (sciatica) following lifting/twisting injury. Pain follows dermatomal distribution — most commonly L4-L5 or L5-S1. Exam: positive straight leg raise test (pain <70° elevation). Neurologic exam to identify affected root: L4 (patellar reflex, medial leg), L5 (foot drop, great toe dorsiflexion, dorsal foot), S1 (Achilles reflex, plantar flexion, lateral foot). Cauda equina RED FLAGS: bilateral sciatica, saddle anesthesia, urinary retention/incontinence, fecal incontinence — surgical emergency. Conservative management for uncomplicated herniation: NSAIDs, physical therapy, continue activity as tolerated (bed rest NOT recommended). Most resolve in 6 weeks. MRI if not improving or neurologic deficit (not urgent CT/bone scan — but MRI is gold standard). Epidural steroid injection for radicular pain. Surgery (microdiscectomy) if severe deficit, cauda equina, or failed 6+ weeks conservative.

exam: Acutely ill appearance consistent with back pain.
Soft, non-distended, no focal peritoneal signs on initial exam.
Motor strength and reflexes tested for fatigability and focal deficits.
No acute rash; capillary refill and perfusion assessed.
099.hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} presents with severe low back pain, bilateral leg weakness and numbness, saddle anesthesia (perineal numbness), urinary retention/incontinence, fecal incontinence, and decreased rectal tone. These are the RED FLAG symptoms of cauda equina syndrome — compression of the cauda equina nerve roots below the conus medullaris. This is a SURGICAL EMERGENCY. Delay in decompression leads to permanent paralysis, incontinence, and sexual dysfunction. Most common cause: massive central disc herniation. Other causes: trauma, tumor, abscess, hematoma. Diagnosis: EMERGENCY MRI of lumbar spine (do NOT wait). Post-void residual (PVR) >200mL supports diagnosis. Treatment: EMERGENCY neurosurgical decompression (laminectomy + discectomy) within 24-48 hours of symptom onset.
099.clinical_tip: Cauda Equina Syndrome — follow CCS review orders.
099.objective: Complete diagnosis and treatment orders for Cauda Equina Syndrome.
